facts.fact_text: [F10] $X(c)$ has the ordered pairwise-edge definition, $X(\sigma)$ and $X(\sigma,\rho)$ are full subcomplexes with $X(\sigma,\tau_i)$ on vertices $\tau_1,\dots,\tau_i$, and $c[\emptyset]=\{0\}$. [[def-cg-brady-watt-ordered-spherical-root-complex]] (1)-(3)

proof_step_texts.3.1: 3.1 For $i<j$, the two-root instance of (1) says $R(a_j)R(a_i)\le_Tc\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mu(a_j)\cdot a_i=0,$ since the product of two distinct positive-root reflections has length $2$ by step 1.2. If $F=\{a_1<\dots<a_k\}$ is a simplex, every pair is an edge by [F10], so these pairwise equivalences make $D=(\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j)$ upper triangular with diagonal $1$. Pairing a vanishing combination $\sum_j\lambda_j a_j=0$ with each $\mu(a_i)$ gives $D\lambda=0$; hence every $\lambda_j=0$. Thus the vertices of every nonempty face are linearly independent. Conversely, if the reverse product of an increasing tuple lies below $c$ and has length $k$, step 1.2 applied to its reduced factorization shows each pair product is below $c$, so the tuple is a simplex. The empty tuple is the empty simplex by [F10]. [F2, F3, F6, F10, F14, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 Let $f_0:=\sum_{s\in S}\beta_s$, with the dual vectors from [F13]. Then $B(f_0,\alpha_s)=1$ for every simple root; since each positive root is a nonzero nonnegative combination of simple roots by [F7], every positive root has positive pairing with $f_0$. Also [F7] gives positive pairing with every $f\in\mathcal C^\circ$ by the chamber transfer [F17]. For a nonempty face $F$, its independent unit roots have a positive-definite Gram matrix with diagonal $1$. By [F12], $c[F]\cap S^{n-1}$ is the associated spherical simplex of dimension $|F|-1$. The independence of the cone generators makes $c[F]$ pointed and simplicial. For the empty face, [F10] gives $c[\emptyset]=\{0\}$ and its sphere section is empty. [F3, F7, F10, F12, F13, F17, step 3.1]
proof_step_texts.4.2: 4.2 The roots of $P_\sigma$ lie in $M(\sigma)$: if $a\in P_\sigma$, then $t_a\le_T\sigma$ by definition; [F2] identifies its linear reflection, [F8] gives $M(t_a)=\mathbb R a$, and [F3] gives $M(t_a)\subseteq M(\sigma)$. Thus a face of $X(\sigma)$ has at most $\dim M(\sigma)=\ell_T(\sigma)$ vertices by step 3.1 and Carter's formula. If $\sigma=1$, then $P_\sigma=\emptyset$ and $X(1)=\{\emptyset\}$ has dimension $-1$. If $n=1$ and $\sigma\ne1$, the rank-one data give $W=\{1,c\}$, $\sigma=c$, and $P_\sigma=\{\alpha_1\}$; hence $X(\sigma)$ has one vertex and dimension $0=\ell_T(\sigma)-1$. If $n\ge2$ and $\sigma\ne1$, [F9] gives $\Delta=\{\delta_1,\dots,\delta_k\}\subseteq P_\sigma$ and $\varepsilon_i=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{i-1})\delta_i$. Each $R(\delta_j)$ lies in the reflection subgroup $W_\sigma$ of [F9], so every $\varepsilon_i$ is a root of that subgroup; its positivity from [F9] puts it in $P_\sigma$. Hence the increasing reordering $\theta_1<\dots<\theta_k$ lies in $P_\sigma$. Its reverse product is below $c$ with length $k=\ell_T(\sigma)$ by [F9], so step 3.1 makes it a $k$-vertex simplex. Therefore $\dim X(\sigma)=k-1$. Finiteness follows from finiteness of $\Phi_+$ in [F1], and the full-subcomplex and $X(\sigma,\rho)$ claims follow from [F10]. [F1, F2, F3, F8, F9, F10, step 3.1]
proof_step_texts.4.3: 4.3 Let $K_i:=X(\sigma,\tau_i)$. By [F10], $K_i$ has vertices $\tau_1,\dots,\tau_i$. Any new simplex of $K_{i+1}$ must contain the new vertex $\tau_{i+1}$. Its other vertices form a face $B$ of $K_i$, and the two-root criterion of step 3.1 says each such vertex $b$ is joined to $\tau_{i+1}$ exactly when $\mu(\tau_{i+1})\cdot b=0$. Conversely, any face $B$ of $K_i$ with all vertices in this hyperplane gives a simplex $B\cup\{\tau_{i+1}\}$. This includes $B=\emptyset$, proving the cone-over-link description and the nested inclusions. [F6, F10, step 3.1]
proof_step_texts.5.1: 5.1 Put $K_0:=\{\emptyset\}$ and induct on $i$ to prove the cone intersection formula for all faces of $K_i$. At $i=0$ both cones equal $\{0\}$. Suppose the formula holds at $i$ and consider faces of $K_{i+1}$. If both are in $K_i$, use induction. Otherwise each new face has the form $B\cup\{\tau_{i+1}\}$ with $B\in K_i$ and every vertex of $B$ orthogonal to $\mu(\tau_{i+1})$, by step 4.3. For a cone point in such a face, its coefficient on $\tau_{i+1}$ is its pairing with $\mu(\tau_{i+1})$, because $\mu(\tau_{i+1})\cdot\tau_{i+1}=1$ by [F6] and its pairings with the base vertices are zero. Every old vertex $\tau_j$, $j\le i$, has $\mu(\tau_{i+1})\cdot\tau_j\le0$ by [F6]. Therefore a cone on an old face intersects a cone with apex $\tau_{i+1}$ only where the apex coefficient is zero; there the induction hypothesis identifies the intersection with the cone on the common base face. For two faces both containing the apex, equality of a common cone point gives equality of its apex coefficients after pairing with $\mu(\tau_{i+1})$, and then equality of the base cone points; induction identifies their base intersection. In each case the intersection is exactly the cone on the common face. Since every face of $X(\sigma)$ belongs to $K_t$, this proves the formula in (4). [F6, F10, step 4.3]
proof_step_texts.6.1: 6.1 Define the normalized cone map on a barycentric point of the geometric realization by $\iota\bigl((\lambda_v)_{v\in V(F)}\bigr):=\frac{\sum_v\lambda_vv}{\left\|\sum_v\lambda_vv\right\|_B},\qquad \lambda_v\ge0,\quad\sum_v\lambda_v=1.$ The denominator is nonzero because $B(f_0,v)>0$ for every positive root by step 4.1. Its restriction to each simplex is a homeomorphism onto the corresponding spherical simplex by [F12], and it is continuous globally by the weak-topology definition [F11]. If two such images agree, the two positive combinations lie on the same ray; step 5.1 puts that ray in the cone on the common face, and linear independence of that face plus the barycentric sum-one condition makes the original points equal. Thus $\iota$ is a continuous bijection onto $|X(\sigma)|$. By [F1] and step 4.2, $X(\sigma)$ is a finite abstract simplicial complex, so its ordinary realization is compact by [F15]. If $A$ is closed in that realization, [F15] makes $A$ compact; the open-cover argument in [F15] makes $\iota[A]$ compact, and it is closed in the Hausdorff sphere by [F15] and [F16]. Thus $\iota$ is a closed continuous bijection onto its image and therefore a topological embedding. No Choice is used: the only compactness input is [F15], whose finite-complex proof reduces to finite-dimensional Heine-Borel. [F1, F10, F11, F12, F15, F16, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1] ∎

facts.fact_text: [F2] The map $\Phi_+\to T$, $a\mapsto t_a$, is a bijection; $\rho(t_a)=R(a)$, and distinct positive roots determine distinct reflections. [[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]] (1)-(2) [[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (1)

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 By [F1], $M(c)=V$ and $\ell_T(c)=n$. For every $a\in\Phi_+$, [F2] gives $t_a$ with $\rho(t_a)=R(a)$, and [F8] gives its moved line $\mathbb R a$. Apply the subspace-restriction theorem [F5] to this line inside $M(c)$; its orthogonal restriction is the unique reflection with normal $a$, so Carter's formula gives $t_a\le_Tc$. Thus every positive-root reflection lies below $c$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F8]
proof_step_texts.1.2: 1.2 Let $q=t_1\cdots t_m$ be a reduced reflection factorization. Each factor $t_r$ lies below $q$: if $q=x t_r y$, then $t_rq=(t_rx t_r)y$ is a product of $m-1$ reflections, so the triangle inequality forces $\ell_T(t_rq)=m-1$. If $r<s$, the product $t_rt_s$ has reflection length $2$ when $t_r\ne t_s$: their canonical images are distinct involutions with distinct moved lines, so $\rho(t_r)\rho(t_s)\ne I$; its determinant is $+1$, whereas every reflection has determinant $-1$. Thus $t_rt_s$ is neither the identity nor a reflection, and its reflection length is $2$. Write $q=x t_r y t_s z$. Then $(t_rt_s)^{-1}q=t_s t_r x t_r y t_s z=(t_s t_r x t_r t_s)(t_s y t_s)z,$ a product of $m-2$ reflections. The triangle inequality gives the reverse lower bound $m-2$, so $t_rt_s\le_Tq$. [F2, F3, F8]
proof_step_texts.2.1: 2.1 Let $q:=R(a_k)\cdots R(a_1)$. If $\ell_T(R(a_1)\cdots R(a_k)c)=n-k$, then $\ell_T(q)\le k$ and [F1], [F3] give $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(q)+\ell_T(q^{-1}c)\le k+(n-k)=n.$ Thus $\ell_T(q)=k$ and $q\le_Tc$, so the factorization of $q$ is reduced. For $i>j$, step 1.2 gives $R(a_i)R(a_j)\le_Tq\le_Tc$. Since $R(a_i)\le_Tc$ by step 1.1, $\ell_T(R(a_i)c)=n-1$; also $\ell_T(R(a_j)R(a_i)c)=n-2$. Hence $R(a_j)\le_TR(a_i)c$. By [F2] and [F8] the moved line of $R(a_j)$ is $\mathbb R a_j$; by [F3] and [F4] it lies in $M(R(a_i)c)=F(R(a_i)c)^\perp$. The vector $\mu(a_i)$ spans that fixed line by [F6], so $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, F8, step 1.1, step 1.2]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 Conversely, suppose $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$ for all $i>j$. The matrix $D=(\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j)_{i,j=1}^k$ is upper triangular with diagonal $1$ by [F6]; therefore both the roots $a_i$ and the vectors $\mu(a_i)$ are linearly independent, so $k\le n$. For $k=0$ the conclusion is $\ell_T(c)=n$ by [F3], so assume $k\ge1$. Define $q_{k+1}=1$. Descending on $i$, assume $q_{i+1}:=R(a_k)\cdots R(a_{i+1})\le_Tc$ with length $k-i$. Each factor $R(a_j)$, $j>i$, is below $q_{i+1}$ by the first claim of step 1.2. Complements reverse order: if $u\le_Tv\le_Tw$, transitivity gives $u\le_Tw$; writing $v=ux$ and $w=vy$ with additive reflection lengths then gives $\ell_T(xy)=\ell_T(x)+\ell_T(y)$, and conjugation invariance gives $\ell_T(y^{-1}xy)=\ell_T(x)$, hence $y=v^{-1}w\le_Tu^{-1}w=xy$. Put $v:=q_{i+1}^{-1}c$. For every $j>i$, complement reversal gives $v\le_TR(a_j)c$, and [F6] puts $\mu(a_j)$ in $F(R(a_j)c)\subseteq F(v)$. These $k-i$ independent vectors form a basis of $F(v)$: Carter's formula gives $\dim F(v)=n-\ell_T(v)=n-(n-k+i)=k-i.$ The assumed zero pairings put $a_i$ in $F(v)^\perp=M(v)$ by [F4]. Restricting $\rho(v)$ to the line $\mathbb R a_i$ gives the orthogonal reflection $R(a_i)=\rho(t_{a_i})$ by [F2]; the restriction theorem [F5] and Carter's formula therefore give $R(a_i)\le_Tv$. Write $v=R(a_i)z$ with $\ell_T(v)=1+\ell_T(z)$. Then $c=q_{i+1}R(a_i)z$, whose displayed $k-i+1+\ell_T(z)=n$ reflection factors force the factorization to be reduced; consequently $q_i:=q_{i+1}R(a_i)\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(q_i)=k-i+1$. At $i=1$ this yields $\ell_T(q)=k$ and $\ell_T(q^{-1}c)=n-k$. This proves (1). [F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F14, step 1.2]
proof_step_texts.3.1: 3.1 For $i<j$, the two-root instance of (1) says $R(a_j)R(a_i)\le_Tc\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mu(a_j)\cdot a_i=0,$ since the product of two distinct positive-root reflections has length $2$ by step 1.2. If $F=\{a_1<\dots<a_k\}$ is a simplex, every pair is an edge by [F10], so these pairwise equivalences make $D=(\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j)$ upper triangular with diagonal $1$. Pairing a vanishing combination $\sum_j\lambda_j a_j=0$ with each $\mu(a_i)$ gives $D\lambda=0$; hence every $\lambda_j=0$. Thus the vertices of every nonempty face are linearly independent. Conversely, if the reverse product of an increasing tuple lies below $c$ and has length $k$, step 1.2 applied to its reduced factorization shows each pair product is below $c$, so the tuple is a simplex. The empty tuple is the empty simplex by [F10]. [F2, F3, F6, F10, F14, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2]
proof_step_texts.4.2: 4.2 The roots of $P_\sigma$ lie in $M(\sigma)$: if $a\in P_\sigma$, then $t_a\le_T\sigma$ by definition; [F2] identifies its linear reflection, [F8] gives $M(t_a)=\mathbb R a$, and [F3] gives $M(t_a)\subseteq M(\sigma)$. facts.fact_text: [F12] A positive-definite Gram matrix with diagonal $1$ defines a spherical simplex; for linearly independent unit vectors its cone section of the sphere is a spherical simplex of dimension one less than the number of vertices, and the radial normalization of the Euclidean simplex onto that section is a homeomorphism. proof_step_texts.6.1: 6.1 Define the normalized cone map on a barycentric point of the geometric realization by $\iota\bigl((\lambda_v)_{v\in V(F)}\bigr):=\frac{\sum_v\lambda_vv}{\left\|\sum_v\lambda_vv\right\|_B},\qquad \lambda_v\ge0,\quad\sum_v\lambda_v=1.$ The denominator is nonzero because $B(f_0,v)>0$ for every positive root by step 4.1. Its restriction to each simplex is a homeomorphism onto the corresponding spherical simplex by [F12], and it is continuous globally by the weak-topology definition [F11]. If two such images agree, the two positive combinations lie on the same ray; step 5.1 puts that ray in the cone on the common face, and linear independence of that face plus the barycentric sum-one condition makes the original points equal. Thus $\iota$ is a continuous bijection onto $|X(\sigma)|$. By [F1] and step 4.2, $X(\sigma)$ is a finite abstract simplicial complex, so its ordinary realization is compact by [F15]. If $A$ is closed in that realization, [F15] makes $A$ compact; the open-cover argument in [F15] makes $\iota[A]$ compact, and it is closed in the Hausdorff sphere by [F15] and [F16]. Thus $\iota$ is a closed continuous bijection onto its image and therefore a topological embedding. No Choice is used: the only compactness input is [F15], whose finite-complex proof reduces to finite-dimensional Heine-Borel. [F1, F10, F11, F12, F15, F16, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1] ∎

Otherwise each new face has the form $B\cup\{\tau_{i+1}\}$ with $B\in K_i$ and every vertex of $B$ orthogonal to $\mu(\tau_{i+1})$, by step 4.3. For a cone point in such a face, its coefficient on $\tau_{i+1}$ is its pairing with $\mu(\tau_{i+1})$, because $\mu(\tau_{i+1})\cdot\tau_{i+1}=1$ by [F6] and its pairings with the base vertices are zero. Every old vertex $\tau_j$, $j\le i$, has $\mu(\tau_{i+1})\cdot\tau_j\le0$ by [F6]. Therefore a cone on an old face intersects a cone with apex $\tau_{i+1}$ only where the apex coefficient is zero; there the induction hypothesis identifies the intersection with the cone on the common base face. For two faces both containing the apex, equality of a common cone point gives equality of its apex coefficients after pairing with $\mu(\tau_{i+1})$, and then equality of the base cone points; induction identifies their base intersection. In each case the intersection is exactly the cone on the common face. Since every face of $X(\sigma)$ belongs to $K_t$, this proves the formula in (4). [F6, F10, step 4.3]

facts.fact_text: [F9] For $n\ge2$ and $\sigma\ne1$, $P_\sigma$ is the positive-root set of the reflection subgroup $W_\sigma$ and contains the simple system $\Delta=\{\delta_1,\dots,\delta_k\}$. The roots $\varepsilon_i=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{i-1})\delta_i$ are positive, factor $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_k)\cdots R(\varepsilon_1)$, and their increasing reordering $\theta_1<\dots<\theta_k$ has reverse product below $c$ with reflection length $k=\ell_T(\sigma)$. [[lem-cg-ordered-root-pairings-and-simple-systems]] (4)(i)-(ii),(iv)

proof_step_texts.4.2: 4.2 The roots of $P_\sigma$ lie in $M(\sigma)$: if $a\in P_\sigma$, then $t_a\le_T\sigma$ by definition; [F2] identifies its linear reflection, [F8] gives $M(t_a)=\mathbb R a$, and [F3] gives $M(t_a)\subseteq M(\sigma)$. Thus a face of $X(\sigma)$ has at most $\dim M(\sigma)=\ell_T(\sigma)$ vertices by step 3.1 and Carter's formula. If $\sigma=1$, then $P_\sigma=\emptyset$ and $X(1)=\{\emptyset\}$ has dimension $-1$. If $n=1$ and $\sigma\ne1$, the rank-one data give $W=\{1,c\}$, $\sigma=c$, and $P_\sigma=\{\alpha_1\}$; hence $X(\sigma)$ has one vertex and dimension $0=\ell_T(\sigma)-1$. If $n\ge2$ and $\sigma\ne1$, [F9] gives $\Delta=\{\delta_1,\dots,\delta_k\}\subseteq P_\sigma$ and $\varepsilon_i=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{i-1})\delta_i$. Each $R(\delta_j)$ lies in the reflection subgroup $W_\sigma$ of [F9], so every $\varepsilon_i$ is a root of that subgroup; its positivity from [F9] puts it in $P_\sigma$. Hence the increasing reordering $\theta_1<\dots<\theta_k$ lies in $P_\sigma$. Its reverse product is below $c$ with length $k=\ell_T(\sigma)$ by [F9], so step 3.1 makes it a $k$-vertex simplex. Therefore $\dim X(\sigma)=k-1$. Finiteness follows from finiteness of $\Phi_+$ in [F1], and the full-subcomplex and $X(\sigma,\rho)$ claims follow from [F10]. [F1, F2, F3, F8, F9, F10, step 3.1]

direct_paragraphs: With the notation of [[def-cg-brady-watt-ordered-spherical-root-complex]] and the conclusions of [[lem-cg-ordered-root-pairings-and-simple-systems]]:

**Given:** An irreducible finite-type Coxeter system $(W,S)$ with $|S|=n\ge1$, the bipartite Coxeter element $c$, its linear action $C_V=\rho(c)$, the ordered positive roots $\Phi_+$, the vectors $\mu_i$ and map $\mu$ of [[def-cg-bipartite-coxeter-element-and-root-recursion]], [[lem-cg-steinberg-bipartite-root-enumeration]], and [[lem-cg-ordered-root-pairings-and-simple-systems]]. Let $R(a)$ be the reflection with root normal $a$, and use the absolute order, moved spaces and positive-cone complexes of [[def-cg-brady-watt-ordered-spherical-root-complex]].

facts.fact_text: [F4] For orthogonal maps, $M(A)=F(A)^\perp$. [[lem-cg-orthogonal-wall-form-and-subspace-restriction]] (1)

proof_step_texts.2.1: 2.1 Let $q:=R(a_k)\cdots R(a_1)$. If $\ell_T(R(a_1)\cdots R(a_k)c)=n-k$, then $\ell_T(q)\le k$ and [F1], [F3] give $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(q)+\ell_T(q^{-1}c)\le k+(n-k)=n.$ Thus $\ell_T(q)=k$ and $q\le_Tc$, so the factorization of $q$ is reduced. For $i>j$, step 1.2 gives $R(a_i)R(a_j)\le_Tq\le_Tc$. Since $R(a_i)\le_Tc$ by step 1.1, $\ell_T(R(a_i)c)=n-1$; also $\ell_T(R(a_j)R(a_i)c)=n-2$. Hence $R(a_j)\le_TR(a_i)c$. By [F2] and [F8] the moved line of $R(a_j)$ is $\mathbb R a_j$; by [F3] and [F4] it lies in $M(R(a_i)c)=F(R(a_i)c)^\perp$. The vector $\mu(a_i)$ spans that fixed line by [F6], so $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, F8, step 1.1, step 1.2]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 Conversely, suppose $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$ for all $i>j$. The matrix $D=(\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j)_{i,j=1}^k$ is upper triangular with diagonal $1$ by [F6]; therefore both the roots $a_i$ and the vectors $\mu(a_i)$ are linearly independent, so $k\le n$. For $k=0$ the conclusion is $\ell_T(c)=n$ by [F3], so assume $k\ge1$. Define $q_{k+1}=1$. Descending on $i$, assume $q_{i+1}:=R(a_k)\cdots R(a_{i+1})\le_Tc$ with length $k-i$. Each factor $R(a_j)$, $j>i$, is below $q_{i+1}$ by the first claim of step 1.2. Complements reverse order: if $u\le_Tv\le_Tw$, transitivity gives $u\le_Tw$; writing $v=ux$ and $w=vy$ with additive reflection lengths then gives $\ell_T(xy)=\ell_T(x)+\ell_T(y)$, and conjugation invariance gives $\ell_T(y^{-1}xy)=\ell_T(x)$, hence $y=v^{-1}w\le_Tu^{-1}w=xy$. Put $v:=q_{i+1}^{-1}c$. For every $j>i$, complement reversal gives $v\le_TR(a_j)c$, and [F6] puts $\mu(a_j)$ in $F(R(a_j)c)\subseteq F(v)$. These $k-i$ independent vectors form a basis of $F(v)$: Carter's formula gives $\dim F(v)=n-\ell_T(v)=n-(n-k+i)=k-i.$ The assumed zero pairings put $a_i$ in $F(v)^\perp=M(v)$ by [F4]. Restricting $\rho(v)$ to the line $\mathbb R a_i$ gives the orthogonal reflection $R(a_i)=\rho(t_{a_i})$ by [F2]; the restriction theorem [F5] and Carter's formula therefore give $R(a_i)\le_Tv$. Write $v=R(a_i)z$ with $\ell_T(v)=1+\ell_T(z)$. Then $c=q_{i+1}R(a_i)z$, whose displayed $k-i+1+\ell_T(z)=n$ reflection factors force the factorization to be reduced; consequently $q_i:=q_{i+1}R(a_i)\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(q_i)=k-i+1$. At $i=1$ this yields $\ell_T(q)=k$ and $\ell_T(q^{-1}c)=n-k$. This proves (1). [F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F14, step 1.2]

facts.fact_text: [F5] Every subspace $U\subseteq M(A)$ has an orthogonal restriction $A_U\le_{\mathrm O}A$ with moved space $U$, and every line is the moved space of a unique orthogonal reflection. Carter's formula transfers this restriction order to absolute order for group elements. [[lem-cg-orthogonal-wall-form-and-subspace-restriction]] (3)-(4) [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]] (1)

Apply the subspace-restriction theorem [F5] to this line inside $M(c)$; its orthogonal restriction is the unique reflection with normal $a$, so Carter's formula gives $t_a\le_Tc$. facts.fact_text: [F12] A positive-definite Gram matrix with diagonal $1$ defines a spherical simplex; for linearly independent unit vectors its cone section of the sphere is a spherical simplex of dimension one less than the number of vertices, and the radial normalization of the Euclidean simplex onto that section is a homeomorphism. [[def-cg-spherical-gram-simplex-and-angular-link]] [[lem-cg-spherical-simplex-existence-and-link-gram-formula]] (i)-(ii)

proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 Let $f_0:=\sum_{s\in S}\beta_s$, with the dual vectors from [F13]. Then $B(f_0,\alpha_s)=1$ for every simple root; since each positive root is a nonzero nonnegative combination of simple roots by [F7], every positive root has positive pairing with $f_0$. Also [F7] gives positive pairing with every $f\in\mathcal C^\circ$ by the chamber transfer [F17]. For a nonempty face $F$, its independent unit roots have a positive-definite Gram matrix with diagonal $1$. By [F12], $c[F]\cap S^{n-1}$ is the associated spherical simplex of dimension $|F|-1$. The independence of the cone generators makes $c[F]$ pointed and simplicial. For the empty face, [F10] gives $c[\emptyset]=\{0\}$ and its sphere section is empty. [F3, F7, F10, F12, F13, F17, step 3.1]
proof_step_texts.6.1: 6.1 Define the normalized cone map on a barycentric point of the geometric realization by $\iota\bigl((\lambda_v)_{v\in V(F)}\bigr):=\frac{\sum_v\lambda_vv}{\left\|\sum_v\lambda_vv\right\|_B},\qquad \lambda_v\ge0,\quad\sum_v\lambda_v=1.$ The denominator is nonzero because $B(f_0,v)>0$ for every positive root by step 4.1. Its restriction to each simplex is a homeomorphism onto the corresponding spherical simplex by [F12], and it is continuous globally by the weak-topology definition [F11]. If two such images agree, the two positive combinations lie on the same ray; step 5.1 puts that ray in the cone on the common face, and linear independence of that face plus the barycentric sum-one condition makes the original points equal. Thus $\iota$ is a continuous bijection onto $|X(\sigma)|$. By [F1] and step 4.2, $X(\sigma)$ is a finite abstract simplicial complex, so its ordinary realization is compact by [F15]. If $A$ is closed in that realization, [F15] makes $A$ compact; the open-cover argument in [F15] makes $\iota[A]$ compact, and it is closed in the Hausdorff sphere by [F15] and [F16]. Thus $\iota$ is a closed continuous bijection onto its image and therefore a topological embedding. No Choice is used: the only compactness input is [F15], whose finite-complex proof reduces to finite-dimensional Heine-Borel. [F1, F10, F11, F12, F15, F16, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1] ∎

facts.fact_text: [F6] Writing $a=\rho_i$ and using $\mu(\rho_i)=\mu_i$, one has $\mu(a)\in F(R(a)c)$, this fixed space is a line, and $\mu(a)\cdot a=1$. Also $\mu_i\cdot\rho_j\ge0$ if $i\le j$, $\mu_i\cdot\rho_j\le0$ if $i>j$ within the positive-root range, and $\mu_{i+t}\cdot\rho_i=0$ for $1\le t\le n-1$. For $n=1$, $C_V=-\mathrm{id}$ and $\mu=\mathrm{id}$, so $R(\alpha_1)c=1$ has the one-dimensional fixed space $V$ and $B(\mu(\alpha_1),\alpha_1)=1$; the strict-order sign conditions and the range $1\le t\le n-1$ are empty. [[lem-cg-steinberg-bipartite-root-enumeration]] (4) [[lem-cg-ordered-root-pairings-and-simple-systems]] (1)-(2)

proof_step_texts.3.1: 3.1 For $i<j$, the two-root instance of (1) says $R(a_j)R(a_i)\le_Tc\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mu(a_j)\cdot a_i=0,$ since the product of two distinct positive-root reflections has length $2$ by step 1.2. If $F=\{a_1<\dots<a_k\}$ is a simplex, every pair is an edge by [F10], so these pairwise equivalences make $D=(\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j)$ upper triangular with diagonal $1$. Pairing a vanishing combination $\sum_j\lambda_j a_j=0$ with each $\mu(a_i)$ gives $D\lambda=0$; hence every $\lambda_j=0$. Thus the vertices of every nonempty face are linearly independent. Conversely, if the reverse product of an increasing tuple lies below $c$ and has length $k$, step 1.2 applied to its reduced factorization shows each pair product is below $c$, so the tuple is a simplex. The empty tuple is the empty simplex by [F10]. [F2, F3, F6, F10, F14, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2]

Conversely, any face $B$ of $K_i$ with all vertices in this hyperplane gives a simplex $B\cup\{\tau_{i+1}\}$. This includes $B=\emptyset$, proving the cone-over-link description and the nested inclusions. [F6, F10, step 3.1]

In each case the intersection is exactly the cone on the common face. Since every face of $X(\sigma)$ belongs to $K_t$, this proves the formula in (4). [F6, F10, step 4.3]

facts.fact_text: [F3] Since $W$ is finite, $B$ is positive definite and every $\rho(w)$ is a $B$-isometry. Carter's formula gives $\ell_T(w)=\dim M(w)=n-\dim F(w)$ for every $w$. Absolute order is the partial order defined by reflection-length additivity; it has the triangle inequality and conjugation invariance, and $u\le_Tv$ implies $M(u)\subseteq M(v)$ and $F(v)\subseteq F(u)$. [[def-cg-reflection-length-absolute-order-and-moved-space]] [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]] (1)-(2)

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 By [F1], $M(c)=V$ and $\ell_T(c)=n$. For every $a\in\Phi_+$, [F2] gives $t_a$ with $\rho(t_a)=R(a)$, and [F8] gives its moved line $\mathbb R a$. Apply the subspace-restriction theorem [F5] to this line inside $M(c)$; its orthogonal restriction is the unique reflection with normal $a$, so Carter's formula gives $t_a\le_Tc$. Thus every positive-root reflection lies below $c$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F8]
proof_step_texts.1.2: 1.2 Let $q=t_1\cdots t_m$ be a reduced reflection factorization. Each factor $t_r$ lies below $q$: if $q=x t_r y$, then $t_rq=(t_rx t_r)y$ is a product of $m-1$ reflections, so the triangle inequality forces $\ell_T(t_rq)=m-1$. If $r<s$, the product $t_rt_s$ has reflection length $2$ when $t_r\ne t_s$: their canonical images are distinct involutions with distinct moved lines, so $\rho(t_r)\rho(t_s)\ne I$; its determinant is $+1$, whereas every reflection has determinant $-1$. Thus $t_rt_s$ is neither the identity nor a reflection, and its reflection length is $2$. Write $q=x t_r y t_s z$. Then $(t_rt_s)^{-1}q=t_s t_r x t_r y t_s z=(t_s t_r x t_r t_s)(t_s y t_s)z,$ a product of $m-2$ reflections. The triangle inequality gives the reverse lower bound $m-2$, so $t_rt_s\le_Tq$. [F2, F3, F8]
proof_step_texts.2.1: 2.1 Let $q:=R(a_k)\cdots R(a_1)$. If $\ell_T(R(a_1)\cdots R(a_k)c)=n-k$, then $\ell_T(q)\le k$ and [F1], [F3] give $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(q)+\ell_T(q^{-1}c)\le k+(n-k)=n.$ Thus $\ell_T(q)=k$ and $q\le_Tc$, so the factorization of $q$ is reduced. For $i>j$, step 1.2 gives $R(a_i)R(a_j)\le_Tq\le_Tc$. Since $R(a_i)\le_Tc$ by step 1.1, $\ell_T(R(a_i)c)=n-1$; also $\ell_T(R(a_j)R(a_i)c)=n-2$. Hence $R(a_j)\le_TR(a_i)c$. By [F2] and [F8] the moved line of $R(a_j)$ is $\mathbb R a_j$; by [F3] and [F4] it lies in $M(R(a_i)c)=F(R(a_i)c)^\perp$. The vector $\mu(a_i)$ spans that fixed line by [F6], so $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, F8, step 1.1, step 1.2]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 Conversely, suppose $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$ for all $i>j$. The matrix $D=(\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j)_{i,j=1}^k$ is upper triangular with diagonal $1$ by [F6]; therefore both the roots $a_i$ and the vectors $\mu(a_i)$ are linearly independent, so $k\le n$. For $k=0$ the conclusion is $\ell_T(c)=n$ by [F3], so assume $k\ge1$. Define $q_{k+1}=1$. Descending on $i$, assume $q_{i+1}:=R(a_k)\cdots R(a_{i+1})\le_Tc$ with length $k-i$. Each factor $R(a_j)$, $j>i$, is below $q_{i+1}$ by the first claim of step 1.2. Complements reverse order: if $u\le_Tv\le_Tw$, transitivity gives $u\le_Tw$; writing $v=ux$ and $w=vy$ with additive reflection lengths then gives $\ell_T(xy)=\ell_T(x)+\ell_T(y)$, and conjugation invariance gives $\ell_T(y^{-1}xy)=\ell_T(x)$, hence $y=v^{-1}w\le_Tu^{-1}w=xy$. Put $v:=q_{i+1}^{-1}c$. For every $j>i$, complement reversal gives $v\le_TR(a_j)c$, and [F6] puts $\mu(a_j)$ in $F(R(a_j)c)\subseteq F(v)$. These $k-i$ independent vectors form a basis of $F(v)$: Carter's formula gives $\dim F(v)=n-\ell_T(v)=n-(n-k+i)=k-i.$ The assumed zero pairings put $a_i$ in $F(v)^\perp=M(v)$ by [F4]. Restricting $\rho(v)$ to the line $\mathbb R a_i$ gives the orthogonal reflection $R(a_i)=\rho(t_{a_i})$ by [F2]; the restriction theorem [F5] and Carter's formula therefore give $R(a_i)\le_Tv$. Write $v=R(a_i)z$ with $\ell_T(v)=1+\ell_T(z)$. Then $c=q_{i+1}R(a_i)z$, whose displayed $k-i+1+\ell_T(z)=n$ reflection factors force the factorization to be reduced; consequently $q_i:=q_{i+1}R(a_i)\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(q_i)=k-i+1$. At $i=1$ this yields $\ell_T(q)=k$ and $\ell_T(q^{-1}c)=n-k$. This proves (1). [F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F14, step 1.2]
proof_step_texts.3.1: 3.1 For $i<j$, the two-root instance of (1) says $R(a_j)R(a_i)\le_Tc\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mu(a_j)\cdot a_i=0,$ since the product of two distinct positive-root reflections has length $2$ by step 1.2. If $F=\{a_1<\dots<a_k\}$ is a simplex, every pair is an edge by [F10], so these pairwise equivalences make $D=(\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j)$ upper triangular with diagonal $1$. Pairing a vanishing combination $\sum_j\lambda_j a_j=0$ with each $\mu(a_i)$ gives $D\lambda=0$; hence every $\lambda_j=0$. Thus the vertices of every nonempty face are linearly independent. Conversely, if the reverse product of an increasing tuple lies below $c$ and has length $k$, step 1.2 applied to its reduced factorization shows each pair product is below $c$, so the tuple is a simplex. The empty tuple is the empty simplex by [F10]. [F2, F3, F6, F10, F14, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 Let $f_0:=\sum_{s\in S}\beta_s$, with the dual vectors from [F13]. Also [F7] gives positive pairing with every $f\in\mathcal C^\circ$ by the chamber transfer [F17]. For a nonempty face $F$, its independent unit roots have a positive-definite Gram matrix with diagonal $1$. By [F12], $c[F]\cap S^{n-1}$ is the associated spherical simplex of dimension $|F|-1$. The independence of the cone generators makes $c[F]$ pointed and simplicial. For the empty face, [F10] gives $c[\emptyset]=\{0\}$ and its sphere section is empty. [F3, F7, F10, F12, F13, F17, step 3.1]
proof_step_texts.4.2: 4.2 The roots of $P_\sigma$ lie in $M(\sigma)$: if $a\in P_\sigma$, then $t_a\le_T\sigma$ by definition; [F2] identifies its linear reflection, [F8] gives $M(t_a)=\mathbb R a$, and [F3] gives $M(t_a)\subseteq M(\sigma)$. facts.fact_text: [F2] $(C-\mathrm{id})\mu_i=-2\rho_i$ for all $i\ge1$, and $\mu$ is $C$-equivariant. For $1\le i\le n$, $\mu_i=\beta_i$: each preceding reflection fixes $\beta_i$ by duality. The pairing and fixed-line assertions of (1) are derived in step 1.1 below. [[lem-cg-steinberg-bipartite-root-enumeration]] (4) [[def-cg-bipartite-coxeter-element-and-root-recursion]] (3)-(4)

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 For every $i\ge1$, [F2] gives $(C-\mathrm{id})\mu_i=-2\rho_i$. Since $C$ is an isometry and $B(\rho_i,\rho_i)=1$, $B(\mu_i,\rho_i)=1$ follows by expanding $B(C\mu_i,C\mu_i)=B(\mu_i-2\rho_i,\mu_i-2\rho_i)$. The same identity gives $C\mu_i=\mu_i-2\rho_i$, so $r_{\rho_i}C\mu_i=\mu_i$ and $\mu_i\in F(r_{\rho_i}C)$. For $1\le i\le n$, the reflection word $r_{\rho_i}C$ cancels to $R_1\cdots R_{i-1}R_{i+1}\cdots R_n$, so its reflection length is at most $n-1$; the triangle inequality and $\ell_T(c)=n$ give the lower bound $n-1$. Thus its fixed space is one-dimensional. Since $r_{\rho_{i+n}}C=C(r_{\rho_i}C)C^{-1}$, the same dimension holds for all $i$. The vector $\mu_i$ is nonzero because $\mu_i\cdot\rho_i=1$, and it is the unique vector in that line with this pairing. This proves (1). [F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.2: 1.2 For all $i,j\ge1$, $\mu_i\cdot\rho_j=-\mu_{j+n}\cdot\rho_i$. Indeed, $\rho_i=\tfrac12(\mu_i-C\mu_i)$ by [F2], so $-\mu_{j+n}\cdot\rho_i=-C\mu_j\cdot\tfrac12(\mu_i-C\mu_i)=\tfrac12(\mu_j-C\mu_j)\cdot\mu_i=\rho_j\cdot\mu_i$, using the isometry of $C$ and [F1]-[F2]. This is (2)(a). [F1, F2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.3: 1.3 Suppose $1\le i\le j\le nh/2$. If $i>n$, then $j>n$ and $C$-equivariance gives $\mu_i\cdot\rho_j=\mu_{i-n}\cdot\rho_{j-n}$. Repeating reduces to a first index at most $n$ while keeping both indices positive and ordered. For $i\le n$, $\mu_i=\beta_i$, and $\beta_i\cdot\rho_j$ is the coefficient of $\alpha_i$ in the positive root $\rho_j$; this is nonnegative by [F4]. Thus (2)(b) holds. [F1, F2, F4, algebra]
proof_step_texts.2.1: 2.1 To prove (2)(c), first reduce $i$ modulo $n$ using $C$-equivariance, which preserves $\mu_{i+t}\cdot\rho_i$, and assume $1\le i\le n$. If $i+t\le n$, then $\mu_{i+t}=\beta_{i+t}$ and $\rho_i=R_1\cdots R_{i-1}\alpha_i$ has no $\alpha_{i+t}$ coefficient, so the pairing is zero. If $i+t>n$, put $j=i+t-n$, so $1\le j<i$. By (2)(a), $\mu_{i+t}\cdot\rho_i=\mu_{j+n}\cdot\rho_i=-\mu_i\cdot\rho_j=-\beta_i\cdot\rho_j=0$, since $\rho_j$ is supported on $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_j$. Now if $1\le i<j\le nh/2$ and $j<i+n$, (2)(d) is (2)(c) with $t=j-i$; if $j\ge i+n$, (2)(a) and (2)(b) give $\mu_j\cdot\rho_i=-\mu_{i+n}\cdot\rho_j\le0$. This proves (2)(c)-(d). [F1, F2, F4, step 1.3, algebra]
proof_step_texts.2.3: 2.3 For any increasing tuple $a_1<\cdots<a_m$ of positive roots, one has $\ell_T(R(a_1)\cdots R(a_m)c)=n-m$ if and only if $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$ for all $i>j$. If $m=0$, the left side is $\ell_T(c)=n$ by [F1], and the zero-pairing condition is vacuous; hence assume $m\ge1$. Put $r_i=R(a_i)$. The length equality is equivalent to the reverse product $q=r_m\cdots r_1$ being a reduced element below $c$: its complement is $q^{-1}c=r_1\cdots r_m c$. In fact, if $\ell_T(q^{-1}c)=n-m$, then $\ell_T(q)\le m$ and $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(q)+\ell_T(q^{-1}c)\le n$, so both inequalities are equalities; the converse is the defining absolute-order equality. For the forward implication, the pair-product fact in step 1.5 gives $r_i r_j\le_Tc$ whenever $i>j$. Since $\ell_T(r_i c)=n-1$, this gives $r_j\le_Tr_i c$ from $\ell_T(r_j r_i c)=n-2$; hence $M(r_j)\subseteq M(r_i c)=F(r_i c)^\perp$. The vector $\mu(a_i)$ is a nonzero member of the one-dimensional fixed space $F(r_i c)$, so $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$. Conversely, suppose all these pairings vanish. The matrix $[\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j]$ is upper triangular with diagonal $1$ by (1), so both the $a_i$ and the $\mu(a_i)$ are linearly independent; in particular $m\le n$. Induct downward on $i$ to prove $q_i:=r_m\cdots r_i\le_Tc$ with length $m-i+1$. The base $q_m=r_m$ is step 1.4. If $q_{i+1}\le_Tc$, then each factor $r_j$ with $j>i$ satisfies $r_j\le_Tq_{i+1}$: writing a reduced factorization $q_{i+1}=x r_j y$, the product $r_jq_{i+1}=(r_jxr_j)y$ uses one fewer reflections, and the triangle inequality makes that expression reduced. Put $v=q_{i+1}^{-1}c$. Complement order reversal from step 1.5 gives $v\le_Tr_jc$, so $\mu(a_j)\in F(r_jc)\subseteq F(v)$ for every $j>i$. These $m-i$ independent vectors form a basis of $F(v)$, whose dimension is $m-i$ by Carter's formula. The assumed zero pairings give $a_i\in F(v)^\perp=M(v)$. The Wall restriction for the line $\mathbb Ra_i$ gives $r_i\le_Tv$; writing $v=r_i z$ then gives $c=q_{i+1}r_i z$, with lengths adding, so $q_i=q_{i+1}r_i\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(q_i)=m-i+1$. At $i=1$ this proves the claimed equivalence. The same argument applies to every subtuple because the vanishing conditions are inherited. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.4, step 1.5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.6.1:
6.1 Let $q$ be the global index with $\delta_k=ho_q$ and put $
u=C\mu_q=\mu_{q+n}$. For every $ho_j\in P_\sigma$ one has $j\le q$ and, by (2)(a) and $C$-equivariance, $
u\cdotho_j=\mu_{q+n}\cdotho_j=-\mu_{j+n}\cdotho_{q+n}=-\mu_j\cdotho_q\le0$ by (2)(b); at $j=q$ this is $-1$. Since $\mu_q\in F(r c)$, conjugating by $C$ gives $
u\in F(c r)$; and $\ell_T(cr)=n-1$, so $F(cr)=\mathbb R
u$ and $M(cr)=
u^\perp$. Moreover $\sigma'\le_Tc r$: its complement is $\sigma'^{-1}cr=rvr$, of length $n-k$, while $\ell_T(cr)=n-1$; the lengths add to $n-1$. Hence $U:=M(\sigma')$ is contained in $E\cap
u^\perp$, and both have dimension $k-1$ because $
u\cdot\delta_k=-1$. Thus $U=E\cap
u^\perp$. The roots $P_{\sigma'}=\Phi_+\cap U$ span $U$ by step 2.2. Each is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$ and is orthogonal to $
u$; since $
u\cdot\delta_k=-1$ and $
u\cdot\delta_j\le0$ for every $j$, every root in $P_{\sigma'}$ is a combination only of the $\delta_j$ for which $
u\cdot\delta_j=0$. Those zero-pairing simple roots must span the $(k-1)$-space $U$, so they are exactly $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{k-1}$. They form a simple system for $P_{\sigma'}$. Induction gives $\sigma'=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{k-1})$ and proves the reverse selection at each rank. Therefore $\sigma=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_k)$. For each $i$, its prefix $p_i:=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_i)$ and complementary suffix $R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)$ multiply to $\sigma$ and have at most $i$ and $k-i$ reflections, so both lengths attain these bounds. Thus $M(p_i)$, contained in $\operatorname{span}(\delta_1,\dots,\delta_i)$, has dimension $i$ and equals that span. Since $\sigma R(\delta_k)\cdots R(\delta_{i+1})=p_i$, the induction shows that $\delta_i$ is the last root of $P_\sigma$ in this subspace. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.3, step 2.2, step 5.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.8.2: 8.2 Fix $i$. The second factorization in (4)(ii) writes $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_i)q_i'$ where $q_i'$ is the product of the other $k-1$ simple reflections in $\Delta$. Thus $\ell_T(q_i')=k-1$, $R(\varepsilon_i)\le_T\sigma$, and $q_i'=R(\varepsilon_i)\sigma$. Since $c=\sigma v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-k$, $R(\varepsilon_i)c=q_i'v$ is reduced, so $q_i'\le_TR(\varepsilon_i)c$. It follows that $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\in F(q_i')$. The moved space $M(q_i')$ is exactly $\operatorname{span}\{\delta_j:j\ne i\}$: it is contained there because those are its reflection normals, and both dimensions are $k-1$. Hence $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\delta_j=0$ for $j\ne i$. Since $\varepsilon_i-\delta_i$ is a linear combination of $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{i-1}$, (1) gives $1=\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\varepsilon_i=\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\delta_i$. Thus the restrictions to $E$ of the functionals $B(\mu(\varepsilon_i),-)$ form the dual basis to $\Delta$. For $x=\sum_j a_j\delta_j$ with $a_j\ge0$, $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot x=a_i$; intersecting the cone with this zero hyperplane and with the unit sphere proves the wall equality, and the supporting hyperplane in $E$ is $E\cap\mu(\varepsilon_i)^\perp$. This proves (4)(iii). [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 7.2, algebra]

direct_paragraphs: Let $(W,S)$ be an irreducible Coxeter system of finite type with $S$ finite of cardinality $n\ge2$, with the data $\alpha_i$, $\beta_i$, $s_i$, $R_i$, $a$, $b$, $c$, $h$, $(\rho_i)$, $(\mu_i)$ and the linear map $\mu$ of [[def-cg-bipartite-coxeter-element-and-root-recursion]], and assume the conclusions of [[lem-cg-steinberg-bipartite-root-enumeration]] (so that $\Phi_+=\{\rho_1,\dots,\rho_{nh/2}\}$ and $\mu(\rho_i)=\mu_i$). Let $\ell_T$, $\le_T$, $M$, $F$ be reflection length, absolute order and the moved and fixed spaces, and let $P_\sigma:=\{\alpha\in\Phi_+:t_\alpha\le_T\sigma\}$ for $\sigma\le_Tc$, where $t_\alpha\in T$ is the reflection with normal $\alpha$ ([[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (1), [[def-cg-reflection-length-absolute-order-and-moved-space]], [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]]). Then:

**Given:** The finite-type irreducible datum with $|S|=n\ge2$ and the bipartite data $\alpha_i,s_i,R_i,\beta_i,\rho_i,\mu_i,a,b,c,h$ of [[def-cg-bipartite-coxeter-element-and-root-recursion]], the enumeration of [[lem-cg-steinberg-bipartite-root-enumeration]], and an element $\sigma\le_Tc$.

supplier_uses.claim_note: Definition1–4: tree bipartition and commuting color products; cyclic prefix/dual vectors; mu inverse conditional. Definition5 permits reducible/empty componentwise use, with no global equal-h root count.

facts.fact_text: [F9] The root arrangement $\{H_\alpha:\alpha\in\Phi\}$ is finite. [[def-cg-finite-reflection-arrangement-and-spherical-chambers]]

proof_step_texts.1.6: 1.6 Put $E=M(\sigma)$ and $F=E^\perp$. Then $W_\sigma=\{w:M(w)\subseteq E\}$ is the pointwise stabilizer of $F$, because $M(w)=F(w)^\perp$. If $F\ne0$, choose $x\in F$ outside $\{0\}$ and every proper subspace $F\cap H_\alpha$; this is possible by [F9] and [F12]. By [F10], $\operatorname{Stab}_W(x)=gW_Ig^{-1}$ for some $g,I$. Each conjugate simple generator has a root hyperplane containing $x$, hence, by the choice of $x$, containing all of $F$; therefore every generator of this stabilizer fixes $F$ pointwise. Conversely every element fixing $F$ fixes $x$, so $W_\sigma=gW_Ig^{-1}$. If $F=0$, take $g=1$ and $I=S$. [F3, F5, F9, F10, F12]

facts.fact_text: [F3] $B$ is positive definite, every root has $B$-norm $1$, reflections act by $r_\alpha(x)=x-2B(x,\alpha)\alpha$, and $B(Cx,Cy)=B(x,y)$. For each positive root $\alpha$ there is a unique reflection $t_\alpha$ with $\rho(t_\alpha)=r_\alpha$; its moved space is $\mathbb R\alpha$. [[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]] (3) [[lem-cg-reflection-representation-descends-and-root-norms]] (2),(3) [[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (1) [[lem-cg-reflection-form-invariance-and-rank-two-orders]] (2)

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 For every $i\ge1$, [F2] gives $(C-\mathrm{id})\mu_i=-2\rho_i$. Since $C$ is an isometry and $B(\rho_i,\rho_i)=1$, $B(\mu_i,\rho_i)=1$ follows by expanding $B(C\mu_i,C\mu_i)=B(\mu_i-2\rho_i,\mu_i-2\rho_i)$. The same identity gives $C\mu_i=\mu_i-2\rho_i$, so $r_{\rho_i}C\mu_i=\mu_i$ and $\mu_i\in F(r_{\rho_i}C)$. For $1\le i\le n$, the reflection word $r_{\rho_i}C$ cancels to $R_1\cdots R_{i-1}R_{i+1}\cdots R_n$, so its reflection length is at most $n-1$; the triangle inequality and $\ell_T(c)=n$ give the lower bound $n-1$. Thus its fixed space is one-dimensional. Since $r_{\rho_{i+n}}C=C(r_{\rho_i}C)C^{-1}$, the same dimension holds for all $i$. The vector $\mu_i$ is nonzero because $\mu_i\cdot\rho_i=1$, and it is the unique vector in that line with this pairing. This proves (1). [F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.4: 1.4 Every reflection lies below $c$. Indeed, $M(c)=V$ by [F1]. For a positive root $\alpha$, the orthogonal reflection with moved line $\mathbb R\alpha$ is uniquely $r_\alpha=\rho(t_\alpha)$ by [F3],[F6]; the Wall restriction for this line is below $C=\rho(c)$ and has moved space $\mathbb R\alpha$. The Wall dimension identity and Carter's formula therefore give $t_\alpha\le_Tc$. [F1, F3, F5, F6]
proof_step_texts.1.5: 1.5 We use two elementary consequences of absolute order. First, if $w=r_1\cdots r_m$ is a reduced reflection factorization and $p<q$, then $r_pr_q\le_Tw$: distinct root-reflections have product moved space the two-plane spanned by their distinct normal lines, so their product has reflection length $2$ by Carter's formula. Write $w=xr_pyr_qz$; then $(r_pr_q)^{-1}w=r_qr_pxr_pyr_qz=(r_q(r_pxr_p)y r_q)z$, a product of $m-2$ reflections because conjugation preserves reflections. The triangle inequality forces this complement to have length $m-2$. Second, if $u\le_Tv\le_Tw$, then $v^{-1}w\le_Tu^{-1}w$: write $v=ux$, $w=vy$ with additive reflection lengths; then $u^{-1}w=xy$, while $y^{-1}xy$ has the same length as $x$, so $y\le_Txy$. These facts will be used below. [F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.6: 1.6 Put $E=M(\sigma)$ and $F=E^\perp$. Then $W_\sigma=\{w:M(w)\subseteq E\}$ is the pointwise stabilizer of $F$, because $M(w)=F(w)^\perp$. If $F\ne0$, choose $x\in F$ outside $\{0\}$ and every proper subspace $F\cap H_\alpha$; this is possible by [F9] and [F12]. By [F10], $\operatorname{Stab}_W(x)=gW_Ig^{-1}$ for some $g,I$. Each conjugate simple generator has a root hyperplane containing $x$, hence, by the choice of $x$, containing all of $F$; therefore every generator of this stabilizer fixes $F$ pointwise. Conversely every element fixing $F$ fixes $x$, so $W_\sigma=gW_Ig^{-1}$. If $F=0$, take $g=1$ and $I=S$. [F3, F5, F9, F10, F12]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 For every $\sigma\le_Tc$, one has $P_\sigma=\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$. If $\alpha\in P_\sigma$, then $M(t_\alpha)=\mathbb R\alpha\subseteq M(\sigma)$ by [F5]. Conversely, if $\alpha\in\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$, then $t_\alpha\le_Tc$ by step 1.4 and $\sigma\le_Tc$, so moved-space rigidity in [F5] gives $t_\alpha\le_T\sigma$. Also $P_\sigma$ spans $M(\sigma)$: choose a reduced reflection factorization of $\sigma$; its prefix-conjugated normals are a basis of $M(\sigma)$ by [F7], and the reflections with those normals have moved lines in $M(\sigma)$, hence lie below $\sigma$ by the same common-upper-bound argument. Taking the positive sign of each normal puts a spanning set in $P_\sigma$. [F3, F5, F7, F8, step 1.4]
proof_step_texts.2.3: 2.3 For any increasing tuple $a_1<\cdots<a_m$ of positive roots, one has $\ell_T(R(a_1)\cdots R(a_m)c)=n-m$ if and only if $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$ for all $i>j$. If $m=0$, the left side is $\ell_T(c)=n$ by [F1], and the zero-pairing condition is vacuous; hence assume $m\ge1$. Put $r_i=R(a_i)$. The length equality is equivalent to the reverse product $q=r_m\cdots r_1$ being a reduced element below $c$: its complement is $q^{-1}c=r_1\cdots r_m c$. In fact, if $\ell_T(q^{-1}c)=n-m$, then $\ell_T(q)\le m$ and $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(q)+\ell_T(q^{-1}c)\le n$, so both inequalities are equalities; the converse is the defining absolute-order equality. For the forward implication, the pair-product fact in step 1.5 gives $r_i r_j\le_Tc$ whenever $i>j$. Since $\ell_T(r_i c)=n-1$, this gives $r_j\le_Tr_i c$ from $\ell_T(r_j r_i c)=n-2$; hence $M(r_j)\subseteq M(r_i c)=F(r_i c)^\perp$. The vector $\mu(a_i)$ is a nonzero member of the one-dimensional fixed space $F(r_i c)$, so $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$. Conversely, suppose all these pairings vanish. The matrix $[\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j]$ is upper triangular with diagonal $1$ by (1), so both the $a_i$ and the $\mu(a_i)$ are linearly independent; in particular $m\le n$. Induct downward on $i$ to prove $q_i:=r_m\cdots r_i\le_Tc$ with length $m-i+1$. The base $q_m=r_m$ is step 1.4. If $q_{i+1}\le_Tc$, then each factor $r_j$ with $j>i$ satisfies $r_j\le_Tq_{i+1}$: writing a reduced factorization $q_{i+1}=x r_j y$, the product $r_jq_{i+1}=(r_jxr_j)y$ uses one fewer reflections, and the triangle inequality makes that expression reduced. Put $v=q_{i+1}^{-1}c$. Complement order reversal from step 1.5 gives $v\le_Tr_jc$, so $\mu(a_j)\in F(r_jc)\subseteq F(v)$ for every $j>i$. These $m-i$ independent vectors form a basis of $F(v)$, whose dimension is $m-i$ by Carter's formula. The assumed zero pairings give $a_i\in F(v)^\perp=M(v)$. The Wall restriction for the line $\mathbb Ra_i$ gives $r_i\le_Tv$; writing $v=r_i z$ then gives $c=q_{i+1}r_i z$, with lengths adding, so $q_i=q_{i+1}r_i\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(q_i)=m-i+1$. At $i=1$ this proves the claimed equivalence. The same argument applies to every subtuple because the vanishing conditions are inherited. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.4, step 1.5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.3.2: 3.2 Let $\Phi_I=\{\rho(u)\alpha_s:u\in W_I,s\in I\}$ be the intrinsic root system from [F14]; its representation is the restriction to $V_I=\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_s:s\in I\}$, since the reflection formulas agree. An ambient reflection $t\in T\cap W_I$ has a reduced $I$-expression by [F14]. Apply strong exchange to $tt=1$: it expresses $t$ as a prefix-conjugate of a letter of that expression, so its root normal belongs to $\pm\Phi_I$ by [F3]. Conversely every intrinsic root gives an ambient reflection in $W_I$. Conjugating by $g$, the root-reflection dictionary therefore identifies the roots of $gW_Ig^{-1}$ with precisely the ambient roots whose reflections fix $F$ pointwise, namely $\Phi\cap E=\pm P_\sigma$ by step 2.2. Their span is both $\rho(g)V_I$ and $E$, since $P_\sigma$ spans $E$. [F3, F14, step 2.2, step 1.6]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 Choose $f\in\mathcal C^\circ$ and project it orthogonally to $E$. Its pairing with every root of $P_\sigma$ is positive by [F4], so it avoids the subsystem arrangement. Apply [F10] to the finite Coxeter system $(W_I,I)$ and transfer its chambers to $E$ by $\rho(g)$. The chamber containing the projection has inward unit normals $\Delta=\{\rho(gu)\alpha_s:s\in I\}$ for some $u\in W_I$. These are a basis of $E$, their reflections are the conjugates of the simple generators of $W_I$, and their Gram matrix is the restricted Coxeter Gram matrix. In particular distinct normals have nonpositive pairings. By the root-sign theorem [F4] applied to this conjugate Coxeter system, its positive roots are exactly the roots positive on the projection, hence $P_\sigma$, and every such root is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$. This supplies the simple system and the Coxeter presentation used below. [F3, F4, F10, F14, step 3.2]
proof_step_texts.7.2: 7.2 Put $D_i:=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{i-1})$ and $\varepsilon_i:=D_i\delta_i$. The prefix $R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_i)$ has reflection length $i$ by the factorization of $\sigma$ and the triangle inequality, so this simple-generator word in the Coxeter system of $W_\sigma$ is reduced. The root-inversion formula [F13], applied to that parabolic system, gives $\varepsilon_i\in P_\sigma$, hence it is a positive root. Conjugation gives $R(\varepsilon_i)=D_iR(\delta_i)D_i^{-1}$; multiplying these identities and cancelling adjacent inverse prefixes yields $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_k)\cdots R(\varepsilon_1)$. Also $R(\varepsilon_i)D_iR(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)=D_iR(\delta_i)R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)=\sigma$. This proves (4)(ii). [F3, F5, F13, step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.8.1: 8.1 Suppose $\ell_T(\sigma)=2$ and $P_\sigma=\{\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_t\}$. By (4)(i), $\Delta=\{\tau_1,\tau_t\}$ and $\sigma=R(\tau_1)R(\tau_t)$. Step 4.1 realizes this as a canonical rank-two system. If its exponent is $m$, [F11] gives simple-root angle $\pi-\pi/m$ and a rotation of magnitude $2\pi/m$. Write its generators as $r,s$ and $q=rs$. The identities $rqr=q^{-1}$ and $s=rq$ reduce every word to $q^j$ or $q^jr$, $0\le j<m$; their distinct actions are the $m$ rotations and $m$ reflections in lines spaced by $\pi/m$. Every reflection is a conjugate of $r$ or $s$: the conjugates give respectively $q^{2j}r$ and $q^{2j-1}r$. The root-reflection dictionary thus gives $t=m$ positive roots, equally spaced between the simple-root rays. The global order agrees with angular order: a decrease after $\tau_r$ would put $\tau_{r+1}$ in the cone on earlier roots $\tau_1,\tau_r$, contrary to step 3.1. A product of reflections has rotation angle twice the difference of its normal angles, modulo $2\pi$; hence the two-reflection factorizations of $\sigma$ are exactly $R(\tau_1)R(\tau_t)=R(\tau_2)R(\tau_1)=\cdots=R(\tau_t)R(\tau_{t-1})$. These exhaust factorizations in $W$: if $\sigma=R(\alpha)R(\beta)$, then $M(\sigma)\subseteq\operatorname{span}(\alpha,\beta)$, and both spaces have dimension $2$, so the positive representatives of $\alpha,\beta$ lie in $P_\sigma$ by step 2.2. The endpoint angle gives $\tau_1\cdot\tau_t=-\cos(\pi/t)\le0$, while each adjacent angle gives $\tau_i\cdot\tau_{i+1}=\cos(\pi/t)\ge0$. [F3, F5, F11, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.8.2: 8.2 Fix $i$. The second factorization in (4)(ii) writes $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_i)q_i'$ where $q_i'$ is the product of the other $k-1$ simple reflections in $\Delta$. Thus $\ell_T(q_i')=k-1$, $R(\varepsilon_i)\le_T\sigma$, and $q_i'=R(\varepsilon_i)\sigma$. Since $c=\sigma v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-k$, $R(\varepsilon_i)c=q_i'v$ is reduced, so $q_i'\le_TR(\varepsilon_i)c$. It follows that $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\in F(q_i')$. The moved space $M(q_i')$ is exactly $\operatorname{span}\{\delta_j:j\ne i\}$: it is contained there because those are its reflection normals, and both dimensions are $k-1$. Hence $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\delta_j=0$ for $j\ne i$. Since $\varepsilon_i-\delta_i$ is a linear combination of $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{i-1}$, (1) gives $1=\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\varepsilon_i=\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\delta_i$. Thus the restrictions to $E$ of the functionals $B(\mu(\varepsilon_i),-)$ form the dual basis to $\Delta$. For $x=\sum_j a_j\delta_j$ with $a_j\ge0$, $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot x=a_i$; intersecting the cone with this zero hyperplane and with the unit sphere proves the wall equality, and the supporting hyperplane in $E$ is $E\cap\mu(\varepsilon_i)^\perp$. This proves (4)(iii). [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 7.2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.9.1: 9.1 If distinct positive roots $\rho_i,\rho_j$ satisfy $R(\rho_i)R(\rho_j)\le_Tc$, their product has reflection length $2$ and belongs to the rank-two case of step 8.1. Both roots lie in the corresponding $P_\sigma$ by moved-space rigidity. If $i<j$, the only increasing-order two-factorization in step 8.1 is the endpoint factorization, so $\rho_i\cdot\rho_j\le0$. If $i>j$, the factorization is one of the adjacent descending pairs, so $\rho_i\cdot\rho_j\ge0$. This proves (4)(v). [F3, F5, step 8.1]
proof_step_texts.10.1: 10.1 If $i<j$ and $\varepsilon_i>\varepsilon_j$, the factorization $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_k)\cdots R(\varepsilon_1)$ is reduced, and the pair-product fact of step 1.5 gives $R(\varepsilon_j)R(\varepsilon_i)\le_T\sigma\le_Tc$. The rank-two sign result of step 9.1 gives $\varepsilon_i\cdot\varepsilon_j\le0$. On the other hand, since distinct simple roots have nonpositive pairings by step 4.1, applying $R(\delta_{j-1}),\dots,R(\delta_{i+1})$ successively to $\delta_j$ yields a nonnegative combination of $\delta_{i+1},\dots,\delta_j$, and $\varepsilon_i\cdot\varepsilon_j=-\delta_i\cdot(R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_{j-1})\delta_j)\ge0$. Thus the pairing is zero, and the two reflections commute. Sorting the $\varepsilon_i$ into global order uses only swaps of such inverted commuting pairs, so the product is unchanged and $\sigma=R(\theta_k)\cdots R(\theta_1)$. [F3, step 4.1, step 7.2, step 1.5, step 9.1, algebra]

direct_paragraphs: Let $(W,S)$ be an irreducible Coxeter system of finite type with $S$ finite of cardinality $n\ge2$, with the data $\alpha_i$, $\beta_i$, $s_i$, $R_i$, $a$, $b$, $c$, $h$, $(\rho_i)$, $(\mu_i)$ and the linear map $\mu$ of [[def-cg-bipartite-coxeter-element-and-root-recursion]], and assume the conclusions of [[lem-cg-steinberg-bipartite-root-enumeration]] (so that $\Phi_+=\{\rho_1,\dots,\rho_{nh/2}\}$ and $\mu(\rho_i)=\mu_i$). Let $\ell_T$, $\le_T$, $M$, $F$ be reflection length, absolute order and the moved and fixed spaces, and let $P_\sigma:=\{\alpha\in\Phi_+:t_\alpha\le_T\sigma\}$ for $\sigma\le_Tc$, where $t_\alpha\in T$ is the reflection with normal $\alpha$ ([[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (1), [[def-cg-reflection-length-absolute-order-and-moved-space]], [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]]). Then:

facts.fact_text: [F6] On the positive-definite space $(V,B)$, $M(A)=F(A)^\perp$ for orthogonal $A$. For $U\subseteq M(A)$ there is a unique orthogonal restriction $A_U\le_{\mathrm O}A$ with moved space $U$, and every line $L$ is the moved space of the unique orthogonal reflection $\mathrm{id}-2\Pi_L$. For group elements, orthogonal order and reflection order agree by Carter's formula. [[lem-cg-orthogonal-wall-form-and-subspace-restriction]] (1),(3)-(5) [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]] (1),(2)

proof_step_texts.1.4: 1.4 Every reflection lies below $c$. Indeed, $M(c)=V$ by [F1]. For a positive root $\alpha$, the orthogonal reflection with moved line $\mathbb R\alpha$ is uniquely $r_\alpha=\rho(t_\alpha)$ by [F3],[F6]; the Wall restriction for this line is below $C=\rho(c)$ and has moved space $\mathbb R\alpha$. The Wall dimension identity and Carter's formula therefore give $t_\alpha\le_Tc$. [F1, F3, F5, F6]
proof_step_texts.2.3: 2.3 For any increasing tuple $a_1<\cdots<a_m$ of positive roots, one has $\ell_T(R(a_1)\cdots R(a_m)c)=n-m$ if and only if $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$ for all $i>j$. If $m=0$, the left side is $\ell_T(c)=n$ by [F1], and the zero-pairing condition is vacuous; hence assume $m\ge1$. Put $r_i=R(a_i)$. The length equality is equivalent to the reverse product $q=r_m\cdots r_1$ being a reduced element below $c$: its complement is $q^{-1}c=r_1\cdots r_m c$. In fact, if $\ell_T(q^{-1}c)=n-m$, then $\ell_T(q)\le m$ and $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(q)+\ell_T(q^{-1}c)\le n$, so both inequalities are equalities; the converse is the defining absolute-order equality. For the forward implication, the pair-product fact in step 1.5 gives $r_i r_j\le_Tc$ whenever $i>j$. Since $\ell_T(r_i c)=n-1$, this gives $r_j\le_Tr_i c$ from $\ell_T(r_j r_i c)=n-2$; hence $M(r_j)\subseteq M(r_i c)=F(r_i c)^\perp$. The vector $\mu(a_i)$ is a nonzero member of the one-dimensional fixed space $F(r_i c)$, so $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$. Conversely, suppose all these pairings vanish. The matrix $[\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j]$ is upper triangular with diagonal $1$ by (1), so both the $a_i$ and the $\mu(a_i)$ are linearly independent; in particular $m\le n$. Induct downward on $i$ to prove $q_i:=r_m\cdots r_i\le_Tc$ with length $m-i+1$. The base $q_m=r_m$ is step 1.4. If $q_{i+1}\le_Tc$, then each factor $r_j$ with $j>i$ satisfies $r_j\le_Tq_{i+1}$: writing a reduced factorization $q_{i+1}=x r_j y$, the product $r_jq_{i+1}=(r_jxr_j)y$ uses one fewer reflections, and the triangle inequality makes that expression reduced. Put $v=q_{i+1}^{-1}c$. Complement order reversal from step 1.5 gives $v\le_Tr_jc$, so $\mu(a_j)\in F(r_jc)\subseteq F(v)$ for every $j>i$. These $m-i$ independent vectors form a basis of $F(v)$, whose dimension is $m-i$ by Carter's formula. The assumed zero pairings give $a_i\in F(v)^\perp=M(v)$. The Wall restriction for the line $\mathbb Ra_i$ gives $r_i\le_Tv$; writing $v=r_i z$ then gives $c=q_{i+1}r_i z$, with lengths adding, so $q_i=q_{i+1}r_i\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(q_i)=m-i+1$. At $i=1$ this proves the claimed equivalence. The same argument applies to every subtuple because the vanishing conditions are inherited. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.4, step 1.5, algebra]

facts.fact_text: [F7] In a reduced reflection factorization $w=t_1\cdots t_m$, the prefix-conjugated root normals form a basis of $M(w)$. [[lem-cg-reflection-factorizations-and-independent-normals]] (3)

proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 For every $\sigma\le_Tc$, one has $P_\sigma=\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$. If $\alpha\in P_\sigma$, then $M(t_\alpha)=\mathbb R\alpha\subseteq M(\sigma)$ by [F5]. Conversely, if $\alpha\in\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$, then $t_\alpha\le_Tc$ by step 1.4 and $\sigma\le_Tc$, so moved-space rigidity in [F5] gives $t_\alpha\le_T\sigma$. Also $P_\sigma$ spans $M(\sigma)$: choose a reduced reflection factorization of $\sigma$; its prefix-conjugated normals are a basis of $M(\sigma)$ by [F7], and the reflections with those normals have moved lines in $M(\sigma)$, hence lie below $\sigma$ by the same common-upper-bound argument. Taking the positive sign of each normal puts a spanning set in $P_\sigma$. [F3, F5, F7, F8, step 1.4]

facts.fact_text: [F8] Every nonidentity $w$ has a reduced reflection factorization of length $\dim M(w)$; the factorization lemma also supplies a root normal in $M(w)$ for its induction step. [[lem-cg-reflection-factorizations-and-independent-normals]] (1)-(3)

facts.fact_text: [F3] $B$ is positive definite, every root has $B$-norm $1$, reflections act by $r_\alpha(x)=x-2B(x,\alpha)\alpha$, and $B(Cx,Cy)=B(x,y)$. For each positive root $\alpha$ there is a unique reflection $t_\alpha$ with $\rho(t_\alpha)=r_\alpha$; its moved space is $\mathbb R\alpha$. [[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]] (3) [[lem-cg-reflection-representation-descends-and-root-norms]] (2),(3) [[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (1) [[lem-cg-reflection-form-invariance-and-rank-two-orders]] (2)

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 For every $i\ge1$, [F2] gives $(C-\mathrm{id})\mu_i=-2\rho_i$. Since $C$ is an isometry and $B(\rho_i,\rho_i)=1$, $B(\mu_i,\rho_i)=1$ follows by expanding $B(C\mu_i,C\mu_i)=B(\mu_i-2\rho_i,\mu_i-2\rho_i)$. The same identity gives $C\mu_i=\mu_i-2\rho_i$, so $r_{\rho_i}C\mu_i=\mu_i$ and $\mu_i\in F(r_{\rho_i}C)$. For $1\le i\le n$, the reflection word $r_{\rho_i}C$ cancels to $R_1\cdots R_{i-1}R_{i+1}\cdots R_n$, so its reflection length is at most $n-1$; the triangle inequality and $\ell_T(c)=n$ give the lower bound $n-1$. Thus its fixed space is one-dimensional. Since $r_{\rho_{i+n}}C=C(r_{\rho_i}C)C^{-1}$, the same dimension holds for all $i$. The vector $\mu_i$ is nonzero because $\mu_i\cdot\rho_i=1$, and it is the unique vector in that line with this pairing. This proves (1). [F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.4: 1.4 Every reflection lies below $c$. Indeed, $M(c)=V$ by [F1]. For a positive root $\alpha$, the orthogonal reflection with moved line $\mathbb R\alpha$ is uniquely $r_\alpha=\rho(t_\alpha)$ by [F3],[F6]; the Wall restriction for this line is below $C=\rho(c)$ and has moved space $\mathbb R\alpha$. The Wall dimension identity and Carter's formula therefore give $t_\alpha\le_Tc$. [F1, F3, F5, F6]
proof_step_texts.1.5: 1.5 We use two elementary consequences of absolute order. First, if $w=r_1\cdots r_m$ is a reduced reflection factorization and $p<q$, then $r_pr_q\le_Tw$: distinct root-reflections have product moved space the two-plane spanned by their distinct normal lines, so their product has reflection length $2$ by Carter's formula. Write $w=xr_pyr_qz$; then $(r_pr_q)^{-1}w=r_qr_pxr_pyr_qz=(r_q(r_pxr_p)y r_q)z$, a product of $m-2$ reflections because conjugation preserves reflections. The triangle inequality forces this complement to have length $m-2$. Second, if $u\le_Tv\le_Tw$, then $v^{-1}w\le_Tu^{-1}w$: write $v=ux$, $w=vy$ with additive reflection lengths; then $u^{-1}w=xy$, while $y^{-1}xy$ has the same length as $x$, so $y\le_Txy$. These facts will be used below. [F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.6: 1.6 Put $E=M(\sigma)$ and $F=E^\perp$. Then $W_\sigma=\{w:M(w)\subseteq E\}$ is the pointwise stabilizer of $F$, because $M(w)=F(w)^\perp$. If $F\ne0$, choose $x\in F$ outside $\{0\}$ and every proper subspace $F\cap H_\alpha$; this is possible by [F9] and [F12]. By [F10], $\operatorname{Stab}_W(x)=gW_Ig^{-1}$ for some $g,I$. Each conjugate simple generator has a root hyperplane containing $x$, hence, by the choice of $x$, containing all of $F$; therefore every generator of this stabilizer fixes $F$ pointwise. Conversely every element fixing $F$ fixes $x$, so $W_\sigma=gW_Ig^{-1}$. If $F=0$, take $g=1$ and $I=S$. [F3, F5, F9, F10, F12]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 For every $\sigma\le_Tc$, one has $P_\sigma=\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$. If $\alpha\in P_\sigma$, then $M(t_\alpha)=\mathbb R\alpha\subseteq M(\sigma)$ by [F5]. Conversely, if $\alpha\in\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$, then $t_\alpha\le_Tc$ by step 1.4 and $\sigma\le_Tc$, so moved-space rigidity in [F5] gives $t_\alpha\le_T\sigma$. Also $P_\sigma$ spans $M(\sigma)$: choose a reduced reflection factorization of $\sigma$; its prefix-conjugated normals are a basis of $M(\sigma)$ by [F7], and the reflections with those normals have moved lines in $M(\sigma)$, hence lie below $\sigma$ by the same common-upper-bound argument. Taking the positive sign of each normal puts a spanning set in $P_\sigma$. [F3, F5, F7, F8, step 1.4]

These $m-i$ independent vectors form a basis of $F(v)$, whose dimension is $m-i$ by Carter's formula. The assumed zero pairings give $a_i\in F(v)^\perp=M(v)$. At $i=1$ this proves the claimed equivalence. The same argument applies to every subtuple because the vanishing conditions are inherited. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.4, step 1.5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.3.2: 3.2 Let $\Phi_I=\{\rho(u)\alpha_s:u\in W_I,s\in I\}$ be the intrinsic root system from [F14]; its representation is the restriction to $V_I=\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_s:s\in I\}$, since the reflection formulas agree. An ambient reflection $t\in T\cap W_I$ has a reduced $I$-expression by [F14]. Apply strong exchange to $tt=1$: it expresses $t$ as a prefix-conjugate of a letter of that expression, so its root normal belongs to $\pm\Phi_I$ by [F3]. Conversely every intrinsic root gives an ambient reflection in $W_I$. Conjugating by $g$, the root-reflection dictionary therefore identifies the roots of $gW_Ig^{-1}$ with precisely the ambient roots whose reflections fix $F$ pointwise, namely $\Phi\cap E=\pm P_\sigma$ by step 2.2. Their span is both $\rho(g)V_I$ and $E$, since $P_\sigma$ spans $E$. [F3, F14, step 2.2, step 1.6]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 Choose $f\in\mathcal C^\circ$ and project it orthogonally to $E$. Its pairing with every root of $P_\sigma$ is positive by [F4], so it avoids the subsystem arrangement. Apply [F10] to the finite Coxeter system $(W_I,I)$ and transfer its chambers to $E$ by $\rho(g)$. The chamber containing the projection has inward unit normals $\Delta=\{\rho(gu)\alpha_s:s\in I\}$ for some $u\in W_I$. These are a basis of $E$, their reflections are the conjugates of the simple generators of $W_I$, and their Gram matrix is the restricted Coxeter Gram matrix. In particular distinct normals have nonpositive pairings. By the root-sign theorem [F4] applied to this conjugate Coxeter system, its positive roots are exactly the roots positive on the projection, hence $P_\sigma$, and every such root is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$. This supplies the simple system and the Coxeter presentation used below. [F3, F4, F10, F14, step 3.2]
proof_step_texts.7.2: 7.2 Put $D_i:=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{i-1})$ and $\varepsilon_i:=D_i\delta_i$. The prefix $R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_i)$ has reflection length $i$ by the factorization of $\sigma$ and the triangle inequality, so this simple-generator word in the Coxeter system of $W_\sigma$ is reduced. The root-inversion formula [F13], applied to that parabolic system, gives $\varepsilon_i\in P_\sigma$, hence it is a positive root. Conjugation gives $R(\varepsilon_i)=D_iR(\delta_i)D_i^{-1}$; multiplying these identities and cancelling adjacent inverse prefixes yields $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_k)\cdots R(\varepsilon_1)$. Also $R(\varepsilon_i)D_iR(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)=D_iR(\delta_i)R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)=\sigma$. This proves (4)(ii). [F3, F5, F13, step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.8.1: 8.1 Suppose $\ell_T(\sigma)=2$ and $P_\sigma=\{\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_t\}$. By (4)(i), $\Delta=\{\tau_1,\tau_t\}$ and $\sigma=R(\tau_1)R(\tau_t)$. Step 4.1 realizes this as a canonical rank-two system. If its exponent is $m$, [F11] gives simple-root angle $\pi-\pi/m$ and a rotation of magnitude $2\pi/m$. Write its generators as $r,s$ and $q=rs$. The identities $rqr=q^{-1}$ and $s=rq$ reduce every word to $q^j$ or $q^jr$, $0\le j<m$; their distinct actions are the $m$ rotations and $m$ reflections in lines spaced by $\pi/m$. Every reflection is a conjugate of $r$ or $s$: the conjugates give respectively $q^{2j}r$ and $q^{2j-1}r$. The root-reflection dictionary thus gives $t=m$ positive roots, equally spaced between the simple-root rays. The global order agrees with angular order: a decrease after $\tau_r$ would put $\tau_{r+1}$ in the cone on earlier roots $\tau_1,\tau_r$, contrary to step 3.1. A product of reflections has rotation angle twice the difference of its normal angles, modulo $2\pi$; hence the two-reflection factorizations of $\sigma$ are exactly $R(\tau_1)R(\tau_t)=R(\tau_2)R(\tau_1)=\cdots=R(\tau_t)R(\tau_{t-1})$. These exhaust factorizations in $W$: if $\sigma=R(\alpha)R(\beta)$, then $M(\sigma)\subseteq\operatorname{span}(\alpha,\beta)$, and both spaces have dimension $2$, so the positive representatives of $\alpha,\beta$ lie in $P_\sigma$ by step 2.2. The endpoint angle gives $\tau_1\cdot\tau_t=-\cos(\pi/t)\le0$, while each adjacent angle gives $\tau_i\cdot\tau_{i+1}=\cos(\pi/t)\ge0$. [F3, F5, F11, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.8.2: 8.2 Fix $i$. The second factorization in (4)(ii) writes $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_i)q_i'$ where $q_i'$ is the product of the other $k-1$ simple reflections in $\Delta$. Thus $\ell_T(q_i')=k-1$, $R(\varepsilon_i)\le_T\sigma$, and $q_i'=R(\varepsilon_i)\sigma$. Since $c=\sigma v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-k$, $R(\varepsilon_i)c=q_i'v$ is reduced, so $q_i'\le_TR(\varepsilon_i)c$. It follows that $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\in F(q_i')$. The moved space $M(q_i')$ is exactly $\operatorname{span}\{\delta_j:j\ne i\}$: it is contained there because those are its reflection normals, and both dimensions are $k-1$. Hence $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\delta_j=0$ for $j\ne i$. Since $\varepsilon_i-\delta_i$ is a linear combination of $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{i-1}$, (1) gives $1=\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\varepsilon_i=\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\delta_i$. Thus the restrictions to $E$ of the functionals $B(\mu(\varepsilon_i),-)$ form the dual basis to $\Delta$. For $x=\sum_j a_j\delta_j$ with $a_j\ge0$, $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot x=a_i$; intersecting the cone with this zero hyperplane and with the unit sphere proves the wall equality, and the supporting hyperplane in $E$ is $E\cap\mu(\varepsilon_i)^\perp$. This proves (4)(iii). [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 7.2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.9.1: 9.1 If distinct positive roots $\rho_i,\rho_j$ satisfy $R(\rho_i)R(\rho_j)\le_Tc$, their product has reflection length $2$ and belongs to the rank-two case of step 8.1. Both roots lie in the corresponding $P_\sigma$ by moved-space rigidity. If $i<j$, the only increasing-order two-factorization in step 8.1 is the endpoint factorization, so $\rho_i\cdot\rho_j\le0$. If $i>j$, the factorization is one of the adjacent descending pairs, so $\rho_i\cdot\rho_j\ge0$. This proves (4)(v). [F3, F5, step 8.1]
proof_step_texts.10.1: 10.1 If $i<j$ and $\varepsilon_i>\varepsilon_j$, the factorization $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_k)\cdots R(\varepsilon_1)$ is reduced, and the pair-product fact of step 1.5 gives $R(\varepsilon_j)R(\varepsilon_i)\le_T\sigma\le_Tc$. The rank-two sign result of step 9.1 gives $\varepsilon_i\cdot\varepsilon_j\le0$. On the other hand, since distinct simple roots have nonpositive pairings by step 4.1, applying $R(\delta_{j-1}),\dots,R(\delta_{i+1})$ successively to $\delta_j$ yields a nonnegative combination of $\delta_{i+1},\dots,\delta_j$, and $\varepsilon_i\cdot\varepsilon_j=-\delta_i\cdot(R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_{j-1})\delta_j)\ge0$. Thus the pairing is zero, and the two reflections commute. Sorting the $\varepsilon_i$ into global order uses only swaps of such inverted commuting pairs, so the product is unchanged and $\sigma=R(\theta_k)\cdots R(\theta_1)$. [F3, step 4.1, step 7.2, step 1.5, step 9.1, algebra]
