supplier_uses.claim_note: Statement1 real basis/form;2 involution, B-invariance and fixed hyperplane for nonisotropic normal;3 Gram/complement/product. Finite exact order is on all V via fixed complement; infinite nilpotent formulas are explicitly on P.

facts.fact_text: [F3] $B$ is positive definite, every root has $B$-norm $1$, reflections act by $r_\alpha(x)=x-2B(x,\alpha)\alpha$, and $B(Cx,Cy)=B(x,y)$. For each positive root $\alpha$ there is a unique reflection $t_\alpha$ with $\rho(t_\alpha)=r_\alpha$; its moved space is $\mathbb R\alpha$. [[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]] (3) [[lem-cg-reflection-representation-descends-and-root-norms]] (2),(3) [[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (1) [[lem-cg-reflection-form-invariance-and-rank-two-orders]] (2)

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 For every $i\ge1$, [F2] gives $(C-\mathrm{id})\mu_i=-2\rho_i$. Since $C$ is an isometry and $B(\rho_i,\rho_i)=1$, $B(\mu_i,\rho_i)=1$ follows by expanding $B(C\mu_i,C\mu_i)=B(\mu_i-2\rho_i,\mu_i-2\rho_i)$. The same identity gives $C\mu_i=\mu_i-2\rho_i$, so $r_{\rho_i}C\mu_i=\mu_i$ and $\mu_i\in F(r_{\rho_i}C)$. For $1\le i\le n$, the reflection word $r_{\rho_i}C$ cancels to $R_1\cdots R_{i-1}R_{i+1}\cdots R_n$, so its reflection length is at most $n-1$; the triangle inequality and $\ell_T(c)=n$ give the lower bound $n-1$. Thus its fixed space is one-dimensional. Since $r_{\rho_{i+n}}C=C(r_{\rho_i}C)C^{-1}$, the same dimension holds for all $i$. The vector $\mu_i$ is nonzero because $\mu_i\cdot\rho_i=1$, and it is the unique vector in that line with this pairing. This proves (1). [F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.4: 1.4 Every reflection lies below $c$. Indeed, $M(c)=V$ by [F1]. For a positive root $\alpha$, the orthogonal reflection with moved line $\mathbb R\alpha$ is uniquely $r_\alpha=\rho(t_\alpha)$ by [F3],[F6]; the Wall restriction for this line is below $C=\rho(c)$ and has moved space $\mathbb R\alpha$. The Wall dimension identity and Carter's formula therefore give $t_\alpha\le_Tc$. [F1, F3, F5, F6]
proof_step_texts.1.5: 1.5 We use two elementary consequences of absolute order. First, if $w=r_1\cdots r_m$ is a reduced reflection factorization and $p<q$, then $r_pr_q\le_Tw$: distinct root-reflections have product moved space the two-plane spanned by their distinct normal lines, so their product has reflection length $2$ by Carter's formula. Write $w=xr_pyr_qz$; then $(r_pr_q)^{-1}w=r_qr_pxr_pyr_qz=(r_q(r_pxr_p)y r_q)z$, a product of $m-2$ reflections because conjugation preserves reflections. The triangle inequality forces this complement to have length $m-2$. Second, if $u\le_Tv\le_Tw$, then $v^{-1}w\le_Tu^{-1}w$: write $v=ux$, $w=vy$ with additive reflection lengths; then $u^{-1}w=xy$, while $y^{-1}xy$ has the same length as $x$, so $y\le_Txy$. These facts will be used below. [F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.6: 1.6 Put $E=M(\sigma)$ and $F=E^\perp$. Then $W_\sigma=\{w:M(w)\subseteq E\}$ is the pointwise stabilizer of $F$, because $M(w)=F(w)^\perp$. If $F\ne0$, choose $x\in F$ outside $\{0\}$ and every proper subspace $F\cap H_\alpha$; this is possible by [F9] and [F12]. By [F10], $\operatorname{Stab}_W(x)=gW_Ig^{-1}$ for some $g,I$. Each conjugate simple generator has a root hyperplane containing $x$, hence, by the choice of $x$, containing all of $F$; therefore every generator of this stabilizer fixes $F$ pointwise. Conversely every element fixing $F$ fixes $x$, so $W_\sigma=gW_Ig^{-1}$. If $F=0$, take $g=1$ and $I=S$. [F3, F5, F9, F10, F12]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 For every $\sigma\le_Tc$, one has $P_\sigma=\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$. If $\alpha\in P_\sigma$, then $M(t_\alpha)=\mathbb R\alpha\subseteq M(\sigma)$ by [F5]. Conversely, if $\alpha\in\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$, then $t_\alpha\le_Tc$ by step 1.4 and $\sigma\le_Tc$, so moved-space rigidity in [F5] gives $t_\alpha\le_T\sigma$. Also $P_\sigma$ spans $M(\sigma)$: choose a reduced reflection factorization of $\sigma$; its prefix-conjugated normals are a basis of $M(\sigma)$ by [F7], and the reflections with those normals have moved lines in $M(\sigma)$, hence lie below $\sigma$ by the same common-upper-bound argument. Taking the positive sign of each normal puts a spanning set in $P_\sigma$. [F3, F5, F7, F8, step 1.4]
proof_step_texts.2.3: 2.3 For any increasing tuple $a_1<\cdots<a_m$ of positive roots, one has $\ell_T(R(a_1)\cdots R(a_m)c)=n-m$ if and only if $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$ for all $i>j$. If $m=0$, the left side is $\ell_T(c)=n$ by [F1], and the zero-pairing condition is vacuous; hence assume $m\ge1$. Put $r_i=R(a_i)$. The length equality is equivalent to the reverse product $q=r_m\cdots r_1$ being a reduced element below $c$: its complement is $q^{-1}c=r_1\cdots r_m c$. In fact, if $\ell_T(q^{-1}c)=n-m$, then $\ell_T(q)\le m$ and $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(q)+\ell_T(q^{-1}c)\le n$, so both inequalities are equalities; the converse is the defining absolute-order equality. For the forward implication, the pair-product fact in step 1.5 gives $r_i r_j\le_Tc$ whenever $i>j$. Since $\ell_T(r_i c)=n-1$, this gives $r_j\le_Tr_i c$ from $\ell_T(r_j r_i c)=n-2$; hence $M(r_j)\subseteq M(r_i c)=F(r_i c)^\perp$. The vector $\mu(a_i)$ is a nonzero member of the one-dimensional fixed space $F(r_i c)$, so $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$. Conversely, suppose all these pairings vanish. The matrix $[\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j]$ is upper triangular with diagonal $1$ by (1), so both the $a_i$ and the $\mu(a_i)$ are linearly independent; in particular $m\le n$. Induct downward on $i$ to prove $q_i:=r_m\cdots r_i\le_Tc$ with length $m-i+1$. The base $q_m=r_m$ is step 1.4. If $q_{i+1}\le_Tc$, then each factor $r_j$ with $j>i$ satisfies $r_j\le_Tq_{i+1}$: writing a reduced factorization $q_{i+1}=x r_j y$, the product $r_jq_{i+1}=(r_jxr_j)y$ uses one fewer reflections, and the triangle inequality makes that expression reduced. Put $v=q_{i+1}^{-1}c$. Complement order reversal from step 1.5 gives $v\le_Tr_jc$, so $\mu(a_j)\in F(r_jc)\subseteq F(v)$ for every $j>i$. These $m-i$ independent vectors form a basis of $F(v)$, whose dimension is $m-i$ by Carter's formula. The assumed zero pairings give $a_i\in F(v)^\perp=M(v)$. The Wall restriction for the line $\mathbb Ra_i$ gives $r_i\le_Tv$; writing $v=r_i z$ then gives $c=q_{i+1}r_i z$, with lengths adding, so $q_i=q_{i+1}r_i\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(q_i)=m-i+1$. At $i=1$ this proves the claimed equivalence. The same argument applies to every subtuple because the vanishing conditions are inherited. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.4, step 1.5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.3.2: 3.2 Let $\Phi_I=\{\rho(u)\alpha_s:u\in W_I,s\in I\}$ be the intrinsic root system from [F14]; its representation is the restriction to $V_I=\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_s:s\in I\}$, since the reflection formulas agree. An ambient reflection $t\in T\cap W_I$ has a reduced $I$-expression by [F14]. Apply strong exchange to $tt=1$: it expresses $t$ as a prefix-conjugate of a letter of that expression, so its root normal belongs to $\pm\Phi_I$ by [F3]. Conversely every intrinsic root gives an ambient reflection in $W_I$. Conjugating by $g$, the root-reflection dictionary therefore identifies the roots of $gW_Ig^{-1}$ with precisely the ambient roots whose reflections fix $F$ pointwise, namely $\Phi\cap E=\pm P_\sigma$ by step 2.2. Their span is both $\rho(g)V_I$ and $E$, since $P_\sigma$ spans $E$. [F3, F14, step 2.2, step 1.6]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 Choose $f\in\mathcal C^\circ$ and project it orthogonally to $E$. Its pairing with every root of $P_\sigma$ is positive by [F4], so it avoids the subsystem arrangement. Apply [F10] to the finite Coxeter system $(W_I,I)$ and transfer its chambers to $E$ by $\rho(g)$. The chamber containing the projection has inward unit normals $\Delta=\{\rho(gu)\alpha_s:s\in I\}$ for some $u\in W_I$. These are a basis of $E$, their reflections are the conjugates of the simple generators of $W_I$, and their Gram matrix is the restricted Coxeter Gram matrix. In particular distinct normals have nonpositive pairings. By the root-sign theorem [F4] applied to this conjugate Coxeter system, its positive roots are exactly the roots positive on the projection, hence $P_\sigma$, and every such root is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$. This supplies the simple system and the Coxeter presentation used below. [F3, F4, F10, F14, step 3.2]
proof_step_texts.7.2: 7.2 Put $D_i:=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{i-1})$ and $\varepsilon_i:=D_i\delta_i$. The prefix $R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_i)$ has reflection length $i$ by the factorization of $\sigma$ and the triangle inequality, so this simple-generator word in the Coxeter system of $W_\sigma$ is reduced. The root-inversion formula [F13], applied to that parabolic system, gives $\varepsilon_i\in P_\sigma$, hence it is a positive root. Conjugation gives $R(\varepsilon_i)=D_iR(\delta_i)D_i^{-1}$; multiplying these identities and cancelling adjacent inverse prefixes yields $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_k)\cdots R(\varepsilon_1)$. Also $R(\varepsilon_i)D_iR(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)=D_iR(\delta_i)R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)=\sigma$. This proves (4)(ii). [F3, F5, F13, step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.8.1: 8.1 Suppose $\ell_T(\sigma)=2$ and $P_\sigma=\{\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_t\}$. By (4)(i), $\Delta=\{\tau_1,\tau_t\}$ and $\sigma=R(\tau_1)R(\tau_t)$. Step 4.1 realizes this as a canonical rank-two system. If its exponent is $m$, [F11] gives simple-root angle $\pi-\pi/m$ and a rotation of magnitude $2\pi/m$. Write its generators as $r,s$ and $q=rs$. The identities $rqr=q^{-1}$ and $s=rq$ reduce every word to $q^j$ or $q^jr$, $0\le j<m$; their distinct actions are the $m$ rotations and $m$ reflections in lines spaced by $\pi/m$. Every reflection is a conjugate of $r$ or $s$: the conjugates give respectively $q^{2j}r$ and $q^{2j-1}r$. The root-reflection dictionary thus gives $t=m$ positive roots, equally spaced between the simple-root rays. The global order agrees with angular order: a decrease after $\tau_r$ would put $\tau_{r+1}$ in the cone on earlier roots $\tau_1,\tau_r$, contrary to step 3.1. A product of reflections has rotation angle twice the difference of its normal angles, modulo $2\pi$; hence the two-reflection factorizations of $\sigma$ are exactly $R(\tau_1)R(\tau_t)=R(\tau_2)R(\tau_1)=\cdots=R(\tau_t)R(\tau_{t-1})$. These exhaust factorizations in $W$: if $\sigma=R(\alpha)R(\beta)$, then $M(\sigma)\subseteq\operatorname{span}(\alpha,\beta)$, and both spaces have dimension $2$, so the positive representatives of $\alpha,\beta$ lie in $P_\sigma$ by step 2.2. The endpoint angle gives $\tau_1\cdot\tau_t=-\cos(\pi/t)\le0$, while each adjacent angle gives $\tau_i\cdot\tau_{i+1}=\cos(\pi/t)\ge0$. [F3, F5, F11, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.8.2: 8.2 Fix $i$. The second factorization in (4)(ii) writes $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_i)q_i'$ where $q_i'$ is the product of the other $k-1$ simple reflections in $\Delta$. Thus $\ell_T(q_i')=k-1$, $R(\varepsilon_i)\le_T\sigma$, and $q_i'=R(\varepsilon_i)\sigma$. Since $c=\sigma v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-k$, $R(\varepsilon_i)c=q_i'v$ is reduced, so $q_i'\le_TR(\varepsilon_i)c$. It follows that $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\in F(q_i')$. The moved space $M(q_i')$ is exactly $\operatorname{span}\{\delta_j:j\ne i\}$: it is contained there because those are its reflection normals, and both dimensions are $k-1$. Hence $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\delta_j=0$ for $j\ne i$. Since $\varepsilon_i-\delta_i$ is a linear combination of $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{i-1}$, (1) gives $1=\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\varepsilon_i=\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\delta_i$. Thus the restrictions to $E$ of the functionals $B(\mu(\varepsilon_i),-)$ form the dual basis to $\Delta$. For $x=\sum_j a_j\delta_j$ with $a_j\ge0$, $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot x=a_i$; intersecting the cone with this zero hyperplane and with the unit sphere proves the wall equality, and the supporting hyperplane in $E$ is $E\cap\mu(\varepsilon_i)^\perp$. This proves (4)(iii). [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 7.2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.9.1: 9.1 If distinct positive roots $\rho_i,\rho_j$ satisfy $R(\rho_i)R(\rho_j)\le_Tc$, their product has reflection length $2$ and belongs to the rank-two case of step 8.1. Both roots lie in the corresponding $P_\sigma$ by moved-space rigidity. If $i<j$, the only increasing-order two-factorization in step 8.1 is the endpoint factorization, so $\rho_i\cdot\rho_j\le0$. If $i>j$, the factorization is one of the adjacent descending pairs, so $\rho_i\cdot\rho_j\ge0$. This proves (4)(v). [F3, F5, step 8.1]
proof_step_texts.10.1: 10.1 If $i<j$ and $\varepsilon_i>\varepsilon_j$, the factorization $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_k)\cdots R(\varepsilon_1)$ is reduced, and the pair-product fact of step 1.5 gives $R(\varepsilon_j)R(\varepsilon_i)\le_T\sigma\le_Tc$. The rank-two sign result of step 9.1 gives $\varepsilon_i\cdot\varepsilon_j\le0$. On the other hand, since distinct simple roots have nonpositive pairings by step 4.1, applying $R(\delta_{j-1}),\dots,R(\delta_{i+1})$ successively to $\delta_j$ yields a nonnegative combination of $\delta_{i+1},\dots,\delta_j$, and $\varepsilon_i\cdot\varepsilon_j=-\delta_i\cdot(R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_{j-1})\delta_j)\ge0$. Thus the pairing is zero, and the two reflections commute. Sorting the $\varepsilon_i$ into global order uses only swaps of such inverted commuting pairs, so the product is unchanged and $\sigma=R(\theta_k)\cdots R(\theta_1)$. [F3, step 4.1, step 7.2, step 1.5, step 9.1, algebra]

supplier_uses.claim_note: Statement1 relators/unique descent;2 all rho(w) preserve B;3 unit norm for all orbit roots;4 conjugation assumes invertible B-preserving g and gives rho(wsw^−1)=r_rho(w)e_s.

facts.fact_text: [F1] $\Phi_+=\{\rho_1,\dots,\rho_{nh/2}\}$ with the $\rho_i$ pairwise distinct and $\rho_{i+n}=C\rho_i$, $\mu_{i+n}=C\mu_i$ for all $i\ge1$, where $C:=\rho(c)$; $C-\mathrm{id}$ is invertible, $\mu(\rho_i)=\mu_i$, and $M(c)=V$. Hence $\ell_T(c)=n$. [[lem-cg-steinberg-bipartite-root-enumeration]] (1)-(4) [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]] (1)

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 For every $i\ge1$, [F2] gives $(C-\mathrm{id})\mu_i=-2\rho_i$. Since $C$ is an isometry and $B(\rho_i,\rho_i)=1$, $B(\mu_i,\rho_i)=1$ follows by expanding $B(C\mu_i,C\mu_i)=B(\mu_i-2\rho_i,\mu_i-2\rho_i)$. The same identity gives $C\mu_i=\mu_i-2\rho_i$, so $r_{\rho_i}C\mu_i=\mu_i$ and $\mu_i\in F(r_{\rho_i}C)$. For $1\le i\le n$, the reflection word $r_{\rho_i}C$ cancels to $R_1\cdots R_{i-1}R_{i+1}\cdots R_n$, so its reflection length is at most $n-1$; the triangle inequality and $\ell_T(c)=n$ give the lower bound $n-1$. The vector $\mu_i$ is nonzero because $\mu_i\cdot\rho_i=1$, and it is the unique vector in that line with this pairing. This proves (1). [F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.2: 1.2 For all $i,j\ge1$, $\mu_i\cdot\rho_j=-\mu_{j+n}\cdot\rho_i$. Indeed, $\rho_i=\tfrac12(\mu_i-C\mu_i)$ by [F2], so $-\mu_{j+n}\cdot\rho_i=-C\mu_j\cdot\tfrac12(\mu_i-C\mu_i)=\tfrac12(\mu_j-C\mu_j)\cdot\mu_i=\rho_j\cdot\mu_i$, using the isometry of $C$ and [F1]-[F2]. This is (2)(a). [F1, F2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.3: 1.3 Suppose $1\le i\le j\le nh/2$. If $i>n$, then $j>n$ and $C$-equivariance gives $\mu_i\cdot\rho_j=\mu_{i-n}\cdot\rho_{j-n}$. Repeating reduces to a first index at most $n$ while keeping both indices positive and ordered. For $i\le n$, $\mu_i=\beta_i$, and $\beta_i\cdot\rho_j$ is the coefficient of $\alpha_i$ in the positive root $\rho_j$; this is nonnegative by [F4]. Thus (2)(b) holds. [F1, F2, F4, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.4: 1.4 Every reflection lies below $c$. Indeed, $M(c)=V$ by [F1]. For a positive root $\alpha$, the orthogonal reflection with moved line $\mathbb R\alpha$ is uniquely $r_\alpha=\rho(t_\alpha)$ by [F3],[F6]; the Wall restriction for this line is below $C=\rho(c)$ and has moved space $\mathbb R\alpha$. The Wall dimension identity and Carter's formula therefore give $t_\alpha\le_Tc$. [F1, F3, F5, F6]
proof_step_texts.2.1: 2.1 To prove (2)(c), first reduce $i$ modulo $n$ using $C$-equivariance, which preserves $\mu_{i+t}\cdot\rho_i$, and assume $1\le i\le n$. If $i+t\le n$, then $\mu_{i+t}=\beta_{i+t}$ and $\rho_i=R_1\cdots R_{i-1}\alpha_i$ has no $\alpha_{i+t}$ coefficient, so the pairing is zero. If $i+t>n$, put $j=i+t-n$, so $1\le j<i$. By (2)(a), $\mu_{i+t}\cdot\rho_i=\mu_{j+n}\cdot\rho_i=-\mu_i\cdot\rho_j=-\beta_i\cdot\rho_j=0$, since $\rho_j$ is supported on $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_j$. Now if $1\le i<j\le nh/2$ and $j<i+n$, (2)(d) is (2)(c) with $t=j-i$; if $j\ge i+n$, (2)(a) and (2)(b) give $\mu_j\cdot\rho_i=-\mu_{i+n}\cdot\rho_j\le0$. This proves (2)(c)-(d). [F1, F2, F4, step 1.3, algebra]
proof_step_texts.2.3: 2.3 For any increasing tuple $a_1<\cdots<a_m$ of positive roots, one has $\ell_T(R(a_1)\cdots R(a_m)c)=n-m$ if and only if $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$ for all $i>j$. If $m=0$, the left side is $\ell_T(c)=n$ by [F1], and the zero-pairing condition is vacuous; hence assume $m\ge1$. Put $r_i=R(a_i)$. The length equality is equivalent to the reverse product $q=r_m\cdots r_1$ being a reduced element below $c$: its complement is $q^{-1}c=r_1\cdots r_m c$. In fact, if $\ell_T(q^{-1}c)=n-m$, then $\ell_T(q)\le m$ and $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(q)+\ell_T(q^{-1}c)\le n$, so both inequalities are equalities; the converse is the defining absolute-order equality. For the forward implication, the pair-product fact in step 1.5 gives $r_i r_j\le_Tc$ whenever $i>j$. The matrix $[\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j]$ is upper triangular with diagonal $1$ by (1), so both the $a_i$ and the $\mu(a_i)$ are linearly independent; in particular $m\le n$. Induct downward on $i$ to prove $q_i:=r_m\cdots r_i\le_Tc$ with length $m-i+1$. The base $q_m=r_m$ is step 1.4. If $q_{i+1}\le_Tc$, then each factor $r_j$ with $j>i$ satisfies $r_j\le_Tq_{i+1}$: writing a reduced factorization $q_{i+1}=x r_j y$, the product $r_jq_{i+1}=(r_jxr_j)y$ uses one fewer reflections, and the triangle inequality makes that expression reduced. Put $v=q_{i+1}^{-1}c$. Complement order reversal from step 1.5 gives $v\le_Tr_jc$, so $\mu(a_j)\in F(r_jc)\subseteq F(v)$ for every $j>i$. These $m-i$ independent vectors form a basis of $F(v)$, whose dimension is $m-i$ by Carter's formula. The assumed zero pairings give $a_i\in F(v)^\perp=M(v)$. The Wall restriction for the line $\mathbb Ra_i$ gives $r_i\le_Tv$; writing $v=r_i z$ then gives $c=q_{i+1}r_i z$, with lengths adding, so $q_i=q_{i+1}r_i\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(q_i)=m-i+1$. At $i=1$ this proves the claimed equivalence. The same argument applies to every subtuple because the vanishing conditions are inherited. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.4, step 1.5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.4.2: 4.2 In any such positive root subsystem with simple system $\Gamma$, its first root in the global order is a member of $\Gamma$. For if the first root $\eta$ were not simple, write $\eta=\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}b_\gamma\gamma$ with $b_\gamma\ge0$; each $\gamma$ is later than $\eta$, so (2)(d) gives $\mu(\gamma)\cdot\eta\le0$. Linearity of $\mu$ and (1) would give $1=\mu(\eta)\cdot\eta=\sum b_\gamma(\mu(\gamma)\cdot\eta)\le0$, impossible. Also the last root of $P_\sigma$ belongs to $\Delta$: otherwise it is a nonnegative combination of the earlier simple roots, contrary to step 3.1. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.6.1:
6.1 Let $q$ be the global index with $\delta_k=ho_q$ and put $
u=C\mu_q=\mu_{q+n}$. For every $ho_j\in P_\sigma$ one has $j\le q$ and, by (2)(a) and $C$-equivariance, $
u\cdotho_j=\mu_{q+n}\cdotho_j=-\mu_{j+n}\cdotho_{q+n}=-\mu_j\cdotho_q\le0$ by (2)(b); at $j=q$ this is $-1$. Since $\mu_q\in F(r c)$, conjugating by $C$ gives $
u\in F(c r)$; and $\ell_T(cr)=n-1$, so $F(cr)=\mathbb R
u$ and $M(cr)=
u^\perp$. Moreover $\sigma'\le_Tc r$: its complement is $\sigma'^{-1}cr=rvr$, of length $n-k$, while $\ell_T(cr)=n-1$; the lengths add to $n-1$. Hence $U:=M(\sigma')$ is contained in $E\cap
u^\perp$, and both have dimension $k-1$ because $
u\cdot\delta_k=-1$. Thus $U=E\cap
u^\perp$. The roots $P_{\sigma'}=\Phi_+\cap U$ span $U$ by step 2.2. Each is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$ and is orthogonal to $
u$; since $
u\cdot\delta_k=-1$ and $
u\cdot\delta_j\le0$ for every $j$, every root in $P_{\sigma'}$ is a combination only of the $\delta_j$ for which $
u\cdot\delta_j=0$. Those zero-pairing simple roots must span the $(k-1)$-space $U$, so they are exactly $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{k-1}$. They form a simple system for $P_{\sigma'}$. Induction gives $\sigma'=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{k-1})$ and proves the reverse selection at each rank. Therefore $\sigma=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_k)$. For each $i$, its prefix $p_i:=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_i)$ and complementary suffix $R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)$ multiply to $\sigma$ and have at most $i$ and $k-i$ reflections, so both lengths attain these bounds. Thus $M(p_i)$, contained in $\operatorname{span}(\delta_1,\dots,\delta_i)$, has dimension $i$ and equals that span. Since $\sigma R(\delta_k)\cdots R(\delta_{i+1})=p_i$, the induction shows that $\delta_i$ is the last root of $P_\sigma$ in this subspace. proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 For every $i\ge1$, [F2] gives $(C-\mathrm{id})\mu_i=-2\rho_i$. The same identity gives $C\mu_i=\mu_i-2\rho_i$, so $r_{\rho_i}C\mu_i=\mu_i$ and $\mu_i\in F(r_{\rho_i}C)$. For $1\le i\le n$, the reflection word $r_{\rho_i}C$ cancels to $R_1\cdots R_{i-1}R_{i+1}\cdots R_n$, so its reflection length is at most $n-1$; the triangle inequality and $\ell_T(c)=n$ give the lower bound $n-1$. Thus its fixed space is one-dimensional. Since $r_{\rho_{i+n}}C=C(r_{\rho_i}C)C^{-1}$, the same dimension holds for all $i$. The vector $\mu_i$ is nonzero because $\mu_i\cdot\rho_i=1$, and it is the unique vector in that line with this pairing. This proves (1). [F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]

For $i\le n$, $\mu_i=\beta_i$, and $\beta_i\cdot\rho_j$ is the coefficient of $\alpha_i$ in the positive root $\rho_j$; this is nonnegative by [F4]. Thus (2)(b) holds. [F1, F2, F4, algebra]

If $F\ne0$, choose $x\in F$ outside $\{0\}$ and every proper subspace $F\cap H_\alpha$; this is possible by [F9] and [F12]. By [F10], $\operatorname{Stab}_W(x)=gW_Ig^{-1}$ for some $g,I$. Each conjugate simple generator has a root hyperplane containing $x$, hence, by the choice of $x$, containing all of $F$; therefore every generator of this stabilizer fixes $F$ pointwise. Conversely every element fixing $F$ fixes $x$, so $W_\sigma=gW_Ig^{-1}$. If $F=0$, take $g=1$ and $I=S$. [F3, F5, F9, F10, F12]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 For every $\sigma\le_Tc$, one has $P_\sigma=\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$. If $\alpha\in P_\sigma$, then $M(t_\alpha)=\mathbb R\alpha\subseteq M(\sigma)$ by [F5]. Conversely, if $\alpha\in\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$, then $t_\alpha\le_Tc$ by step 1.4 and $\sigma\le_Tc$, so moved-space rigidity in [F5] gives $t_\alpha\le_T\sigma$. Also $P_\sigma$ spans $M(\sigma)$: choose a reduced reflection factorization of $\sigma$; its prefix-conjugated normals are a basis of $M(\sigma)$ by [F7], and the reflections with those normals have moved lines in $M(\sigma)$, hence lie below $\sigma$ by the same common-upper-bound argument. Taking the positive sign of each normal puts a spanning set in $P_\sigma$. [F3, F5, F7, F8, step 1.4]
proof_step_texts.2.3: 2.3 For any increasing tuple $a_1<\cdots<a_m$ of positive roots, one has $\ell_T(R(a_1)\cdots R(a_m)c)=n-m$ if and only if $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$ for all $i>j$. If $m=0$, the left side is $\ell_T(c)=n$ by [F1], and the zero-pairing condition is vacuous; hence assume $m\ge1$. Put $r_i=R(a_i)$. The length equality is equivalent to the reverse product $q=r_m\cdots r_1$ being a reduced element below $c$: its complement is $q^{-1}c=r_1\cdots r_m c$. In fact, if $\ell_T(q^{-1}c)=n-m$, then $\ell_T(q)\le m$ and $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(q)+\ell_T(q^{-1}c)\le n$, so both inequalities are equalities; the converse is the defining absolute-order equality. For the forward implication, the pair-product fact in step 1.5 gives $r_i r_j\le_Tc$ whenever $i>j$. Since $\ell_T(r_i c)=n-1$, this gives $r_j\le_Tr_i c$ from $\ell_T(r_j r_i c)=n-2$; hence $M(r_j)\subseteq M(r_i c)=F(r_i c)^\perp$. The vector $\mu(a_i)$ is a nonzero member of the one-dimensional fixed space $F(r_i c)$, so $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$. Conversely, suppose all these pairings vanish. The matrix $[\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j]$ is upper triangular with diagonal $1$ by (1), so both the $a_i$ and the $\mu(a_i)$ are linearly independent; in particular $m\le n$. Induct downward on $i$ to prove $q_i:=r_m\cdots r_i\le_Tc$ with length $m-i+1$. The base $q_m=r_m$ is step 1.4. If $q_{i+1}\le_Tc$, then each factor $r_j$ with $j>i$ satisfies $r_j\le_Tq_{i+1}$: writing a reduced factorization $q_{i+1}=x r_j y$, the product $r_jq_{i+1}=(r_jxr_j)y$ uses one fewer reflections, and the triangle inequality makes that expression reduced. Put $v=q_{i+1}^{-1}c$. Complement order reversal from step 1.5 gives $v\le_Tr_jc$, so $\mu(a_j)\in F(r_jc)\subseteq F(v)$ for every $j>i$. These $m-i$ independent vectors form a basis of $F(v)$, whose dimension is $m-i$ by Carter's formula. The assumed zero pairings give $a_i\in F(v)^\perp=M(v)$. The Wall restriction for the line $\mathbb Ra_i$ gives $r_i\le_Tv$; writing $v=r_i z$ then gives $c=q_{i+1}r_i z$, with lengths adding, so $q_i=q_{i+1}r_i\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(q_i)=m-i+1$. At $i=1$ this proves the claimed equivalence. The same argument applies to every subtuple because the vanishing conditions are inherited. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.4, step 1.5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.5.1: 5.1 We prove the recursive selection and the factorization $\sigma=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_k)$ by induction on $k$. For $k=1$, $W_\sigma$ has rank one, $P_\sigma$ has its single positive root $\delta_1$, and $\sigma=R(\delta_1)$. For $k>1$, order the simple roots increasingly; step 4.2 makes the last one $\delta_k=\tau_t$. Put $r=R(\delta_k)$. Since $r\le_T\sigma$, write $\sigma=ru$ with $\ell_T(u)=k-1$; then $\sigma':=\sigma r=rur$ has length $k-1$. Write $c=\sigma v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-k$. The identity $c=\sigma'(rv)$ and the bounds $\ell_T(rv)\le n-k+1$ and $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(\sigma')+\ell_T(rv)$ force $\ell_T(rv)=n-k+1$, so $\sigma'\le_Tc$. Also $\sigma'$ fixes $F$ pointwise, hence $M(\sigma')\subseteq E$. [F5, step 1.4, step 1.6, step 4.1, step 4.2]
proof_step_texts.6.1:

u=C\mu_q=\mu_{q+n}$. For every $ho_j\in P_\sigma$ one has $j\le q$ and, by (2)(a) and $C$-equivariance, $

u$ and $M(cr)=
u^\perp$. Moreover $\sigma'\le_Tc r$: its complement is $\sigma'^{-1}cr=rvr$, of length $n-k$, while $\ell_T(cr)=n-1$; the lengths add to $n-1$. Hence $U:=M(\sigma')$ is contained in $E\cap
u^\perp$, and both have dimension $k-1$ because $
u\cdot\delta_k=-1$. Thus $U=E\cap
u^\perp$. The roots $P_{\sigma'}=\Phi_+\cap U$ span $U$ by step 2.2. Each is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$ and is orthogonal to $
u$; since $

u\cdot\delta_j\le0$ for every $j$, every root in $P_{\sigma'}$ is a combination only of the $\delta_j$ for which $

Induction gives $\sigma'=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{k-1})$ and proves the reverse selection at each rank. Therefore $\sigma=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_k)$. For each $i$, its prefix $p_i:=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_i)$ and complementary suffix $R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)$ multiply to $\sigma$ and have at most $i$ and $k-i$ reflections, so both lengths attain these bounds. Thus $M(p_i)$, contained in $\operatorname{span}(\delta_1,\dots,\delta_i)$, has dimension $i$ and equals that span. Since $\sigma R(\delta_k)\cdots R(\delta_{i+1})=p_i$, the induction shows that $\delta_i$ is the last root of $P_\sigma$ in this subspace. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.3, step 2.2, step 5.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.7.1: 7.1 The other recursive description follows by considering the suffix $q_i:=R(\delta_i)\cdots R(\delta_k)$. The factorization in step 6.1 gives $\ell_T(q_i)=k-i+1$: its prefix and suffix factors together multiply to $\sigma$ of length $k$, and their lengths are bounded by their numbers of reflections, whose sum is $k$. Writing $p_i:=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{i-1})$, the same length equality forces $\ell_T(p_i)=i-1$, so $q_i^{-1}\sigma=q_i^{-1}p_iq_i$ has length $i-1$ and $q_i\le_T\sigma$. If $c=\sigma v$ as above, then $q_i^{-1}c=q_i^{-1}(R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{i-1}))q_i v$ has length at most $(i-1)+(n-k)=n-\ell_T(q_i)$; the triangle inequality forces equality, so $q_i\le_Tc$. Its moved space is $\operatorname{span}(\delta_i,\dots,\delta_k)$, since its factors fix the orthogonal complement of that span and its moved dimension is $k-i+1$. Thus $P_{q_i}=P_\sigma\cap M(q_i)$, and $\{\delta_i,\dots,\delta_k\}$ is a simple system for this subsystem: a root in the tail span has zero coefficients on $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{i-1}$ in its nonnegative $\Delta$-expansion. By step 4.2 the first root of $P_{q_i}$ is a simple root of this tail system; its first simple root is $\delta_i$. Finally $R(\delta_{i-1})\cdots R(\delta_1)\sigma=q_i$ by cancellation, so $\delta_i$ is the first root of $P_\sigma$ in the moved space in (4)(i), and $\delta_1=\tau_1$. This proves (4)(i). Step 4.1 realizes this as a canonical rank-two system. If its exponent is $m$, [F11] gives simple-root angle $\pi-\pi/m$ and a rotation of magnitude $2\pi/m$. Write its generators as $r,s$ and $q=rs$. The identities $rqr=q^{-1}$ and $s=rq$ reduce every word to $q^j$ or $q^jr$, $0\le j<m$; their distinct actions are the $m$ rotations and $m$ reflections in lines spaced by $\pi/m$. Every reflection is a conjugate of $r$ or $s$: the conjugates give respectively $q^{2j}r$ and $q^{2j-1}r$. The root-reflection dictionary thus gives $t=m$ positive roots, equally spaced between the simple-root rays. The global order agrees with angular order: a decrease after $\tau_r$ would put $\tau_{r+1}$ in the cone on earlier roots $\tau_1,\tau_r$, contrary to step 3.1. [F3, F5, F11, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]

proof_step_texts.11.1: 11.1 The tuple $\theta_1<\cdots<\theta_k$ has reverse product $\sigma\le_Tc$ of length $k$, so it is among the tuples in (4)(iv). If $\eta_r<\theta_r$, the $r$ independent roots $\eta_1,\dots,\eta_r$ all lie in that kernel, a contradiction. Hence $\eta_r\ge\theta_r$ for every $r$, which proves componentwise domination (4)(vi) and the lexicographic minimality in (4)(iv). No Choice is used. [F4, F5, step 8.2, step 2.3, step 2.1, step 10.1] ∎

facts.fact_text: [F6] On the positive-definite space $(V,B)$, $M(A)=F(A)^\perp$ for orthogonal $A$. For $U\subseteq M(A)$ there is a unique orthogonal restriction $A_U\le_{\mathrm O}A$ with moved space $U$, and every line $L$ is the moved space of the unique orthogonal reflection $\mathrm{id}-2\Pi_L$. For group elements, orthogonal order and reflection order agree by Carter's formula. facts.fact_text: [F10] For every nonzero point $x\in g\mathcal C_I$, its stabilizer is $gW_Ig^{-1}$. In a finite Coxeter system the chambers are translates of the simplicial fundamental chamber, whose inward unit normals are its simple roots. [[thm-cg-finite-chamber-tiling-and-coset-face-identification]] (1)-(3)

proof_step_texts.1.6: 1.6 Put $E=M(\sigma)$ and $F=E^\perp$. Then $W_\sigma=\{w:M(w)\subseteq E\}$ is the pointwise stabilizer of $F$, because $M(w)=F(w)^\perp$. If $F\ne0$, choose $x\in F$ outside $\{0\}$ and every proper subspace $F\cap H_\alpha$; this is possible by [F9] and [F12]. By [F10], $\operatorname{Stab}_W(x)=gW_Ig^{-1}$ for some $g,I$. Each conjugate simple generator has a root hyperplane containing $x$, hence, by the choice of $x$, containing all of $F$; therefore every generator of this stabilizer fixes $F$ pointwise. Conversely every element fixing $F$ fixes $x$, so $W_\sigma=gW_Ig^{-1}$. If $F=0$, take $g=1$ and $I=S$. [F3, F5, F9, F10, F12]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 Choose $f\in\mathcal C^\circ$ and project it orthogonally to $E$. Its pairing with every root of $P_\sigma$ is positive by [F4], so it avoids the subsystem arrangement. Apply [F10] to the finite Coxeter system $(W_I,I)$ and transfer its chambers to $E$ by $\rho(g)$. The chamber containing the projection has inward unit normals $\Delta=\{\rho(gu)\alpha_s:s\in I\}$ for some $u\in W_I$. These are a basis of $E$, their reflections are the conjugates of the simple generators of $W_I$, and their Gram matrix is the restricted Coxeter Gram matrix. In particular distinct normals have nonpositive pairings. By the root-sign theorem [F4] applied to this conjugate Coxeter system, its positive roots are exactly the roots positive on the projection, hence $P_\sigma$, and every such root is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$. This supplies the simple system and the Coxeter presentation used below. [F3, F4, F10, F14, step 3.2]

facts.fact_text: [F3] $B$ is positive definite, every root has $B$-norm $1$, reflections act by $r_\alpha(x)=x-2B(x,\alpha)\alpha$, and $B(Cx,Cy)=B(x,y)$. For each positive root $\alpha$ there is a unique reflection $t_\alpha$ with $\rho(t_\alpha)=r_\alpha$; its moved space is $\mathbb R\alpha$. [[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]] (3) [[lem-cg-reflection-representation-descends-and-root-norms]] (2),(3) [[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (1) [[lem-cg-reflection-form-invariance-and-rank-two-orders]] (2)

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 For every $i\ge1$, [F2] gives $(C-\mathrm{id})\mu_i=-2\rho_i$. Since $C$ is an isometry and $B(\rho_i,\rho_i)=1$, $B(\mu_i,\rho_i)=1$ follows by expanding $B(C\mu_i,C\mu_i)=B(\mu_i-2\rho_i,\mu_i-2\rho_i)$. The same identity gives $C\mu_i=\mu_i-2\rho_i$, so $r_{\rho_i}C\mu_i=\mu_i$ and $\mu_i\in F(r_{\rho_i}C)$. For $1\le i\le n$, the reflection word $r_{\rho_i}C$ cancels to $R_1\cdots R_{i-1}R_{i+1}\cdots R_n$, so its reflection length is at most $n-1$; the triangle inequality and $\ell_T(c)=n$ give the lower bound $n-1$. Thus its fixed space is one-dimensional. Since $r_{\rho_{i+n}}C=C(r_{\rho_i}C)C^{-1}$, the same dimension holds for all $i$. The vector $\mu_i$ is nonzero because $\mu_i\cdot\rho_i=1$, and it is the unique vector in that line with this pairing. This proves (1). [F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.4: 1.4 Every reflection lies below $c$. Indeed, $M(c)=V$ by [F1]. For a positive root $\alpha$, the orthogonal reflection with moved line $\mathbb R\alpha$ is uniquely $r_\alpha=\rho(t_\alpha)$ by [F3],[F6]; the Wall restriction for this line is below $C=\rho(c)$ and has moved space $\mathbb R\alpha$. The Wall dimension identity and Carter's formula therefore give $t_\alpha\le_Tc$. [F1, F3, F5, F6]
proof_step_texts.1.5: 1.5 We use two elementary consequences of absolute order. First, if $w=r_1\cdots r_m$ is a reduced reflection factorization and $p<q$, then $r_pr_q\le_Tw$: distinct root-reflections have product moved space the two-plane spanned by their distinct normal lines, so their product has reflection length $2$ by Carter's formula. Write $w=xr_pyr_qz$; then $(r_pr_q)^{-1}w=r_qr_pxr_pyr_qz=(r_q(r_pxr_p)y r_q)z$, a product of $m-2$ reflections because conjugation preserves reflections. The triangle inequality forces this complement to have length $m-2$. Second, if $u\le_Tv\le_Tw$, then $v^{-1}w\le_Tu^{-1}w$: write $v=ux$, $w=vy$ with additive reflection lengths; then $u^{-1}w=xy$, while $y^{-1}xy$ has the same length as $x$, so $y\le_Txy$. These facts will be used below. [F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.6: 1.6 Put $E=M(\sigma)$ and $F=E^\perp$. Then $W_\sigma=\{w:M(w)\subseteq E\}$ is the pointwise stabilizer of $F$, because $M(w)=F(w)^\perp$. If $F\ne0$, choose $x\in F$ outside $\{0\}$ and every proper subspace $F\cap H_\alpha$; this is possible by [F9] and [F12]. By [F10], $\operatorname{Stab}_W(x)=gW_Ig^{-1}$ for some $g,I$. Each conjugate simple generator has a root hyperplane containing $x$, hence, by the choice of $x$, containing all of $F$; therefore every generator of this stabilizer fixes $F$ pointwise. Conversely every element fixing $F$ fixes $x$, so $W_\sigma=gW_Ig^{-1}$. If $F=0$, take $g=1$ and $I=S$. [F3, F5, F9, F10, F12]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 For every $\sigma\le_Tc$, one has $P_\sigma=\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$. If $\alpha\in P_\sigma$, then $M(t_\alpha)=\mathbb R\alpha\subseteq M(\sigma)$ by [F5]. Conversely, if $\alpha\in\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$, then $t_\alpha\le_Tc$ by step 1.4 and $\sigma\le_Tc$, so moved-space rigidity in [F5] gives $t_\alpha\le_T\sigma$. Also $P_\sigma$ spans $M(\sigma)$: choose a reduced reflection factorization of $\sigma$; its prefix-conjugated normals are a basis of $M(\sigma)$ by [F7], and the reflections with those normals have moved lines in $M(\sigma)$, hence lie below $\sigma$ by the same common-upper-bound argument. Taking the positive sign of each normal puts a spanning set in $P_\sigma$. [F3, F5, F7, F8, step 1.4]
proof_step_texts.2.3: 2.3 For any increasing tuple $a_1<\cdots<a_m$ of positive roots, one has $\ell_T(R(a_1)\cdots R(a_m)c)=n-m$ if and only if $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$ for all $i>j$. If $m=0$, the left side is $\ell_T(c)=n$ by [F1], and the zero-pairing condition is vacuous; hence assume $m\ge1$. Put $r_i=R(a_i)$. The length equality is equivalent to the reverse product $q=r_m\cdots r_1$ being a reduced element below $c$: its complement is $q^{-1}c=r_1\cdots r_m c$. In fact, if $\ell_T(q^{-1}c)=n-m$, then $\ell_T(q)\le m$ and $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(q)+\ell_T(q^{-1}c)\le n$, so both inequalities are equalities; the converse is the defining absolute-order equality. For the forward implication, the pair-product fact in step 1.5 gives $r_i r_j\le_Tc$ whenever $i>j$. Since $\ell_T(r_i c)=n-1$, this gives $r_j\le_Tr_i c$ from $\ell_T(r_j r_i c)=n-2$; hence $M(r_j)\subseteq M(r_i c)=F(r_i c)^\perp$. The vector $\mu(a_i)$ is a nonzero member of the one-dimensional fixed space $F(r_i c)$, so $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$. Conversely, suppose all these pairings vanish. The matrix $[\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j]$ is upper triangular with diagonal $1$ by (1), so both the $a_i$ and the $\mu(a_i)$ are linearly independent; in particular $m\le n$. Induct downward on $i$ to prove $q_i:=r_m\cdots r_i\le_Tc$ with length $m-i+1$. The base $q_m=r_m$ is step 1.4. If $q_{i+1}\le_Tc$, then each factor $r_j$ with $j>i$ satisfies $r_j\le_Tq_{i+1}$: writing a reduced factorization $q_{i+1}=x r_j y$, the product $r_jq_{i+1}=(r_jxr_j)y$ uses one fewer reflections, and the triangle inequality makes that expression reduced. Put $v=q_{i+1}^{-1}c$. Complement order reversal from step 1.5 gives $v\le_Tr_jc$, so $\mu(a_j)\in F(r_jc)\subseteq F(v)$ for every $j>i$. These $m-i$ independent vectors form a basis of $F(v)$, whose dimension is $m-i$ by Carter's formula. The assumed zero pairings give $a_i\in F(v)^\perp=M(v)$. The Wall restriction for the line $\mathbb Ra_i$ gives $r_i\le_Tv$; writing $v=r_i z$ then gives $c=q_{i+1}r_i z$, with lengths adding, so $q_i=q_{i+1}r_i\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(q_i)=m-i+1$. At $i=1$ this proves the claimed equivalence. The same argument applies to every subtuple because the vanishing conditions are inherited. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.4, step 1.5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.3.2: 3.2 Let $\Phi_I=\{\rho(u)\alpha_s:u\in W_I,s\in I\}$ be the intrinsic root system from [F14]; its representation is the restriction to $V_I=\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_s:s\in I\}$, since the reflection formulas agree. An ambient reflection $t\in T\cap W_I$ has a reduced $I$-expression by [F14]. Apply strong exchange to $tt=1$: it expresses $t$ as a prefix-conjugate of a letter of that expression, so its root normal belongs to $\pm\Phi_I$ by [F3]. Conversely every intrinsic root gives an ambient reflection in $W_I$. Conjugating by $g$, the root-reflection dictionary therefore identifies the roots of $gW_Ig^{-1}$ with precisely the ambient roots whose reflections fix $F$ pointwise, namely $\Phi\cap E=\pm P_\sigma$ by step 2.2. Their span is both $\rho(g)V_I$ and $E$, since $P_\sigma$ spans $E$. [F3, F14, step 2.2, step 1.6]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 Choose $f\in\mathcal C^\circ$ and project it orthogonally to $E$. Its pairing with every root of $P_\sigma$ is positive by [F4], so it avoids the subsystem arrangement. Apply [F10] to the finite Coxeter system $(W_I,I)$ and transfer its chambers to $E$ by $\rho(g)$. The chamber containing the projection has inward unit normals $\Delta=\{\rho(gu)\alpha_s:s\in I\}$ for some $u\in W_I$. These are a basis of $E$, their reflections are the conjugates of the simple generators of $W_I$, and their Gram matrix is the restricted Coxeter Gram matrix. In particular distinct normals have nonpositive pairings. By the root-sign theorem [F4] applied to this conjugate Coxeter system, its positive roots are exactly the roots positive on the projection, hence $P_\sigma$, and every such root is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$. This supplies the simple system and the Coxeter presentation used below. [F3, F4, F10, F14, step 3.2]
proof_step_texts.7.2: 7.2 Put $D_i:=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{i-1})$ and $\varepsilon_i:=D_i\delta_i$. The prefix $R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_i)$ has reflection length $i$ by the factorization of $\sigma$ and the triangle inequality, so this simple-generator word in the Coxeter system of $W_\sigma$ is reduced. The root-inversion formula [F13], applied to that parabolic system, gives $\varepsilon_i\in P_\sigma$, hence it is a positive root. Conjugation gives $R(\varepsilon_i)=D_iR(\delta_i)D_i^{-1}$; multiplying these identities and cancelling adjacent inverse prefixes yields $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_k)\cdots R(\varepsilon_1)$. Also $R(\varepsilon_i)D_iR(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)=D_iR(\delta_i)R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)=\sigma$. This proves (4)(ii). [F3, F5, F13, step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.8.1: 8.1 Suppose $\ell_T(\sigma)=2$ and $P_\sigma=\{\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_t\}$. By (4)(i), $\Delta=\{\tau_1,\tau_t\}$ and $\sigma=R(\tau_1)R(\tau_t)$. Step 4.1 realizes this as a canonical rank-two system. If its exponent is $m$, [F11] gives simple-root angle $\pi-\pi/m$ and a rotation of magnitude $2\pi/m$. Write its generators as $r,s$ and $q=rs$. The identities $rqr=q^{-1}$ and $s=rq$ reduce every word to $q^j$ or $q^jr$, $0\le j<m$; their distinct actions are the $m$ rotations and $m$ reflections in lines spaced by $\pi/m$. Every reflection is a conjugate of $r$ or $s$: the conjugates give respectively $q^{2j}r$ and $q^{2j-1}r$. The root-reflection dictionary thus gives $t=m$ positive roots, equally spaced between the simple-root rays. The global order agrees with angular order: a decrease after $\tau_r$ would put $\tau_{r+1}$ in the cone on earlier roots $\tau_1,\tau_r$, contrary to step 3.1. A product of reflections has rotation angle twice the difference of its normal angles, modulo $2\pi$; hence the two-reflection factorizations of $\sigma$ are exactly $R(\tau_1)R(\tau_t)=R(\tau_2)R(\tau_1)=\cdots=R(\tau_t)R(\tau_{t-1})$. These exhaust factorizations in $W$: if $\sigma=R(\alpha)R(\beta)$, then $M(\sigma)\subseteq\operatorname{span}(\alpha,\beta)$, and both spaces have dimension $2$, so the positive representatives of $\alpha,\beta$ lie in $P_\sigma$ by step 2.2. The endpoint angle gives $\tau_1\cdot\tau_t=-\cos(\pi/t)\le0$, while each adjacent angle gives $\tau_i\cdot\tau_{i+1}=\cos(\pi/t)\ge0$. [F3, F5, F11, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.8.2: 8.2 Fix $i$. The second factorization in (4)(ii) writes $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_i)q_i'$ where $q_i'$ is the product of the other $k-1$ simple reflections in $\Delta$. Thus $\ell_T(q_i')=k-1$, $R(\varepsilon_i)\le_T\sigma$, and $q_i'=R(\varepsilon_i)\sigma$. Since $c=\sigma v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-k$, $R(\varepsilon_i)c=q_i'v$ is reduced, so $q_i'\le_TR(\varepsilon_i)c$. It follows that $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\in F(q_i')$. The moved space $M(q_i')$ is exactly $\operatorname{span}\{\delta_j:j\ne i\}$: it is contained there because those are its reflection normals, and both dimensions are $k-1$. Hence $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\delta_j=0$ for $j\ne i$. Since $\varepsilon_i-\delta_i$ is a linear combination of $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{i-1}$, (1) gives $1=\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\varepsilon_i=\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\delta_i$. Thus the restrictions to $E$ of the functionals $B(\mu(\varepsilon_i),-)$ form the dual basis to $\Delta$. For $x=\sum_j a_j\delta_j$ with $a_j\ge0$, $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot x=a_i$; intersecting the cone with this zero hyperplane and with the unit sphere proves the wall equality, and the supporting hyperplane in $E$ is $E\cap\mu(\varepsilon_i)^\perp$. This proves (4)(iii). [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 7.2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.9.1: 9.1 If distinct positive roots $\rho_i,\rho_j$ satisfy $R(\rho_i)R(\rho_j)\le_Tc$, their product has reflection length $2$ and belongs to the rank-two case of step 8.1. Both roots lie in the corresponding $P_\sigma$ by moved-space rigidity. If $i<j$, the only increasing-order two-factorization in step 8.1 is the endpoint factorization, so $\rho_i\cdot\rho_j\le0$. If $i>j$, the factorization is one of the adjacent descending pairs, so $\rho_i\cdot\rho_j\ge0$. This proves (4)(v). [F3, F5, step 8.1]
proof_step_texts.10.1: 10.1 If $i<j$ and $\varepsilon_i>\varepsilon_j$, the factorization $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_k)\cdots R(\varepsilon_1)$ is reduced, and the pair-product fact of step 1.5 gives $R(\varepsilon_j)R(\varepsilon_i)\le_T\sigma\le_Tc$. The rank-two sign result of step 9.1 gives $\varepsilon_i\cdot\varepsilon_j\le0$. On the other hand, since distinct simple roots have nonpositive pairings by step 4.1, applying $R(\delta_{j-1}),\dots,R(\delta_{i+1})$ successively to $\delta_j$ yields a nonnegative combination of $\delta_{i+1},\dots,\delta_j$, and $\varepsilon_i\cdot\varepsilon_j=-\delta_i\cdot(R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_{j-1})\delta_j)\ge0$. Thus the pairing is zero, and the two reflections commute. Sorting the $\varepsilon_i$ into global order uses only swaps of such inverted commuting pairs, so the product is unchanged and $\sigma=R(\theta_k)\cdots R(\theta_1)$. [F3, step 4.1, step 7.2, step 1.5, step 9.1, algebra]

proof_step_texts.1.3: 1.3 Suppose $1\le i\le j\le nh/2$. If $i>n$, then $j>n$ and $C$-equivariance gives $\mu_i\cdot\rho_j=\mu_{i-n}\cdot\rho_{j-n}$. Repeating reduces to a first index at most $n$ while keeping both indices positive and ordered. For $i\le n$, $\mu_i=\beta_i$, and $\beta_i\cdot\rho_j$ is the coefficient of $\alpha_i$ in the positive root $\rho_j$; this is nonnegative by [F4]. Thus (2)(b) holds. [F1, F2, F4, algebra]
proof_step_texts.2.1: 2.1 To prove (2)(c), first reduce $i$ modulo $n$ using $C$-equivariance, which preserves $\mu_{i+t}\cdot\rho_i$, and assume $1\le i\le n$. If $i+t\le n$, then $\mu_{i+t}=\beta_{i+t}$ and $\rho_i=R_1\cdots R_{i-1}\alpha_i$ has no $\alpha_{i+t}$ coefficient, so the pairing is zero. If $i+t>n$, put $j=i+t-n$, so $1\le j<i$. By (2)(a), $\mu_{i+t}\cdot\rho_i=\mu_{j+n}\cdot\rho_i=-\mu_i\cdot\rho_j=-\beta_i\cdot\rho_j=0$, since $\rho_j$ is supported on $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_j$. Now if $1\le i<j\le nh/2$ and $j<i+n$, (2)(d) is (2)(c) with $t=j-i$; if $j\ge i+n$, (2)(a) and (2)(b) give $\mu_j\cdot\rho_i=-\mu_{i+n}\cdot\rho_j\le0$. This proves (2)(c)-(d). proof_step_texts.6.1:
6.1 Let $q$ be the global index with $\delta_k=ho_q$ and put $
u=C\mu_q=\mu_{q+n}$. For every $ho_j\in P_\sigma$ one has $j\le q$ and, by (2)(a) and $C$-equivariance, $
u\cdotho_j=\mu_{q+n}\cdotho_j=-\mu_{j+n}\cdotho_{q+n}=-\mu_j\cdotho_q\le0$ by (2)(b); at $j=q$ this is $-1$. Since $\mu_q\in F(r c)$, conjugating by $C$ gives $
u\in F(c r)$; and $\ell_T(cr)=n-1$, so $F(cr)=\mathbb R
u$ and $M(cr)=
u^\perp$. Moreover $\sigma'\le_Tc r$: its complement is $\sigma'^{-1}cr=rvr$, of length $n-k$, while $\ell_T(cr)=n-1$; the lengths add to $n-1$. Hence $U:=M(\sigma')$ is contained in $E\cap
u^\perp$, and both have dimension $k-1$ because $
u\cdot\delta_k=-1$. Thus $U=E\cap
u^\perp$. The roots $P_{\sigma'}=\Phi_+\cap U$ span $U$ by step 2.2. Each is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$ and is orthogonal to $
u$; since $
u\cdot\delta_k=-1$ and $
u\cdot\delta_j\le0$ for every $j$, every root in $P_{\sigma'}$ is a combination only of the $\delta_j$ for which $
u\cdot\delta_j=0$. Those zero-pairing simple roots must span the $(k-1)$-space $U$, so they are exactly $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{k-1}$. They form a simple system for $P_{\sigma'}$. Induction gives $\sigma'=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{k-1})$ and proves the reverse selection at each rank. Therefore $\sigma=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_k)$. For each $i$, its prefix $p_i:=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_i)$ and complementary suffix $R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)$ multiply to $\sigma$ and have at most $i$ and $k-i$ reflections, so both lengths attain these bounds. Thus $M(p_i)$, contained in $\operatorname{span}(\delta_1,\dots,\delta_i)$, has dimension $i$ and equals that span. Since $\sigma R(\delta_k)\cdots R(\delta_{i+1})=p_i$, the induction shows that $\delta_i$ is the last root of $P_\sigma$ in this subspace. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.3, step 2.2, step 5.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.11.1: 11.1 The tuple $\theta_1<\cdots<\theta_k$ has reverse product $\sigma\le_Tc$ of length $k$, so it is among the tuples in (4)(iv). Let $\eta_1<\cdots<\eta_k$ be any other such tuple. By step 2.3 every prefix $\eta_1<\cdots<\eta_r$ also has reverse product below $c$ of length $r$, so its $r$ roots are linearly independent. For each $s\ge r$, every root $\tau\in P_\sigma$ with $\tau<\theta_r$ has $\mu(\theta_s)\cdot\tau=0$: its pairing is nonnegative because $\tau$ is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$ and the restricted pairing functionals $B(\mu(\varepsilon_i),-)|_E$ are dual to $\Delta$ by step 8.2, while it is nonpositive by (2)(d). The restrictions to $E$ of the $k-r+1$ functionals $\mu(\theta_r),\dots,\mu(\theta_k)$ are independent, again by the dual-basis property. Their common kernel in $E$ therefore has dimension $r-1$. If $\eta_r<\theta_r$, the $r$ independent roots $\eta_1,\dots,\eta_r$ all lie in that kernel, a contradiction. Hence $\eta_r\ge\theta_r$ for every $r$, which proves componentwise domination (4)(vi) and the lexicographic minimality in (4)(iv). No Choice is used. [F4, F5, step 8.2, step 2.3, step 2.1, step 10.1] ∎

facts.fact_text: [F6] $M(A)=\operatorname{im}(A-\mathrm{id})$, $F(A)=\ker(A-\mathrm{id})$ and $B\le_{\mathrm O}A$ holds if and only if $\dim M(A)=\dim M(B)+\dim M(B^{-1}A)$; no order property of $\le_{\mathrm O}$ is asserted by the definition. [[def-cg-reflection-length-absolute-order-and-moved-space]]

proof_step_texts.7.1: 7.1 Fix $U\subseteq M(A)$ and let $A_U$ be as in step 6.1. In the direct sum $V=M(A)\oplus F(A)$ of step 1.1 write $x=m+f$; then $(A-A_U)x=(A-\mathrm{id})m-H_U^{-1}\Pi_Um$, so $x\in\ker(A-A_U)$ exactly when $(A-\mathrm{id})m=H_U^{-1}\Pi_Um$. With $u:=\Pi_Um\in U$ this equation reads $m=S_AH_U^{-1}u$, and it is consistent because $\Pi_US_A\Pi_U=H_U$ is step 5.1: the solutions are exactly the $x=S_AH_U^{-1}u+f$ with $u\in U$ and $f\in F(A)$ arbitrary. Hence $\ker(A-A_U)=S_AH_U^{-1}(U)\oplus F(A)$ has dimension $\dim U+\dim F(A)$, so $\operatorname{rank}(A-A_U)=\dim M(A)-\dim U$. Since $A_U^{-1}A-\mathrm{id}=A_U^{-1}(A-A_U)$, the space $M(A_U^{-1}A)$ is the image of $A-A_U$ under $A_U^{-1}$ and has the same dimension $\operatorname{rank}(A-A_U)$; therefore $\dim M(A)=\dim U+\dim M(A_U^{-1}A)$, that is, $A_U\le_{\mathrm O}A$ by [F6]. [step 1.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, F1, F6, algebra]
proof_step_texts.7.2: 7.2 Let $B\le_{\mathrm O}A$ and put $C:=B^{-1}A$, so that $\dim M(A)=\dim M(B)+\dim M(C)$ by [F6]. Since $A-\mathrm{id}=(B-\mathrm{id})C+(C-\mathrm{id})$, one has $M(A)\subseteq M(B)+M(C)$, and comparing dimensions gives $M(A)=M(B)\oplus M(C)$; in particular $M(B)\subseteq M(A)$. Fix $w\in U:=M(B)$ and write $m:=S_Aw=m_B+m_C$ with $m_B\in M(B)$ and $m_C\in M(C)$; then $w=(A-\mathrm{id})m=(B-\mathrm{id})(Cm)+(C-\mathrm{id})m$ with $(B-\mathrm{id})(Cm)\in M(B)$ and $(C-\mathrm{id})m\in M(C)$, so comparing the two direct summands gives $Cm=m$ and $(B-\mathrm{id})m=w$. Hence $m-S_Bw\in F(B)=M(B)^\perp=U^\perp$, where the first equality uses step 1.1 applied to $B$; therefore for all $u,v\in U$ one has $\chi_A(u,v)=B(S_Au,v)=B(S_Bu,v)=\chi_B(u,v)$, because $S_Au-S_Bu\in U^\perp$. Thus the operator defined by $\chi_A$ on $U$ in step 5.1 is $H_U=S_B$, and the construction of step 6.1 for $A$ and $U$ gives $A_{M(B)}=\mathrm{id}+S_B^{-1}$ on $U$ and $\mathrm{id}$ on $U^\perp$, while $B=\mathrm{id}+S_B^{-1}$ on $U$ and $B=\mathrm{id}$ on $U^\perp=F(B)$ by step 1.1, so $B=A_{M(B)}$. [step 1.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, F6, algebra]
proof_step_texts.9.2: 9.2 Suppose $A=r_1\cdots r_m$ with $m=\dim M(A)$ and $B=r_1\cdots r_k$; the $r_i$ are involutions by step 2.2, so $B^{-1}A=r_{k+1}\cdots r_m$, whence $\dim M(B)\le k$ and $\dim M(B^{-1}A)\le m-k$ by step 8.2, while $\dim M(A)\le\dim M(B)+\dim M(B^{-1}A)$ by step 1.2; both inequalities are therefore equalities and $B\le_{\mathrm O}A$ by [F6]. [step 1.2, step 2.2, step 8.2, F6, algebra]
proof_step_texts.10.1: 10.1 Conversely, if $B\le_{\mathrm O}A$, write $B=r_1\cdots r_k$ with $k=\dim M(B)$ and $B^{-1}A=s_1\cdots s_l$ with $l=\dim M(B^{-1}A)$, both by the factorization clause of step 8.2; then $A=r_1\cdots r_ks_1\cdots s_l$ is a product of $k+l=\dim M(A)$ reflections by [F6], that is, a shortest factorization of $A$ by step 8.2, of which $B$ is the prefix of length $k$. [step 8.2, F6] ∎

Let $M$, $F$ and $\le_{\mathrm O}$ be as in [[def-cg-reflection-length-absolute-order-and-moved-space]]. Then:

**Given:** A finite-dimensional real inner product space $(V,B)$ with the positive definite Coxeter form of a finite-type Coxeter system, an element $A\in\mathrm O(V)$, and the moved space $M(A)=\operatorname{im}(A-\mathrm{id})$, the fixed space $F(A)=\ker(A-\mathrm{id})$ and the relation $\le_{\mathrm O}$ of [[def-cg-reflection-length-absolute-order-and-moved-space]].

facts.fact_text: [F5] $B$ is symmetric and bilinear, and positive definite: $B(u,u)\ge0$ with $B(u,u)=0$ only for $u=0$; consequently $B$ is nondegenerate, so $B(x,y)=0$ for all $y\in V$ implies $x=0$, and the same holds for the restriction of $B$ to any subspace. [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] [[thm-cg-finite-type-positive-definite-criterion]]

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 For $y\in V$ one has $B((A-\mathrm{id})x,y)=B(x,(A^{-1}-\mathrm{id})y)$ for all $x\in V$ by [F4], so $y\in M(A)^\perp$ holds exactly when $(A^{-1}-\mathrm{id})y=0$ and hence exactly when $A^{-1}y=y$, that is, when $y\in F(A^{-1})$; thus $M(A)^\perp=F(A^{-1})$. Since $A^{-1}y=y$ holds exactly when $Ay=y$, one has $F(A^{-1})=F(A)$, and $A^{-1}-\mathrm{id}=-A^{-1}(A-\mathrm{id})$ shows $M(A^{-1})=M(A)$. Consequently $M(A)^\perp=F(A)$, and [F2] gives $M(A)=M(A)^{\perp\perp}=F(A)^\perp$, $V=M(A)\oplus F(A)$ and $\dim M(A)+\dim F(A)=\dim V$. Moreover $A(A-\mathrm{id})=(A-\mathrm{id})A$, so $A(M(A))=M(A)$; and $A(F(A))\subseteq F(A)$ with equality because $A$ is injective. [F2, F4, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 Let $A\in\mathrm O(V)$ with $\dim M(A)=1$, put $L:=M(A)$ and let $\Pi_L$ be the orthogonal projection onto $L$ [F3]. By step 1.1 the line $L$ and the space $F(A)=L^\perp$ are $A$-stable, so $A$ fixes $L^\perp$ pointwise; for $0\ne u\in L$ one has $Au=cu$ with $c\in\mathbb R$, and since $A$ preserves $B$ by [F4] and $B(u,u)\ne0$ by [F5], $c^2B(u,u)=B(Au,Au)=B(u,u)$ forces $c^2=1$, while $c=1$ would put $u\in L\cap F(A)=\{0\}$; hence $c=-1$ and $A=\mathrm{id}-2\Pi_L$. Conversely if $L$ is a line then $A':=\mathrm{id}-2\Pi_L$ acts as $-1$ on $L$ and as the identity on $L^\perp$, so it preserves $B$ and is invertible, and $M(A')=L$ has dimension one; if $A'\in\mathrm O(V)$ is a reflection with $M(A')=L$, the first part applied to $A'$ gives $A'=\mathrm{id}-2\Pi_L$. Hence every line $L\subseteq V$ is the moved space of exactly one reflection of $\mathrm O(V)$, namely $\mathrm{id}-2\Pi_L$. [step 1.1, F3, F4, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.3.1: 3.1 Applying step 2.1 to the orthogonal element $A^{-1}$, whose moved space is $M(A)$ by step 1.1, gives the bijection $T_A:=((A^{-1}-\mathrm{id})|_{M(A)})^{-1}:M(A)\to M(A)$. For $u,v\in M(A)$ put $w:=S_Au$ and $z:=T_Av$, so that $(A-\mathrm{id})w=u$ and $(A^{-1}-\mathrm{id})z=v$; then $B(S_Au,v)=B(w,(A^{-1}-\mathrm{id})z)=B(w,A^{-1}z)-B(w,z)=B(Aw,z)-B(w,z)=B((A-\mathrm{id})w,z)=B(u,T_Av)$, using [F4] and symmetry of $B$. Moreover $A^{-1}-\mathrm{id}=-A^{-1}(A-\mathrm{id})$ on the $A$-stable space $M(A)$, so the inverse there is $T_A=-S_AA$ and $S_A+T_A=S_A(\mathrm{id}-A)=-((A-\mathrm{id})|_{M(A)})^{-1}(A-\mathrm{id})|_{M(A)}=-\mathrm{id}_{M(A)}$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F4, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 The Wall form $\chi_A(u,v)=B(S_Au,v)$ is bilinear on $M(A)$, and for $u,v\in M(A)$ the transpose identity of step 3.1 gives $B(S_Av,u)=B(v,T_Au)=B(T_Au,v)$, so $\chi_A(u,v)+\chi_A(v,u)=B(S_Au,v)+B(T_Au,v)=B((S_A+T_A)u,v)=-B(u,v)$. If $\chi_A(u,v)=0$ for all $v\in M(A)$, then $B(S_Au,\cdot)$ vanishes on $M(A)$ and, since $S_Au\in M(A)=F(A)^\perp$, also on $F(A)$, hence on $V$; by [F5] $S_Au=0$, and $S_A$ is injective, so $u=0$: the form $\chi_A$ is nondegenerate, and its symmetric part is $\tfrac12(\chi_A(u,v)+\chi_A(v,u))=-\tfrac12B(u,v)$ on $M(A)$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, F4, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.5.1: 5.1 Let $U\subseteq M(A)$ and define $H_U:=\Pi_US_A|_U:U\to U$. For $u,v\in U$, [F3] gives $B(H_Uu,v)=B(S_Au,v)=\chi_A(u,v)$; if another operator has these pairings, its difference from $H_U$ pairs to zero with every $v\in U$, so it equals $H_U$ by [F5]. Define $H_U^t:=\Pi_UT_A|_U$, with $T_A$ from step 3.1. That step and [F3] give $B(H_U^tu,v)=B(T_Au,v)=B(u,S_Av)=B(u,H_Uv)$, so $H_U^t$ is the adjoint $H_U^*$ of [[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]. Since $S_A+T_A=-\mathrm{id}_{M(A)}$, compression to $U$ gives $H_U+H_U^t=-\mathrm{id}_U$. If $H_Uu=0$, then $0=B(H_Uu,u)=\chi_A(u,u)=-\tfrac12B(u,u)$ by step 4.1, hence $u=0$; thus $H_U$ is injective and invertible by [F1], including when $U=0$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.6.1: 6.1 Define $A_U\in\operatorname{End}(V)$ by $A_Uu=u+H_U^{-1}u$ for $u\in U$ and $A_U=\mathrm{id}$ on $U^\perp$; this is well defined and linear because $V=U\oplus U^\perp$ [F2]. Then $A_U-\mathrm{id}=H_U^{-1}\Pi_U$ has image $U$, so $M(A_U)=U$ and $(A_U-\mathrm{id})|_U^{-1}=H_U$. Put $T:=H_U^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}(U)$ and $T^t:=(H_U^t)^{-1}$; inverting the transpose relation of step 5.1 shows that $T^t$ is the transpose of $T$, that is, $B(Tx,y)=B(x,T^ty)$ for all $x,y\in U$. Multiplying $H_U+H_U^t=-\mathrm{id}_U$ on the left by $T$ and on the right by $T^t$, and also on the left by $T^t$ and on the right by $T$, gives $T+T^t=-TT^t=-T^tT$, hence $(\mathrm{id}+T)(\mathrm{id}+T^t)=\mathrm{id}_U=(\mathrm{id}+T^t)(\mathrm{id}+T)$. Therefore $B(A_Uu,A_Uv)=B((\mathrm{id}+T^t)(\mathrm{id}+T)u,v)=B(u,v)$ for all $u,v\in U$, the transpose of $\mathrm{id}+T$ being $\mathrm{id}+T^t$; on $U^\perp$ the operator $A_U$ is the identity, and $U\perp U^\perp$, so $A_U$ preserves $B$ on $V$. If $A_Ux=0$, then $B(x,y)=B(A_Ux,A_Uy)=0$ for every $y\in V$, so $x=0$ by [F5] and $A_U$ is injective, hence invertible by [F1]: thus $A_U\in\mathrm O(V)$. [step 5.1, F1, F2, F5, algebra]

contract_anchors.quote:
Fix the following definitions and conventions for this page.

**(1) Models.** $\mathbb E^2$ is $\mathbb R^2$ with the Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). The comparison sphere is $S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$ with the round metric $d_S(x,y):=\arccos(x\cdot y)$ ([[def-cg-spherical-gram-simplex-and-angular-link]], [[def-principal-inverse-sine-and-cosine]]); more generally $d_S(x,y):=\arccos(x\cdot y)$ is defined on every sphere $S^{n-1}$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]).

**(2) Geodesic triangles and comparison.** A geodesic triangle in a metric space $X$ consists of three points $p,q,r\in X$ and a choice of geodesic segments $[p,q]$, $[q,r]$, $[r,p]$ joining them ([[def-geodesic-and-geodesic-metric-space]]); its perimeter is $d(p,q)+d(q,r)+d(r,p)$. A comparison triangle for it in $\mathbb E^2$, or in $S^2$ when its perimeter is $<2\pi$, is a triangle $(\bar p,\bar q,\bar r)$ in that model with the same three side lengths; it is unique up to an isometry of the model ([[lem-cg-comparison-convexity-and-model-spaces]]). For an occurrence of a point $x$ on a specified chosen side, the comparison point $\bar x$ is the point of the corresponding side of the comparison triangle at the same distance from the corresponding vertex; a vertex corresponds to itself. If a point belongs to more than one side, each side occurrence has its own comparison point, and the CAT inequalities quantify over every pair of side occurrences.

**(3) The CAT inequalities.** A metric space $X$ is **CAT(0)** if it is geodesic and for every geodesic triangle in $X$ and all points $x,y$ of that triangle, $d(x,y)\le d_2(\bar x,\bar y)$. It is **CAT(1)** if every pair of points of $X$ at distance $<D_1:=\pi$ is joined by a geodesic segment in $X$, and every geodesic triangle in $X$ of perimeter $<2\pi$ satisfies $d(x,y)\le d_S(\bar x,\bar y)$ for all points $x,y$ of the triangle. Thus for CAT(1) only triangles of perimeter $<2\pi$ are tested, and geodesic segments are demanded only for pairs at distance $<\pi$; a triangle of perimeter $<2\pi$ has all sides $<\pi$, so its sides are available by hypothesis. A metric space is **locally CAT(0)**, equivalently of curvature $\le0$, if every point has a closed ball $\bar B(x,r)$, $r>0$, such that the induced metric on $\bar B(x,r)$ is CAT(0); **locally CAT(1)** is defined in the same way.

**(4) Truncated angular metrics on links.** Let $F$ be a face of an isometric polyhedral gluing with its chain metric ([[def-cg-abstract-isometric-polyhedral-gluing-and-chain-metric]]) and let $L:=\operatorname{Lk}_X(F)$ be its angular link with the auxiliary extended componentwise path metric $d_{\mathrm{path}}$ and the finite angular metric $d_\pi:=\min\{\pi,d_{\mathrm{path}}\}$ ([[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]], [[lem-cg-spherical-simplex-existence-and-link-gram-formula]]). Then every $d_\pi$-triangle of perimeter $<2\pi$ has all sides $<\pi$: if one side were $\pi$, the triangle inequality would make the perimeter at least $2\pi$. Thus its vertices lie in one intrinsic component of $L$, and its side lengths equal the untruncated intrinsic path distances. It also holds between any two side points: the shorter of the two boundary routes has length at most half the perimeter, hence $<\pi$, so their truncated distance is $<\pi$ and equals their intrinsic path distance. Hence the CAT(1) tests in $(L,d_\pi)$ of perimeter $<2\pi$ agree with componentwise intrinsic tests ([[thm-cg-cone-join-metric-and-local-product-chart]]). The empty metric space carries no triangles and satisfies the CAT(0) and CAT(1) tests vacuously; a one-point space is CAT(0) and CAT(1). With the conventions $C(\varnothing)=\{o\}$ and $L*\varnothing=L$ ([[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]]), the empty link satisfies the CAT(1) tests vacuously and its cone is a point.

**(5) Local geodesics.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval. A map $c:I\to X$ is a **constant-speed local geodesic** if there is a fixed $\lambda\ge0$ such that for every $t\in I$ some $\varepsilon>0$ satisfies $d(c(t'),c(t''))=\lambda|t'-t''|$ whenever $t',t''\in(t-\varepsilon,t+\varepsilon)\cap I$. Here $\lambda$ is its speed; $\lambda=1$ is the unit-speed convention and $\lambda=0$ gives the constant paths. In this chapter “local geodesic” includes these linear reparametrizations. It is a **minimizing geodesic** precisely when the same distance equality holds for every pair $t',t''\in I$.

**(6) Length.** A continuous path $\gamma:[a,b]\to X$ has length $L(\gamma)\in[0,\infty]$, the supremum of its polygonal sums, and is rectifiable if $L(\gamma)<\infty$ ([[lem-cg-metric-target-length-reparametrization-and-lower-semicontinuity]], [[def-upper-bound]]). $X$ is a **length space** if for all $x,y\in X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a path from $x$ to $y$ of length $<d(x,y)+\varepsilon$.

**(7) Round circles.** For $\ell>0$ let $S^1_\ell:=\mathbb R/\ell\mathbb Z$ be the circle of circumference $\ell$, with $d_\ell(x,y):=\min\{|x-y+k\ell|:k\in\mathbb Z\}$; for $\ell=2\pi$ this is the unit circle. An **isometrically embedded circle of length $\ell$** in a metric space $X$ is an isometric embedding $S^1_\ell\to X$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]); its image is a subset of $X$ isometric to $(S^1_\ell,d_\ell)$.

consumed_current_paragraphs.text: Let $X$ be compact and locally CAT(1), and let $l$, $n\ge3$ and $h<l$ be as in [[def-cg-cyclic-small-mesh-polygon-and-midpoint-energy]]. Then:

[F1] [[def-cg-cyclic-small-mesh-polygon-and-midpoint-energy]]: $l$ is a uniform local CAT(1) radius when all closed balls of radius at most $l$ are CAT(1); for $\operatorname{mesh}(x)<l$ consecutive vertices are joined by a unique geodesic inside $B(x_i,l)$ and $f(x)_i=\operatorname{mid}(x_i,x_{i+1})$; $P_h(n)=\{x\in X^n:\operatorname{mesh}(x)\le h\}$; $C^0_h(n)=\{x\in P_h(n):\lim_kL(f^kx)=0\}$; a constant tuple has $\operatorname{mesh}=L=E=0$ and is fixed by $f$, and a degenerate pair has midpoint the point itself.

contract_anchors.quote:
Let $X$ be a compact locally CAT(1) metric space ([[def-cg-cat-zero-cat-one-and-local-geodesic]], [[def-metric-compactness]]).

**(1) Uniform local CAT(1) radius.** A real number $l>0$ is a **uniform local CAT(1) radius** for $X$ if every closed ball $\bar B(x,r)\subseteq X$ with $x\in X$ and $0<r\le l$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), with the induced metric, is a CAT(1) space. Such an $l$ exists and may be chosen with $l<\pi/2$ ([[cor-pi-is-the-first-positive-sine-zero]]); the existence proof is part of [[lem-cg-polygon-midpoint-drop-and-equality]] and is not asserted by this definition. Fix such an $l$ for the remainder of the page.

**(2) Cyclic tuples, mesh, length, energy.** Fix an integer $n\ge3$ and a real $h$ with $0<h<l$. For a tuple $x=(x_0,\dots,x_{n-1})\in X^n$ the indices are read modulo $n$, and
$$\operatorname{mesh}(x):=\max_{0\le i<n}d(x_i,x_{i+1}),\qquad L(x):=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}d(x_i,x_{i+1}),\qquad E(x):=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}d(x_i,x_{i+1})^2 .$$
The **mesh-$h$ polygon space** is $P_h(n):=\{x\in X^n:\operatorname{mesh}(x)\le h\}$; its points are called **cyclic small-mesh polygons**. Fixing $n$ (rather than letting the vertex count grow) is essential: the quantitative constants of this page depend on $n$ but not on $h$, and they are not uniform in a variable vertex count.

**(3) The midpoint operation.** For $x\in X^n$ with $\operatorname{mesh}(x)<l$, consecutive vertices satisfy $d(x_i,x_{i+1})<l<\pi/2$, and the closed ball $\bar B(x_i,l)$ is CAT(1); by the convexity and uniqueness clause for balls of radius $<\pi/2$ ([[lem-cg-comparison-convexity-and-model-spaces]]) the geodesic segment $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ inside that ball is unique ([[def-geodesic-and-geodesic-metric-space]]) and has a unique midpoint. Define $f(x)\in X^n$ by $f(x)_i:=\operatorname{mid}(x_i,x_{i+1})$ for $0\le i<n$. Continuity of $f$ on $\{\operatorname{mesh}<l\}$ and the invariance $\operatorname{mesh}(fx)\le\operatorname{mesh}(x)$, which make $f$ a self-map of $P_h(n)$, are proved in [[lem-cg-polygon-midpoint-drop-and-equality]]. Write $f^k$ for the $k$-fold iterate.

**(4) The zero-limit basin.** $C^0_h(n):=\{x\in P_h(n): f^k(x)\text{ is defined for every }k\ge0\text{ and }\lim_{k\to\infty}L(f^k x)=0\}$ ([[def-real-limit]]). By (3) the definability condition is automatic on $P_h(n)$, so $C^0_h(n)=\{x\in P_h(n):\lim_k L(f^k x)=0\}$; this set is the **zero-limit basin**. It is defined purely through the iterated lengths, without reference to short-loop homotopy; its identification with a short-loop class is proved later on this page, after its topological properties are established.

**(5) Conventions.** A tuple is **constant** if all its entries are equal; a constant tuple has $\operatorname{mesh}=L=E=0$ and is fixed by $f$ (the midpoint of a degenerate segment is its point, in accordance with [[def-geodesic-and-geodesic-metric-space]]). If some consecutive vertices coincide while the tuple is not constant, the corresponding edge contributes $0$ to mesh, length and energy, and the midpoint operation is applied to the (possibly degenerate) pair by the same rule.

contract_anchors.quote:
Let $X$ be a CAT(1) space ([[def-cg-cat-zero-cat-one-and-local-geodesic]]). Then:

**(i) Unique short geodesics.** Every two points $p,q\in X$ with $d(p,q)<\pi$ are joined by exactly one geodesic segment up to reparametrization ([[def-geodesic-and-geodesic-metric-space]]); moreover the segment depends continuously on its endpoints: if $p_k\to p$, $q_k\to q$ and $d(p,q)<\pi$, then the linear parametrizations of $[p_k,q_k]$ converge uniformly to the linear parametrization of $[p,q]$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]).

**(ii) Local geodesics of length at most $\pi$ are geodesics.** If $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval ([[def-interval]]) and $c\colon I\to X$ is a constant-speed local geodesic of speed $\lambda\ge0$ with $L(c)\le\pi$, then $d(c(s),c(t))=\lambda|s-t|$ for all $s,t\in I$. Here, for an arbitrary interval, $L(c)$ means the supremum of the lengths on its nonempty compact subintervals, with value $0$ for an empty interval. Every compact restriction, after translation and arclength reparametrization when $\lambda>0$, is a geodesic segment; speed zero gives a constant map.

**(iii) Closed local geodesics are at least $2\pi$ long.** If $c\colon S^1_\ell\to X$ is a nonconstant closed local geodesic (i.e. it is locally isometric and parametrized by arclength, as in [[def-cg-cat-zero-cat-one-and-local-geodesic]]), then $\ell\ge2\pi$; and the image of $c$ has diameter at least $\pi$. Consequently no nonconstant closed local geodesic is contained in a ball of diameter $<\pi$ ([[def-metric-ball]]).

consumed_current_paragraphs.text: [F4] [[lem-cg-comparison-convexity-and-model-spaces]]: comparison triangles of perimeter $<2\pi$ exist in $S^2$; the spherical cosine rule $\cos c=\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b\cos\gamma$; balls of radius $<\pi/2$ in a CAT(1) space are convex; the CAT(1) inequality holds for all pairs of points of a triangle of perimeter $<2\pi$.

contract_anchors.quote:
**(i) Euclidean comparison.** For all reals $a,b,c\ge0$ with $a\le b+c$, $b\le c+a$, $c\le a+b$ there are $\bar p,\bar q,\bar r\in\mathbb E^2$ with the three prescribed distances, and any two such triangles are related by an isometry of $\mathbb E^2$ ([[def-cg-cat-zero-cat-one-and-local-geodesic]]). Consequently every geodesic triangle in every metric space has a comparison triangle in $\mathbb E^2$, and the plane is CAT(0): for a triangle in $\mathbb E^2$ the comparison triangle is congruent to it and the defining inequality is an equality.

**(ii) The round sphere.** For $n\ge2$ the function $d_S(x,y)=\arccos(x\cdot y)$ is a metric on $S^{n-1}\subset\mathbb R^n$; $(S^{n-1},d_S)$ is a geodesic space whose geodesic segments are the minimal great-circle arcs; two points at distance $<\pi$ are joined by a unique geodesic segment; and every closed ball of radius $<\pi/2$ is convex ([[def-metric-ball]]). For every triple of side lengths with perimeter $<2\pi$ satisfying the triangle inequalities there is a comparison triangle in $S^2$, unique up to an isometry of $S^2$. Hence $S^2$ is CAT(1), the CAT(1) inequality for a triangle in $S^2$ of perimeter $<2\pi$ being an equality.

**(iii) Spherical cosine rule and midpoint identity.** For $A,B,C\in S^2$ with $a=d_S(B,C),b=d_S(C,A)\in(0,\pi)$, $c=d_S(A,B)<\pi$ and vertex angle $\gamma$ at $C$, $\cos c=\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b\cos\gamma$. If $c<\pi$, $a$ is the midpoint of a geodesic $[y,z]$ of length $c$ and $x\in S^2$, then $$\cos d_S(x,a)=\frac{\cos d_S(x,y)+\cos d_S(x,z)}{2\cos(c/2)},\qquad \cos(c/2)>0.$$

**(iv) Consequences of CAT(0).** Let $X$ be CAT(0). Then: (a) geodesic segments between two points are unique and vary continuously with their endpoints ([[def-geodesic-and-geodesic-metric-space]]); (b) if $\gamma,\delta$ are geodesics with a common initial point and proportional parametrizations, then $d(\gamma(t),\delta(t))\le(1-t)d(\gamma(0),\delta(0))+t\,d(\gamma(1),\delta(1))$ for $t\in[0,1]$; (c) (hinged criterion) for a geodesic triangle with vertices $z,x,y$ and the point $p_t$ on $[x,y]$ at distance $t\,d(x,y)$ from $x$, the CAT(0) inequality $d(z,p_t)\le d_2(\bar z,\bar p_t)$ holds if and only if $$d(z,p_t)^2\le(1-t)d(z,x)^2+t\,d(z,y)^2-t(1-t)d(x,y)^2,$$ the right-hand side being the squared Euclidean comparison distance; consequently a geodesic space is CAT(0) if and only if for every geodesic triangle and every point $x$ on a side the comparison inequality $d(p,x)\le d_2(\bar p,\bar x)$ with the opposite vertex $p$ holds; (d) for every pair $y,y'$, every midpoint $m$ of a geodesic segment $[y,y']$ and every $z$, $d(z,m)^2\le\tfrac12(d(z,y)^2+d(z,y')^2)-\tfrac14 d(y,y')^2$.

**(v) CAT(1) short-geodesic estimates.** Let $X$ be CAT(1), $p\in X$, $0<r<\pi/2$ and $x,y,z\in B(p,r)$. Then $B(p,r)$ is convex, $[y,z]$ is unique with midpoint $a$, and, **whenever the CAT(1) test is admissible, i.e. $d(x,y)+d(y,z)+d(z,x)<2\pi$**, $$\cos d(x,a)\ge\frac{\cos d(x,y)+\cos d(x,z)}{2\cos(d(y,z)/2)},$$ where $d(y,z)\le2r<\pi$ makes the denominator positive. The admissibility bound is a hypothesis and not a consequence of $r<\pi/2$: a triple in such a ball has perimeter $<6r$ only, and the CAT(1) inequality is stated for triangles of perimeter $<2\pi$.

**(vi) The round circle.** For every $\ell>0$, $d_\ell$ is a metric on $S^1_\ell$ ([[def-cg-cat-zero-cat-one-and-local-geodesic]]); $(S^1_\ell,d_\ell)$ is a compact complete geodesic space locally isometric to $\mathbb R$, contains an isometrically embedded circle of length $\ell$, and is CAT(1) if and only if $\ell\ge2\pi$. For $\ell<2\pi$ the points $0,\ell/3,2\ell/3$ form a triangle of perimeter $\ell<2\pi$ whose side midpoint is at distance $\ell/2$ from the opposite vertex, which exceeds the distance in the spherical comparison triangle; for $\ell\ge2\pi$ every triangle of perimeter $<2\pi$ lies in an arc of length $<\pi$, hence is degenerate and realizes its comparison triangle isometrically.
