citation_contexts: Let $X$ be an isometric polyhedral gluing with standing hypotheses (H1)-(H3) of [[def-cg-abstract-isometric-polyhedral-gluing-and-chain-metric]], with chain metric candidate $d$, maximal dimension $D$ and finite model list. Write $P^{*}:=P\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ and let $K$ be the order complex ([[def-face-poset-and-order-complex]]) of $P^{*}$: its vertices are the elements of $P^{*}$ and its simplices are the finite chains in $P^{*}$.

[F6] The chain length of a chain is the sum of the Euclidean distances of its steps computed in any common cells, $d$ is the infimum of chain lengths, (H1)-(H3) hold, and $D$ is the maximum of the dimensions of the cells. [[def-cg-abstract-isometric-polyhedral-gluing-and-chain-metric]]

proof_uses.text: 3.1 The family of all convex hulls $\operatorname{conv}(b_{F_0},\dots,b_{F_k})$ over strict chains $F_0>\dots>F_k$ in $P^{*}$ is a well-defined family of subsets of $X$, the map $\Phi\colon|K|\to X$ that is affine on each simplex of $K$ with the corresponding vertex values is well defined, and it is a bijection. Each such hull lies in the cell $C_{F_0}$ and is computed there; if the same chain is regarded inside a larger cell the hull is unchanged because all its points lie in the face $C_{F_0}$ and that face is convex, so the subset of $X$ is unambiguous. The images of the simplices of $K$ are exactly the simplices of the triangulations of the cells of [step 2.1], so they cover $X$, and distinct ones have disjoint relative interiors: within one cell this is the triangulation property of [step 2.1]; and if $x$ lies in the relative interior of simplices with top faces $F$ and $G$, then $x\in\operatorname{relint}F\cap\operatorname{relint}G$ by the coning description of [step 2.1], while $x\in C_F\cap C_G=C_{F\wedge G}$ by the intersection condition of [F6]; as $C_{F\wedge G}$ is a face of $C_F$ containing $x$ and $x$ is relatively interior in $F$, that face must be $F$ itself, and likewise $G\subseteq C_{F\wedge G}$, so $F$ and $G$ are faces of one cell with a common relative interior point and hence coincide by [F2]; then the two simplices are two cells of one triangulation with a common relative interior point and hence coincide. Therefore every point of $X$ is in the relative interior of exactly one of the simplices, so $\Phi$ is bijective, and its carrier is unique. [F5, F6, step 2.1]

3.2 There is a real $L$ with $1\le L<\infty$, depending only on the finite model list, such that for every simplex of $K$ and every vertex $v$ the function $\lambda_v$ restricted to that simplex is $L$-Lipschitz for the Euclidean metric of its image. On a singleton simplex all coordinates are constant, with slope $0$. On a positive-dimensional simplex of $K$ with chain $F_0>\dots>F_k$ the function $\lambda_v$ either vanishes identically, when $v$ is not one of the $F_i$, or equals the barycentric coordinate at $b_v$; its linear part has norm $1/h$, where $h>0$ is the distance from $b_v$ to the affine hull of the remaining barycentres, because its gradient is perpendicular to that affine hull and the coordinate changes from $0$ there to $1$ over the perpendicular displacement of length $h$. Each such configuration is isometric to a configuration in a model cell, because the cells of $X$ fall into finitely many isometry classes and the face isometries are affine and isometric, so the positive-dimensional model simplices supply only finitely many positive numbers $h$. Take $L$ to be the maximum of $1$ and their reciprocals; when no such simplex exists take $L=1$. This bounds every coordinate slope. [F3, F5, F6, step 2.1]

4.2 Every point of $X$ lies in the relative interior of exactly one simplex of $K$, its carrier, of dimension at most $D$. Uniqueness and existence are [step 3.1]. A simplex of $K$ is a strict chain $F_0>\dots>F_k$ of nonempty faces; passing from $F_{i+1}$ to $F_i$ is passing to a proper face, which by [F2] lies in a supporting hyperplane, so the dimensions strictly increase along the chain: $k\le\dim F_0\le D$; the simplex therefore has $k+1\le D+1$ vertices and dimension at most $D$. [F2, F6, step 3.1]

5.1 For all $x,y\in X$ and every vertex $v$ one has $|\lambda_v(x)-\lambda_v(y)|\le L\,d(x,y)$. Let $x=x_0,\dots,x_m=y$ be a chain as in [F6]; each consecutive pair lies in a common cell, so [step 4.4] gives $|\lambda_v(x_{i-1})-\lambda_v(x_i)|\le L\,d_{p_i}(x_{i-1},x_i)$, and summing the at most $m$ inequalities and using the triangle inequality for real numbers gives $|\lambda_v(x)-\lambda_v(y)|\le L\,\ell(x_0,\dots,x_m)$. Taking the infimum over all chains from $x$ to $y$ gives the claim, since $L>0$. [F6, step 4.4, algebra]

7.1 For every vertex $v$ the closed star of $v$ is compact and metrizable, and its open star is open and hence a neighbourhood of each of its own points. The closed star is $\Phi(|S|)$ where $S$ is the subcomplex of $K$ consisting of every simplex containing $v$ together with all its faces: the simplices containing $v$ are chains in $P^{*}$ containing $v$, and the elements of $P^{*}$ comparable with $v$ are finitely many, because $P_{\le v}$ is finite by the shape condition of [F6] and the faces $q\ge v$ are finitely many by (H2) of [F6] (a cell $C_q$ meets the relative interior of $C_v$ exactly when $v\le q$). There are finitely many such chains, and each has finitely many faces, so $S$ is a finite subcomplex, $|S|$ is compact and metrizable by [F4], and its image under the homeomorphism of [step 4.1] is compact and metrizable. The open star is the union of the relative interiors of precisely the simplices containing $v$, not of all faces in $S$. Equivalently it is $\{x:\lambda_v(x)>0\}$, which is open: on each cell the coordinate is continuous by step 4.4, or for the chain metric it is Lipschitz by step 5.1. It is contained in the closed star and is a neighbourhood of each of its own points; and every $x\in X$ lies in the relative interior of its carrier, which has at least one vertex, so the open stars cover $X$. Finally, if a vertex $w$ lies in a common cell with $v$, then $w\le q$ for some $q\ge v$; there are finitely many such $q$ as just shown and each $P_{\le q}$ is finite, so only finitely many such $w$ exist. [F4, F6, F7, step 4.1, step 4.4, step 5.1] ∎

Let $S$ be a finite set with Coxeter matrix $m$ and diagram $\Gamma$
([[def-cg-coxeter-diagram-components-and-finite-type]]), let $V=\mathbb R^S$ and
let $B$ be the Coxeter form
([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]]). For $s\ne t$ in $S$ write
$$c(s,t):=-B(e_s,e_t)=\cos(\pi/m(s,t))\ (\text{finite }m(s,t)),\qquad c(s,t):=1\ (m(s,t)=\infty),$$
so that $c(s,t)\in[0,1]$, $c(s,t)=0$ exactly when $m(s,t)=2$, and
$c(s,t)\ge1/2$ whenever $m(s,t)\ge3$. The **cosine matrix** is
$C:=(B(e_s,e_t))_{s,t\in S}$, so $C$ has diagonal entries $1$ and off-diagonal
entries $-c(s,t)$. Assume that $\Gamma$ is connected and that $B$ is positive
definite ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]). Then:

[F1] In the diagram $\Gamma$, distinct vertices $s\ne t$ are joined by an edge exactly when $m(s,t)\ge3$, and the neighbours of $s$ are $N(s)=\{t\in S:t\ne s,\ m(s,t)\ge3\}$; the components of $\Gamma$ partition $S$, and a cycle of $\Gamma$ is a cycle of the underlying simple graph ([[def-cg-coxeter-diagram-components-and-finite-type]]).

contract_anchors.quote:
**(1) The diagram.** The **Coxeter diagram** $\Gamma(W,S)$ of $(W,S)$ has vertex
set $S$, and two distinct vertices $s\ne t$ are joined by an edge exactly when
$m(s,t)\ge3$; that edge carries the **label**
$m(s,t)\in\{3,4,5,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$. By convention the label $3$ is omitted
(an unlabelled edge has label $3$) and no edge is drawn when $m(s,t)=2$. Thus
$\Gamma$ is a finite simple graph whose edges are labelled in
$\{3,4,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$
([[def-graph-adjacency-incidence-neighbourhood-and-degree]]), and $m$ is
recovered from the pair $(S,\Gamma)$ by $m(s,s)=1$; $m(s,t)=m(t,s)=2$ if
$\{s,t\}$ is not an edge; $m(s,t)=3$ if $\{s,t\}$ is an unlabelled edge; and
$m(s,t)=$ the label otherwise. In particular $m\mapsto\Gamma$ is injective on
the Coxeter matrices on $S$. For $T\subseteq S$ the **subdiagram** $\Gamma_T$ is
the induced labelled graph on $T$, i.e. the diagram of the restricted matrix
$m|_{T\times T}$.

**(2) Graph-theoretic vocabulary.** A **cycle** of $\Gamma$ is a cycle of the
underlying simple graph ([[def-graph-walk-trail-path-and-cycle]]); a **path** (or
**chain**) is a diagram whose underlying graph is a path. $\Gamma$ is
**connected** when its underlying graph is connected
([[def-connected-graph-and-connected-component]]); its **components** are the
connected components of the underlying graph, and their vertex sets are
nonempty and partition $S$. For $s\in S$ the **neighbours** of $s$ are
$N(s):=\{t\in S:t\ne s,\ m(s,t)\ge3\}$ and the **degree** of $s$ is $|N(s)|$
([[def-graph-adjacency-incidence-neighbourhood-and-degree]]).

Let $S$ be a finite set with Coxeter matrix $m$ and diagram $\Gamma$
([[def-cg-coxeter-diagram-components-and-finite-type]]), let $V=\mathbb R^S$ and
let $B$ be the Coxeter form
([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]]). For $s\ne t$ in $S$ write
$$c(s,t):=-B(e_s,e_t)=\cos(\pi/m(s,t))\ (\text{finite }m(s,t)),\qquad c(s,t):=1\ (m(s,t)=\infty),$$
so that $c(s,t)\in[0,1]$, $c(s,t)=0$ exactly when $m(s,t)=2$, and
$c(s,t)\ge1/2$ whenever $m(s,t)\ge3$. The **cosine matrix** is
$C:=(B(e_s,e_t))_{s,t\in S}$, so $C$ has diagonal entries $1$ and off-diagonal
entries $-c(s,t)$. Assume that $\Gamma$ is connected and that $B$ is positive
definite ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]). Then:

[F2] $B$ is the unique symmetric bilinear form on $V$ with $B(e_s,e_s)=1$, $B(e_s,e_t)=-\cos(\pi/m(s,t))$ for finite $m(s,t)$ and $B(e_s,e_t)=-1$ for $m(s,t)=\infty$; in particular $C$ is a symmetric matrix and $B(u,w)=\sum_{s,t\in S}u(s)w(t)B(e_s,e_t)$ ([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]], [[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]).

contract_anchors.quote:
**(1) The space and its distinguished functions.** Let $V:=\mathbb R^S$ be the real vector space of all functions $S\to\mathbb R$, with pointwise operations ([[def-function-space]]); it is a vector space over the ordered field $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-reals-ordered-field]]). Write $u(s)$ for the value of $u$ at $s$ and put $e_s(s):=1$, $e_s(t):=0$ for $t\ne s$.

**(2) The Coxeter form.** For finite $m(s,t)$ put $c(s,t):=\cos(\pi/m(s,t))$ ([[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]]) and for $m(s,t)=\infty$ put $c(s,t):=1$; then $c(s,t)=c(t,s)$ and $c(s,s)=\cos\pi=-1$. The **Coxeter form** $B$ is the unique symmetric bilinear form on $V$ with $B(e_s,e_t)=-c(s,t)$ for all $s,t\in S$; in particular $B(e_s,e_s)=1$ and $B(e_s,e_t)=-\cos(\pi/m(s,t))$ for finite $m(s,t)$, while $B(e_s,e_t)=-1$ when $m(s,t)=\infty$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]], [[thm-bilinear-forms-correspond-to-linear-maps-into-the-dual]]). **No positive definiteness, definiteness or nondegeneracy of $B$ is presumed**: $\operatorname{rad}(B):=\{u:B(u,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\}$ may be nonzero ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]), and the form may be indefinite ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]). A linear map $g:V\to V$ is **$B$-preserving** when $B(gu,gw)=B(u,w)$ for all $u,w\in V$.

proof_uses.text: 1.3 (Propagation of zeros along the diagram.) Let $y=\sum_sy_se_s\in\operatorname{rad}(B)$ with $y_s\ge0$ for all $s$, and suppose $y_i=0$ for some $i\in S$. Since $B$ is symmetric and $y$ is radical, $0=B(e_i,y)=\sum_{t}B(e_i,e_t)y_t$ [F1, F2]. Each summand is $\le0$: this follows from $y_t\ge0$ and $B(e_i,e_t)\le0$ for $t\ne i$, while the $t=i$ term is $1\cdot0=0$ [F1]. Hence every summand is $0$; in particular $y_j=0$ for every neighbour $j$ of $i$, because neighbours have $B(e_i,e_j)<0$ by [F1, F4, F7, F12]. Iterating along the connected diagram $\Gamma$ [F11] gives $y_t=0$ for all $t\in S$. [F1, F2, F4, F7, F11, F12, algebra]

Every $v\in W_{s,t}$ preserves $P$ and fixes $P^\perp$ pointwise by [F1], so for $x\in P$ and $f\in V^*$ one has $(v\cdot f)(x)=f(\rho(v)^{-1}x)$ with $\rho(v)^{-1}x\in P$; hence $\pi(v\cdot f)=v\cdot\pi(f)$ and $\pi^{-1}(C_P^\circ)=B_s\cap B_t$, $\pi^{-1}\{g:g(e_{s'})>0\}=B_{s'}$, $\pi^{-1}\{g:g(e_{s'})<0\}=s'B_{s'}$ for $s'\in\{s,t\}$. Consequently $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq B_{s'}$ if and only if $vC_P^\circ\subseteq\{g:g(e_{s'})>0\}$, and $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq s'B_{s'}$ if and only if $vC_P^\circ\subseteq\{g:g(e_{s'})<0\}$. 1.5 **The infinite dihedral group.** Assume $m(s,t)=\infty$, write $u:=st$, and let $u'_k$ be the alternating word of length $k$ beginning with $t$. By [F5], $u$ has infinite order, and by [F6] $\ell_{s,t}(u_k)=k=\ell_{s,t}(u'_k)$ for all $k\ge0$. The union $X:=\{u_k:k\ge0\}\cup\{u'_k:k\ge0\}$ is closed under right multiplication by $s$ and $t$ ($u_{2j}s=u_{2j+1}$, $u_{2j+1}s=u_{2j}$, $u_{2j}t=u_{2j-1}$ for $j\ge1$, $u_0t=u'_1$, $u_{2j+1}t=u_{2j+2}$, symmetrically for $u'_k$), so $X=W_{s,t}$; by [F6] the elements $u_k$ are pairwise distinct with $\ell_{s,t}(u_k)=k$ for every $k\ge0$, and likewise the $u'_k$. The Cayley graph of $W_{s,t}$ for $\{s,t\}$ is connected, and every vertex has degree exactly $2$ (as in 1.4), so it is the two-way infinite path $\cdots u'_2,u'_1,1,u_1,u_2\cdots$, and the graph distance from $1$ to $u_k$, or to $u'_k$, equals $\ell_{s,t}$ of that element, namely $k$. On the affine line $\{f\in P^*:f(e_s+e_t)=1\}$, parametrized by $y_s$, the generators act by $s:y_s\mapsto-y_s$ and $t:y_s\mapsto 2-y_s$ by [F3] (here $c=1$); consequently the affine map of $u_k$ is $y_s\mapsto y_s-2j$ for $k=2j$ and $y_s\mapsto-y_s-2j$ for $k=2j+1$, and that of $u'_k$ is $y_s\mapsto y_s+2j$ for $k=2j$ and $y_s\mapsto-y_s+2j+2$ for $k=2j+1$, by induction on $k$ (each step composes with $s$ or $t$ alternately). Hence the trace of $u_kC_P^\circ$ is the interval $(-k,-k+1)$ and that of $u'_kC_P^\circ$ is $(k,k+1)$. Since these intervals are pairwise distinct, an element of $W_{s,t}=X$ is determined by the trace of its chamber. Writing $v_j$ $(j\in\mathbb Z)$ for the element with trace $(j,j+1)$, namely $v_j=u_{-j}$ for $j\le0$ and $v_j=u'_j$ for $j\ge0$, one therefore has $\ell_{s,t}(v_j)=|j|$ together with $s\cdot v_j=v_{-j-1}$ and $t\cdot v_j=v_{1-j}$, because the affine maps send the interval $(j,j+1)$ to $(-j-1,-j)$, respectively $(1-j,2-j)$. The sign of $y_s$ is constant on each $C_k$ (no $C_k$ meets the line $y_s=0$ by 1.3), is $+$ on $C_0$, and is $-$ on $C_1=sC_P^\circ$ because $s$ negates $y_s$ by [F3]. 9.1 **Converse direction of (4) and conclusion.** Suppose $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$ and put $w':=sw$, so that $\ell(w')=\ell(w)-1$ and $w=sw'$. Let $S$ be a finite set, $m$ a Coxeter matrix on $S$, $W$ the group presented by $(S,m)$ with length function $\ell$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]), $V=\mathbb R^S$, $B$ the Coxeter form, $\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ the canonical reflection homomorphism with root system $\Phi$ ([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]]), and let $V^*$ be the algebraic dual with its dual action, its chamber $C$, its interior $C^\circ$ and its root hyperplanes $H_\alpha$ ([[def-cg-dual-chambers-and-reflection-hyperplanes]]). For $s\in S$ put
$$B_s:=\{f\in V^*:f(e_s)>0\};$$
then $C^\circ=\bigcap_{s\in S}B_s$ and the translate $sB_s=\{f\in V^*:f(e_s)<0\}$ is the opposite open half-space. For distinct $s,t$ let $W_{s,t}:=\langle s,t\rangle\le W$ be the standard parabolic subgroup, with intrinsic length $\ell_{s,t}$, which agrees with $\ell$ on $W_{s,t}$ ([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (2)). For $s\ne t$ and $k\ge0$ let $u_k$ be the alternating word $s\,t\,s\cdots$ of $k$ letters beginning with $s$, so $u_0=1$.

[F5] There is a homomorphism $\operatorname{sgn}:W\to\{\pm1\}$ with $\operatorname{sgn}(s)=-1$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(w)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}$ for all $w\in W$; hence $\ell(ws)=\ell(w)\pm1$ for all $w\in W$ and $s\in S$. Also $\ell(s)=1$ for every $s\in S$, so $s\ne1$ in $W$. Distinct generators are distinct in $W$, the product $st$ has order exactly $m(s,t)$ in $W$, the standard parabolic subgroup $W_{s,t}$ is the Coxeter system presented by the restricted matrix on $\{s,t\}$ with intrinsic length $\ell_{s,t}$ equal to $\ell$ on $W_{s,t}$, and every right coset $W_{s,t}a$ has a unique minimal-length representative $d$, characterized by $\ell(s'd)>\ell(d)$ for $s'\in\{s,t\}$ and satisfying $\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ for all $u\in W_{s,t}$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], [[thm-hh-coxeter-exchange-deletion-and-faithfulness]], [[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]]).

For $s\ne t$, in the coordinates $(y_s,y_t)$ of $P^*=\mathbb Rf_s+\mathbb Rf_t$ with dual basis $f_s(e_t)=\delta_{st}$, the dual generators act by $(y_s,y_t)\mapsto(-y_s,\ 2cy_s+y_t)$ for $s$ and $(y_s,y_t)\mapsto(y_s+2cy_t,\ -y_t)$ for $t$, each fixing the line $H_{e_s}\cap P^*$ respectively $H_{e_t}\cap P^*$ pointwise; when $m(s,t)=\infty$ the functional $f\mapsto f(e_s+e_t)$ is $W_{s,t}$-invariant ([[def-cg-dual-chambers-and-reflection-hyperplanes]], [[lem-cg-dual-action-and-chamber-faces-exist]]).

[F4] Let $C_P:=\{f\in P^*:f(e_s)\ge0,\ f(e_t)\ge0\}$ and $\Phi_P:=W_{s,t}\{e_s,e_t\}$. If $m:=m(s,t)<\infty$, then $W_{s,t}$ has order $2m$ and the $2m$ chambers $wC_P$ $(w\in W_{s,t})$ are exactly the $2m$ closed sectors cut out in $P^*$ by the $m$ root lines $H_\beta\cap P^*$ $(\beta\in\Phi_P)$; they have pairwise disjoint interiors, their union is $P^*$, $W_{s,t}$ acts simply transitively on them, and distinct chambers are separated by a root line. If $m=\infty$, the chambers $wC_P$ have pairwise disjoint interiors with union $\{f\in P^*:f(e_s+e_t)>0\}\cup\{0\}$ (so every chamber meets the boundary line $\{f:f(e_s+e_t)=0\}$ only in $0$), distinct chambers are separated by a root line, and the traces of the root lines on the affine line $\{f:f(e_s+e_t)=1\}$ are exactly the integers in the coordinate $y_s$ ([[lem-cg-dual-action-and-chamber-faces-exist]]).

proof_uses.text: 1.1 **Set-up.** For the rank-two calculation fix $s\ne t$ in $S$ and adopt the notation of [F1] and [F3]. For $r\in S$ the sets $B_r=\{f\in V^*:f(e_r)>0\}$ and $rB_r=\{f\in V^*:f(e_r)<0\}$ are disjoint and $C^\circ=\bigcap_{r\in S}B_r$; the dual action satisfies $v(B_s\cap B_t)=\{v\cdot f:f\in B_s\cap B_t\}$, and the action of $v\in W_{s,t}$ on $V^*$ is linear. By [F5] the intrinsic length satisfies $\ell_{s,t}(x)=\ell(x)$ for $x\in W_{s,t}$. [F1, F3, F5, given]

1.2 **Reduction to the rank-two plane.** Put $C_P^\circ:=\{g\in P^*:g(e_s)>0,\ g(e_t)>0\}$ and let $\pi:V^*\to P^*$, $\pi(f):=f|_P$. Then $\pi$ is linear and surjective, because a functional prescribed on $P$ extends to a functional on $V$ by $0$ on the remaining basis vectors. Every $v\in W_{s,t}$ preserves $P$ and fixes $P^\perp$ pointwise by [F1], so for $x\in P$ and $f\in V^*$ one has $(v\cdot f)(x)=f(\rho(v)^{-1}x)$ with $\rho(v)^{-1}x\in P$; hence $\pi(v\cdot f)=v\cdot\pi(f)$ and $\pi^{-1}(C_P^\circ)=B_s\cap B_t$, $\pi^{-1}\{g:g(e_{s'})>0\}=B_{s'}$, $\pi^{-1}\{g:g(e_{s'})<0\}=s'B_{s'}$ for $s'\in\{s,t\}$. Consequently $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq B_{s'}$ if and only if $vC_P^\circ\subseteq\{g:g(e_{s'})>0\}$, and $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq s'B_{s'}$ if and only if $vC_P^\circ\subseteq\{g:g(e_{s'})<0\}$. [F1, F3, algebra]

1.3 **Sectors avoid the walls.** By [F4] the interiors of the chambers $wC_P$ $(w\in W_{s,t})$ are convex open cones that are connected components of the complement of the union of the root lines in $P^*$ (respectively in $\{f\in P^*:f(e_s+e_t)>0\}$ when $m(s,t)=\infty$), so each is disjoint from every root line $H_\beta\cap P^*$ $(\beta\in\Phi_P)$, and $H_{e_s}\cap P^*$, $H_{e_t}\cap P^*$ are root lines because $e_s,e_t\in\Phi_P$. An open convex set disjoint from a line lies in exactly one of the two open half-planes bounded by it. Hence for every $v\in W_{s,t}$ and $s'\in\{s,t\}$ exactly one of $vC_P^\circ\subseteq\{g:g(e_{s'})>0\}$ and $vC_P^\circ\subseteq\{g:g(e_{s'})<0\}$ holds. [F4, F2, algebra]

1.5 **The infinite dihedral group.** Assume $m(s,t)=\infty$, write $u:=st$, and let $u'_k$ be the alternating word of length $k$ beginning with $t$. By [F5], $u$ has infinite order, and by [F6] $\ell_{s,t}(u_k)=k=\ell_{s,t}(u'_k)$ for all $k\ge0$. The union $X:=\{u_k:k\ge0\}\cup\{u'_k:k\ge0\}$ is closed under right multiplication by $s$ and $t$ ($u_{2j}s=u_{2j+1}$, $u_{2j+1}s=u_{2j}$, $u_{2j}t=u_{2j-1}$ for $j\ge1$, $u_0t=u'_1$, $u_{2j+1}t=u_{2j+2}$, symmetrically for $u'_k$), so $X=W_{s,t}$; by [F6] the elements $u_k$ are pairwise distinct with $\ell_{s,t}(u_k)=k$ for every $k\ge0$, and likewise the $u'_k$. The Cayley graph of $W_{s,t}$ for $\{s,t\}$ is connected, and every vertex has degree exactly $2$ (as in 1.4), so it is the two-way infinite path $\cdots u'_2,u'_1,1,u_1,u_2\cdots$, and the graph distance from $1$ to $u_k$, or to $u'_k$, equals $\ell_{s,t}$ of that element, namely $k$. On the affine line $\{f\in P^*:f(e_s+e_t)=1\}$, parametrized by $y_s$, the generators act by $s:y_s\mapsto-y_s$ and $t:y_s\mapsto 2-y_s$ by [F3] (here $c=1$); consequently the affine map of $u_k$ is $y_s\mapsto y_s-2j$ for $k=2j$ and $y_s\mapsto-y_s-2j$ for $k=2j+1$, and that of $u'_k$ is $y_s\mapsto y_s+2j$ for $k=2j$ and $y_s\mapsto-y_s+2j+2$ for $k=2j+1$, by induction on $k$ (each step composes with $s$ or $t$ alternately). Hence the trace of $u_kC_P^\circ$ is the interval $(-k,-k+1)$ and that of $u'_kC_P^\circ$ is $(k,k+1)$. Since these intervals are pairwise distinct, an element of $W_{s,t}=X$ is determined by the trace of its chamber. Writing $v_j$ $(j\in\mathbb Z)$ for the element with trace $(j,j+1)$, namely $v_j=u_{-j}$ for $j\le0$ and $v_j=u'_j$ for $j\ge0$, one therefore has $\ell_{s,t}(v_j)=|j|$ together with $s\cdot v_j=v_{-j-1}$ and $t\cdot v_j=v_{1-j}$, because the affine maps send the interval $(j,j+1)$ to $(-j-1,-j)$, respectively $(1-j,2-j)$. [F3, F5, F6, algebra]

1.6 **Signs in the infinite case.** In the situation of 1.5 the sign of $y_s$ on $v_jC_P^\circ$ is the sign of $y_s$ on the interval $(j,j+1)$, hence negative exactly when $j\le-1$, and the sign of $y_t=1-y_s$ is negative exactly when $j\ge1$. [F3, algebra]

1.7 **(P_0) and (Q_0).** For $w=1$ one has $\ell(w)=0$, $wC^\circ=C^\circ\subseteq B_r$ for every $r\in S$ by 1.1, and choosing $u=1$ gives $C^\circ\subseteq B_s\cap B_t$ and $\ell(1)=0=\ell_{s,t}(1)+\ell(1)$ for all $s\ne t$. [F3, given]

2.1 **Signs of the finite sectors.** In the finite case let $C_k:=u_kC_P^\circ$ $(0\le k<2m)$; by [F4] these are the interiors of all $2m$ sectors. Consecutive $u_k$ differ by right multiplication by a generator $r$, so $u_kC_P$ and $u_krC_P$ share the image under $u_k$ of the wall of $C_P$ fixed by $r$ and lie on its opposite sides, by [F3]. They are adjacent sectors. The distinct vertices of the Cayley cycle in 1.4 therefore list the sectors in cyclic order. The sign of $y_s$ is constant on each $C_k$ (no $C_k$ meets the line $y_s=0$ by 1.3), is $+$ on $C_0$, and is $-$ on $C_1=sC_P^\circ$ because $s$ negates $y_s$ by [F3]. It changes exactly at those transitions whose common boundary ray lies on the line $y_s=0$: that line contains exactly two boundary rays of the arrangement, hence exactly two transitions; and the involution $s$ maps each sector to the sector on the opposite side of $y_s=0$ and fixes no sector, because $s$ swaps the two half-planes and no sector meets the wall. Hence exactly $m$ sectors lie on each side, and the negative side is the contiguous block of $m$ sectors containing $C_1$ but not $C_0$, that is $\{k:y_s<0\text{ on }C_k\}=\{1,\dots,m\}$. Applying the same argument to $t$, which is $u_{2m-1}$ and negates $y_t$, gives $\{k:y_t<0\text{ on }C_k\}=\{m,\dots,2m-1\}$. [F3, F4, step 1.3, step 1.4, algebra]

5.1 **The conditional step for $(\mathrm P)$.** Fix $n\ge0$ and suppose only $(\mathrm Q_n)$. If $S$ is empty there is no $s$ to check. If $S=\{s\}$ then $W=\{1,s\}$ by $s^2=1$ and [F5], and the only positive-length chamber is $sC^\circ\subseteq sB_s$, with $\ell(s)=1$, proving $(\mathrm P_{n+1})$ directly. Now suppose $|S|\ge2$. First $(\mathrm Q_n)$ and (1) imply $(\mathrm P_n)$: for any $a$ of length $n$ and generator $r$, choose $q\ne r$ and use $(\mathrm Q_n)$ to write $a=ud$, with $aC^\circ\subseteq u(B_r\cap B_q)$ and $n=\ell_{r,q}(u)+\ell(d)$. The rank-two dichotomy gives the positive alternative or the negative alternative with $\ell_{r,q}(ru)=\ell_{r,q}(u)-1$; in the latter case $\ell(ra)\le\ell_{r,q}(ru)+\ell(d)=n-1$, hence equality by [F5]. This is $(\mathrm P_n)$. Let $w\in W$ with $\ell(w)=n+1$ and let $s\in S$; choose $t$ with $w=tw'$ and $\ell(w')=n$. If $s=t$, then $(\mathrm P_n)$ applied to $w'$ gives $w'C^\circ\subseteq B_s$: the second alternative would give $\ell(sw')=\ell(w')-1=n-1$, whereas $\ell(sw')=\ell(w)=n+1$ here. Hence $wC^\circ=t(w'C^\circ)\subseteq tB_s=sB_s$ and $\ell(sw)=\ell(w')=n=\ell(w)-1$, the second alternative of $(\mathrm P_{n+1})$. If $s\ne t$, apply $(\mathrm Q_n)$ to $w'$: there is $u\in W_{s,t}$ with $w'C^\circ\subseteq u(B_s\cap B_t)$ and $\ell(w')=\ell_{s,t}(u)+\ell(u^{-1}w')$. Put $v:=tu\in W_{s,t}$. If $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq B_s$, then $wC^\circ\subseteq tu(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq B_s$. Otherwise $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq sB_s$ and $\ell_{s,t}(sv)=\ell_{s,t}(v)-1$ by (1) from 4.1, so with $d:=u^{-1}w'$ one has $wC^\circ\subseteq sB_s$ and $\ell(sw)=\ell(stu\,d)\le\ell_{s,t}(stu)+\ell(d)=\ell_{s,t}(v)-1+\ell(d)\le\ell_{s,t}(u)+\ell(d)=\ell(w')=\ell(w)-1$, where $\ell_{s,t}(tu)\le1+\ell_{s,t}(u)$ follows by prepending $t$ to a shortest word for $u$. The reverse bound $\ell(sw)\ge\ell(w)-1$ follows from [F5], so $\ell(sw)=\ell(w)-1$, the second alternative of $(\mathrm P_{n+1})$. [step 4.1, F3, F5, algebra]

9.1 **Converse direction of (4) and conclusion.** Suppose $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$ and put $w':=sw$, so that $\ell(w')=\ell(w)-1$ and $w=sw'$. By $(\mathrm P_{\ell(w')})$ from 7.1 applied to $w'$, either $w'C^\circ\subseteq B_s$, or $w'C^\circ\subseteq sB_s$ and $\ell(sw')=\ell(w')-1$; the second alternative would give $\ell(w)=\ell(sw')=\ell(w')-1=\ell(w)-2$, which is impossible, so $w'C^\circ\subseteq B_s$. Applying the linear bijection $f\mapsto s\cdot f$ of [F3] gives $wC^\circ=s(w'C^\circ)\subseteq sB_s$. Together with 8.2 this is the equivalence (4); and (1) is 4.1, (2) is 7.1 and (3) is 8.1, so all four clauses of the statement hold. [step 8.2, step 7.1, step 4.1, step 8.1] ∎

citation_contexts: [F5] There is a homomorphism $\operatorname{sgn}:W\to\{\pm1\}$ with $\operatorname{sgn}(s)=-1$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(w)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}$ for all $w\in W$; hence $\ell(ws)=\ell(w)\pm1$ for all $w\in W$ and $s\in S$. Also $\ell(s)=1$ for every $s\in S$, so $s\ne1$ in $W$. Distinct generators are distinct in $W$, the product $st$ has order exactly $m(s,t)$ in $W$, the standard parabolic subgroup $W_{s,t}$ is the Coxeter system presented by the restricted matrix on $\{s,t\}$ with intrinsic length $\ell_{s,t}$ equal to $\ell$ on $W_{s,t}$, and every right coset $W_{s,t}a$ has a unique minimal-length representative $d$, characterized by $\ell(s'd)>\ell(d)$ for $s'\in\{s,t\}$ and satisfying $\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ for all $u\in W_{s,t}$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], [[thm-hh-coxeter-exchange-deletion-and-faithfulness]], [[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]]).

$$B_s:=\{f\in V^*:f(e_s)>0\};$$
then $C^\circ=\bigcap_{s\in S}B_s$ and the translate $sB_s=\{f\in V^*:f(e_s)<0\}$ is the opposite open half-space. This is $(\mathrm P_n)$. Let $w\in W$ with $\ell(w)=n+1$ and let $s\in S$; choose $t$ with $w=tw'$ and $\ell(w')=n$. If $s=t$, then $(\mathrm P_n)$ applied to $w'$ gives $w'C^\circ\subseteq B_s$: the second alternative would give $\ell(sw')=\ell(w')-1=n-1$, whereas $\ell(sw')=\ell(w)=n+1$ here. Hence $wC^\circ=t(w'C^\circ)\subseteq tB_s=sB_s$ and $\ell(sw)=\ell(w')=n=\ell(w)-1$, the second alternative of $(\mathrm P_{n+1})$. If $s\ne t$, apply $(\mathrm Q_n)$ to $w'$: there is $u\in W_{s,t}$ with $w'C^\circ\subseteq u(B_s\cap B_t)$ and $\ell(w')=\ell_{s,t}(u)+\ell(u^{-1}w')$. Put $v:=tu\in W_{s,t}$. If $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq B_s$, then $wC^\circ\subseteq tu(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq B_s$. Otherwise $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq sB_s$ and $\ell_{s,t}(sv)=\ell_{s,t}(v)-1$ by (1) from 4.1, so with $d:=u^{-1}w'$ one has $wC^\circ\subseteq sB_s$ and $\ell(sw)=\ell(stu\,d)\le\ell_{s,t}(stu)+\ell(d)=\ell_{s,t}(v)-1+\ell(d)\le\ell_{s,t}(u)+\ell(d)=\ell(w')=\ell(w)-1$, where $\ell_{s,t}(tu)\le1+\ell_{s,t}(u)$ follows by prepending $t$ to a shortest word for $u$. Let $S$, $m$, $V$, $B$, $W$, $r_s$, $\rho$, $\Phi$, $T$ be as in [[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]].

**Given:** a finite set $S$, a Coxeter matrix $m$, the space $V=\mathbb R^S$, the Coxeter form $B$, the reflections $r_a$ and the presented Coxeter group $W$ with its universal property, all as in the Statement of [[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]]; here $r_s:=r_{e_s}$ for $s\in S$.

[F1] For $a\in V$ with $B(a,a)\ne0$ the map $r_a$ is linear, satisfies $r_a^2=\mathrm{id}_V$ and $B(r_au,r_aw)=B(u,w)$ for all $u,w\in V$; and for distinct $s,t\in S$ with $m(s,t)<\infty$ the product $A=r_sr_t$ satisfies $A^{m(s,t)}=\mathrm{id}_V$ ([[lem-cg-reflection-form-invariance-and-rank-two-orders]], clauses (2) and (3)(iv)).

[F2] The Coxeter form satisfies $B(e_s,e_s)=1$ for every $s\in S$, the symbol $r_s$ abbreviates $r_{e_s}$, and a linear map $g$ is $B$-preserving when $B(gu,gw)=B(u,w)$ for all $u,w\in V$ ([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]]).

**(1) Relators and descent.** For every $s\in S$ one has $r_s^2=\mathrm{id}_V$, and for all $s\ne t$ with $m(s,t)<\infty$ one has $(r_sr_t)^{m(s,t)}=\mathrm{id}_V$. Consequently the assignment $s\mapsto r_s$ sends every relator of the presentation to the identity, and by the universal property of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]] there is a **unique** group homomorphism $\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ with $\rho(s)=r_s$ for all $s\in S$.

2.1 Descent. The assignment $s\mapsto r_s$ sends the relator $s^2$ to $r_s^2=\mathrm{id}_V$ by 1.1 and the relator $(st)^{m(s,t)}$ to $(r_sr_t)^{m(s,t)}=\mathrm{id}_V$ by 1.2; these are exactly the relators of the presented Coxeter group $W$ of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], and the images $r_s$ lie in the group $\mathrm{GL}(V)$. So the universal property of that presentation gives a unique group homomorphism $\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ with $\rho(s)=r_s$ for every $s\in S$. [given, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 $\rho$ preserves the form, and roots have unit norm. Let $H:=\{w\in W:B(\rho(w)u,\rho(w)w')=B(u,w')\text{ for all }u,w'\in V\}$. Every $s\in S$ lies in $H$ by 1.1, since $\rho(s)=r_s$. If $g,h\in H$ then $B(\rho(gh)u,\rho(gh)w')=B(\rho(g)\rho(h)u,\rho(g)\rho(h)w')=B(\rho(h)u,\rho(h)w')=B(u,w')$, using the homomorphism property of 2.1 and the $B$-preservation of $\rho(g)$ and then of $\rho(h)$, so $gh\in H$; and if $g\in H$, then $B(\rho(g^{-1})u,\rho(g^{-1})w')=B(\rho(g)\rho(g^{-1})u,\rho(g)\rho(g^{-1})w')=B(u,w')$, so $g^{-1}\in H$. Thus $H$ is a subgroup containing $S$, and since every element of $W$ is the value of a finite word in $S$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]), so that the images of the elements of $S$ generate $W$, [F3] gives $H=W$. In particular $B(\rho(w)e_s,\rho(w)e_s)=B(e_s,e_s)=1$ for all $w\in W$ and $s\in S$ by [F2], so every root $\alpha\in\Phi$ has $B(\alpha,\alpha)=1\ne0$ and the reflection $r_\alpha$ is defined. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1]

facts.actual_text: [F11] [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]] (7): standard dihedral alternating words of length at most $m(s,t)$ are reduced in the ambient group. [[lem-cg-finite-dihedral-subsystems-and-canonical-roots]] (3) identifies the standard rank-two subgroup with the dihedral group of order $2m$. Its $2m$ elements have alternating representatives of length at most $m$. Indeed, let $A,B$ be the alternating words of length $m$ beginning with $s,t$, respectively. Since $s,t$ are involutions, the concatenation $AB^{-1}$ is alternating of length $2m$ beginning with $s$, so $AB^{-1}=(st)^m=1$ by [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]] (1),(4); hence $A=B$. Thus an alternating length-$m$ word is its longest element, and deleting its first $s$ gives a reduced length-$m-1$ alternating word starting with $t$.

proof_uses.text: 2.4 Links of gluings. Let $X$ be an isometric polyhedral gluing with cells $C_p$ and let $F$ be a face. By step 1.2 the tangent cone $T_FC_p$ and the angular link $\operatorname{Lk}_{C_p}(F)$ depend only on $F$, and for $p\le q$ the isometry $h_{p,q}:C_p\to C_q$ maps $F$ onto $F$, so its linear part maps $T_FC_p$ isometrically into $T_FC_q$ and maps its normal section onto the corresponding link face that is compatible with the cocycle condition; the intersection condition makes the intersections of the resulting images correspond to the common faces, so the cell links glue to a well-defined quotient $\operatorname{Lk}_X(F)$, and replacing the point of $F$ changes nothing by step 1.2. The normal sections in cofaces $G>F$ inherit their polyhedral face incidences; when $X$ is simplicial these correspond to the simplices $G\setminus F$ of its combinatorial link. A general polyhedral face link need not itself be simplicial. [step 1.2, F7]

7.1 Component metrics and topology. The classes under being joined by a chain are finite in number. Each is a union of whole cells: any two points of one cell are joined by a single chain step. The trace of a class on every cell is therefore the entire cell or empty, so every class is weakly open and closed; each class is path connected by cell arcs, hence is a connected component. The corresponding component of $Y$ satisfies (H1)-(H3), so [F7] supplies its metric, weak topology, properness and completeness; step 6.1 transfers these properties to the component of $X$. Each component is compact as a quotient of finitely many compact cells. Its chain metric is a length metric: a chain can be replaced by cell arcs, whose $d$-length is at most its chain length because $d\le d_{\mathrm{ang}}$ on a cell, while every path has length at least the distance of its endpoints. Cellwise radial homeomorphisms descend to a homeomorphism for the quotient (weak) topologies, and the components are open and closed, so $X$ and $Y$ are compact finite disjoint unions of the component metric spaces. Distances between distinct components remain auxiliary infinities; no real-valued global chain metric is asserted. The empty case is vacuous. [step 4.2, step 6.1, F6, F7]

8.1 Minimizing geodesics (AC). Assume AC, fix $x,y$ in one component and put $R=d(x,y)$. AC selects, for each $n\ge1$, a chain of length $L_n<R+1/n$; the infimum definition gives $R\le L_n$. Replace its steps by cell arcs, traversed at angular speed $L_n$ on $[0,1]$ (use the constant path for $L_n=0$). Each arc lies in its cell by the nonnegative-combination argument of step 2.3 applied to $K(C_\sigma)$, and the triangle inequality gives $d(\gamma_n(s),\gamma_n(t))\le L_n|s-t|$, hence $R\le\ell(\gamma_n)\le L_n$. The paths are equicontinuous and pointwise bounded in the compact proper component of step 7.1. The domain $[0,1]$ is compact as a nonempty bounded one-dimensional polyhedral cell by [F5]; with AC it satisfies [F8], giving a uniformly convergent subsequence with continuous limit $\gamma$ and endpoints $x,y$. Since $R\le\ell(\gamma_n)\le L_n\to R$, lower semicontinuity [F7] gives $\ell(\gamma)\le R$, while the endpoint partition gives the reverse bound. Reparametrise by arc length using [F7]. For $0\le u\le v\le R$, the resulting path $\bar\gamma$ is $1$-Lipschitz, and $R=d(x,y)\le u+d(\bar\gamma(u),\bar\gamma(v))+R-v$ forces $d(\bar\gamma(u),\bar\gamma(v))\ge v-u$; thus equality holds and $\bar\gamma$ is a minimizing geodesic. AC is used for the sequence selection and for Ascoli. [step 2.3, step 7.1, F5, F7, F8]

citation_contexts: **(vi) Disconnected components.** If the angular link of a face of a complex is disconnected, the componentwise path distance is $+\infty$ between distinct components; this value is auxiliary notation only and is truncated in the cone formulas of [[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]].

9.1 The $+\infty$ convention. Let $F$ be a face of a finite spherical complex $X$. By step 4.3 the angular link $\operatorname{Lk}_X(F)$ is a finite spherical complex, so step 7.1 applies to it: being joined by a chain of directions inside common cells is reflexive (singleton chains), symmetric (reverse a chain) and transitive (concatenate chains), hence an equivalence relation on $\operatorname{Lk}_X(F)$; the infimum $d_{\mathrm{path}}(x,y)$ is finite whenever a chain from $x$ to $y$ exists and is a metric on each class by step 7.1, while for $x,y$ in different classes no chain joins them and $d_{\mathrm{path}}(x,y)=+\infty$. This infinite value is auxiliary notation, not an ordinary distance of the metric-space definition, and it is replaced by $\pi$ in the truncated metric of [[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]]. citation_contexts: Let $C=(c_{ij})$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ matrix with diagonal $1$, and let $L$, $u_0,\dots,u_n$, $K(C)$, $\Sigma(C)$ be as in [[def-cg-spherical-gram-simplex-and-angular-link]].

**(v) Angular links of Euclidean faces.** For a compact convex polyhedral cell $C$ and a face $F$ as in [[def-cg-spherical-gram-simplex-and-angular-link]], with direction space $U(F)$ and normal cone $N_FC=T_FC\cap U(F)^{\perp}$, after constant defining inequalities are discarded, the two descriptions of the tangent cone agree: $T_FC=\overline{\{\lambda(x-p):x\in C,\ \lambda\ge0\}}$ for every $p$ in the relative interior of $F$, and $T_FC=\{\xi:\langle\xi,n_j\rangle\ge0\ (j\in I(F))\}$ for the inward unit normals of the active defining hyperplanes; the tangent cone and the normal cone depend only on $F$. The cone $N_FC$ is pointed, and is closed under nonnegative combinations, so for $\xi,\eta\in N_FC\cap S(V)$ the shorter great-circle arc between them stays in $N_FC\cap S(V)$ and realises $\arccos\langle\xi,\eta\rangle$ as an intrinsic path in the link; conversely every path in $N_FC\cap S(V)$ has length at least the round distance of its endpoints. Hence the angular distance of [[def-cg-spherical-gram-simplex-and-angular-link]] is the intrinsic path metric of the round sphere restricted to $\operatorname{Lk}_C(F)$, it is a metric of diameter at most $\pi$, and the links $\operatorname{Lk}_{C_p}(F)$ of the cells containing a face $F$ of an isometric polyhedral gluing depend only on $F$, so their quotient $\operatorname{Lk}_X(F)$ is well defined up to canonical isometry.

**Given:** A real symmetric positive-definite $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ matrix $C$ with diagonal $1$, its Cholesky factor $L$, the vectors $u_i$, the cone $K(C)$ and simplex $\Sigma(C)$ of [[def-cg-spherical-gram-simplex-and-angular-link]]; in clauses (iii) and (vi) additionally a finite abstract simplicial complex $K$ with compatible Gram matrices $C_\sigma$ as in the Statement.

citation_contexts: **(iii) Finite spherical complexes.** Let $K$ be a finite abstract simplicial complex ([[def-abstract-simplicial-complex]]) whose nonempty simplices $\sigma$ carry positive-definite Gram matrices $C_\sigma$ of diagonal $1$, compatible with faces. Form $X:=|K|_C$ by gluing the spherical simplices $\Sigma(C_\sigma)$ along their vertex-wise face identifications. On each component define the **chain metric** $d$ as the infimum of $\sum_i d_{p_i}(x_{i-1},x_i)$ over finite chains in common cells, with $d_p$ the angular metric of that cell; equivalently it is the infimum of lengths of continuous paths. Between different components this infimum is $+\infty$, auxiliary notation rather than a metric value ([[def-metric-space]]). The inverse cellwise radial maps descend to a homeomorphism $X\to Y$, where $Y$ is the Euclidean gluing with cells $\Delta(C_\sigma)$; it is bi-Lipschitz on every component. Each component of $X$ is a compact proper complete length space whose metric topology is the weak topology, and $X$ is a finite disjoint union of these components. For the empty complex, $X=Y=\emptyset$. *Under the Axiom of Choice* ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), every two points in a component are joined by a minimizing geodesic of length $d(x,y)$, in particular every pair at distance $<\pi$. The proper-target argument is written locally below, using [[lem-cg-metric-target-length-reparametrization-and-lower-semicontinuity]] and [[cor-arzela-ascoli-subsequence-theorem-for-proper-metric-targets]]; compare [[thm-cg-proper-polyhedral-spaces-have-minimizing-geodesics]].

proof_uses.text: 2.4 Links of gluings. Let $X$ be an isometric polyhedral gluing with cells $C_p$ and let $F$ be a face. By step 1.2 the tangent cone $T_FC_p$ and the angular link $\operatorname{Lk}_{C_p}(F)$ depend only on $F$, and for $p\le q$ the isometry $h_{p,q}:C_p\to C_q$ maps $F$ onto $F$, so its linear part maps $T_FC_p$ isometrically into $T_FC_q$ and maps its normal section onto the corresponding link face that is compatible with the cocycle condition; the intersection condition makes the intersections of the resulting images correspond to the common faces, so the cell links glue to a well-defined quotient $\operatorname{Lk}_X(F)$, and replacing the point of $F$ changes nothing by step 1.2. The normal sections in cofaces $G>F$ inherit their polyhedral face incidences; when $X$ is simplicial these correspond to the simplices $G\setminus F$ of its combinatorial link. A general polyhedral face link need not itself be simplicial. [step 1.2, F7]

7.1 Component metrics and topology. The classes under being joined by a chain are finite in number. Each is a union of whole cells: any two points of one cell are joined by a single chain step. The trace of a class on every cell is therefore the entire cell or empty, so every class is weakly open and closed; each class is path connected by cell arcs, hence is a connected component. The corresponding component of $Y$ satisfies (H1)-(H3), so [F7] supplies its metric, weak topology, properness and completeness; step 6.1 transfers these properties to the component of $X$. Each component is compact as a quotient of finitely many compact cells. Its chain metric is a length metric: a chain can be replaced by cell arcs, whose $d$-length is at most its chain length because $d\le d_{\mathrm{ang}}$ on a cell, while every path has length at least the distance of its endpoints. Cellwise radial homeomorphisms descend to a homeomorphism for the quotient (weak) topologies, and the components are open and closed, so $X$ and $Y$ are compact finite disjoint unions of the component metric spaces. Distances between distinct components remain auxiliary infinities; no real-valued global chain metric is asserted. The empty case is vacuous. [step 4.2, step 6.1, F6, F7]

8.1 Minimizing geodesics (AC). Assume AC, fix $x,y$ in one component and put $R=d(x,y)$. AC selects, for each $n\ge1$, a chain of length $L_n<R+1/n$; the infimum definition gives $R\le L_n$. Replace its steps by cell arcs, traversed at angular speed $L_n$ on $[0,1]$ (use the constant path for $L_n=0$). Each arc lies in its cell by the nonnegative-combination argument of step 2.3 applied to $K(C_\sigma)$, and the triangle inequality gives $d(\gamma_n(s),\gamma_n(t))\le L_n|s-t|$, hence $R\le\ell(\gamma_n)\le L_n$. The paths are equicontinuous and pointwise bounded in the compact proper component of step 7.1. The domain $[0,1]$ is compact as a nonempty bounded one-dimensional polyhedral cell by [F5]; with AC it satisfies [F8], giving a uniformly convergent subsequence with continuous limit $\gamma$ and endpoints $x,y$. Since $R\le\ell(\gamma_n)\le L_n\to R$, lower semicontinuity [F7] gives $\ell(\gamma)\le R$, while the endpoint partition gives the reverse bound. Reparametrise by arc length using [F7]. For $0\le u\le v\le R$, the resulting path $\bar\gamma$ is $1$-Lipschitz, and $R=d(x,y)\le u+d(\bar\gamma(u),\bar\gamma(v))+R-v$ forces $d(\bar\gamma(u),\bar\gamma(v))\ge v-u$; thus equality holds and $\bar\gamma$ is a minimizing geodesic. AC is used for the sequence selection and for Ascoli. [step 2.3, step 7.1, F5, F7, F8]

facts.fact_text: [F1] The defining data have $\Gamma$ connected, $J=\{s_1,\dots,s_r\}$, $K=\{s_{r+1},\dots,s_n\}$, pairwise orthogonal simple roots within each class, and $\rho_{i+n}=C_V\rho_i$, $\mu_{i+n}=C_V\mu_i$ for every $i\ge1$. The vectors $\beta_i$ satisfy $B(\beta_i,\alpha_j)=\delta_{ij}$. [[def-cg-bipartite-coxeter-element-and-root-recursion]] (1)-(3)

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 Write $\|x\|_0^2:=\sum_{s\in S}x_s^2$ for the standard coordinate norm and set $q(x):=x^{\mathsf T}Ax$. If $m(s,t)=\infty$ for distinct $s,t$, then $B(e_s+e_t,e_s+e_t)=0$, contradicting positive definiteness; hence every off-diagonal Coxeter exponent is finite. Therefore $A_{ss}=0$ and $A_{st}=-2B(e_s,e_t)=2\cos(\pi/m(s,t))\ge0$ for $s\ne t$, with $A_{st}>0$ exactly on the edges of the connected diagram. Also $q(x)=2\|x\|_0^2-2B(x,x)<2\|x\|_0^2$ for every nonzero $x$. [F1, F2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.2: 1.2 For $1\le i\le n$, the first $n$ prefix vectors satisfy $\rho_i=\alpha_i$ for $i\le r$ and $\rho_i=\rho(a)\alpha_i=\alpha_i+\sum_{s\in J}A_{si}\alpha_s$ for $i>r$: the earlier reflections in the same color class fix $\alpha_i$, while each reflection in the other class adds its $A_{si}\alpha_s$ and fixes the other roots of that class. Hence the coordinate matrix of $(\rho_1,\dots,\rho_n)$ relative to the ordered basis $(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ is block upper triangular with identity diagonal blocks, so these vectors form a basis. The cyclic definitions give $\rho_{i+n}=C_V\rho_i$ and $\mu_{i+n}=C_V\mu_i$ for every $i\ge1$, because each block of $n$ reflections has product $c$. Each $\rho_i$ is a root, being the image of a simple root by an element of $W$. [F1, F2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 For $1\le i\le n$, duality gives $B(\beta_i,\alpha_j)=0$ for every $j\ne i$, so $R_j\beta_i=\beta_i$ for every $j\ne i$ and in particular $\mu_i=R_1\cdots R_{i-1}\beta_i=\beta_i$. Also $R_i\beta_i=\beta_i-2\alpha_i$. Thus $C_V\beta_i=R_1\cdots R_n\beta_i=R_1\cdots R_{i-1}(\beta_i-2\alpha_i)=\mu_i-2\rho_i=\beta_i-2\rho_i$, so $(C_V-\mathrm{id}_V)\beta_i=-2\rho_i$. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.3.1: 3.1 Since every entry of $A$ is nonnegative, $q(|p|)\ge q(p)=\lambda$, while $\||p|\|_0=1$, so $|p|$ is also a maximizer and satisfies $A|p|=\lambda|p|$ by step 2.1. Put $r:=|p|$. If $r_s>0$ and $A_{st}>0$, then $\lambda r_t=\sum_uA_{tu}r_u\ge A_{ts}r_s>0$; since $\lambda>0$ and the edge graph of $A$ is connected, positivity propagates to every coordinate. Thus we may take $p\in\mathbb R_{>0}^S$, proving the existence claim in (1). [F1, step 2.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.3.2: 3.2 The vectors $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_n$ form a basis by the construction in the preceding definition, and $\rho_1,\dots,\rho_n$ form a basis by 1.2; thus 2.2 shows that $C_V-\mathrm{id}_V$ maps one basis to the other up to the nonzero scalar $-2$, so it is invertible. If $i=mn+j$ with $m\ge0$ and $1\le j\le n$, then the cyclic recursions in F1 and the identity in 2.2 give $(C_V-\mathrm{id}_V)\mu_i=C_V^m(C_V-\mathrm{id}_V)\mu_j=-2C_V^m\rho_j=-2\rho_i$. Applying the conditional map of the preceding definition now yields $\mu(\rho_i)=\mu_i$ for all $i\ge1$, proving (4) and the definition's well-definedness justification. [F1, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 Put $d':=\sum_{t\in K}p_t^2$. Since distinct simple roots in either color class are orthogonal, $B(u,u)=d$ and $B(v,v)=d'$. Multiplying the eigenvector equations $\sum_{t\in K}A_{st}p_t=\lambda p_s$ by $p_s$ and summing over $s\in J$ gives $\sum_{s\in J,t\in K}p_sA_{st}p_t=\lambda d$; summing the equations indexed by $K$ gives the same left side equal to $\lambda d'$, hence $d=d'>0$. Finally $B(u,v)=-\frac12\sum_{s\in J,t\in K}p_sA_{st}p_t=-\lambda d/2$. The Gram matrix on $(u,v)$ is $d\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-\lambda/2\\-\lambda/2&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $d^2(1-\lambda^2/4)>0$, so $u,v$ are independent and $P$ is a plane. [F1, F2, step 3.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.5.1: 5.1 For $s\in J$, $R_s$ fixes $\alpha_{s'}$ for $s'\in J\setminus\{s\}$ and negates $\alpha_s$; the corresponding statement holds in $K$. For $t\in K$, the commuting reflections in $a$ give $\rho(a)\alpha_t=\alpha_t+\sum_{s\in J}A_{st}\alpha_s$, and for $s\in J$, $\rho(b)\alpha_s=\alpha_s+\sum_{t\in K}A_{ts}\alpha_t$. Summing with coefficients $p_t$ and $p_s$ and using $Ap=\lambda p$ yields $\rho(a)u=-u$, $\rho(a)v=v+\lambda u$, $\rho(b)v=-v$, and $\rho(b)u=u+\lambda v$. Thus $P$ is invariant under $\rho(a),\rho(b)$ and $C_V=\rho(a)\rho(b)$. [F1, F2, step 4.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.7.1: 7.1 For $x=\xi u+\eta v\in P$, one has $B(x,\alpha_s)=p_s(\xi-\frac\lambda2\eta)$ for $s\in J$ and $B(x,\alpha_t)=p_t(\eta-\frac\lambda2\xi)$ for $t\in K$. Thus $\mathcal C\cap P$ is given by $\xi\ge\frac\lambda2\eta$ and $\eta\ge\frac\lambda2\xi$; because $0<\lambda/2<1$, these inequalities imply $\xi,\eta\ge0$, and their strict versions place the relative interior in $\mathcal C^\circ$. Its boundary rays are $x_J:=\lambda u+2v$ (the $J$ simple-root hyperplanes) and $x_K:=2u+\lambda v$ (the $K$ simple-root hyperplanes). Their squared $B$-norms are both $d(4-\lambda^2)$ and $B(x_J,x_K)=\lambda d(2-\lambda^2/2)$, so the sector angle has cosine $\lambda/2$ and equals $\theta$. The restrictions of $\rho(a)$ and $\rho(b)$ are reflections in the lines $\mathbb R x_J$ and $\mathbb R x_K$: they fix those lines, are involutions, and are nonidentity on $P$ by 4.1. [F1, F2, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.8.1: 8.1 Let $m_0$ be the order of $C_V|_P$. Since it rotates through $2\theta\in(0,\pi)$, $m_0\ge3$ and $2\theta=2\pi j/m_0$ for an integer $j$ with $1\le j<m_0/2$ and $\gcd(j,m_0)=1$. The subgroup $D:=\langle\rho(a)|_P,\rho(b)|_P\rangle$ consists of the $m_0$ distinct rotations $(C_V|_P)^k$ and the $m_0$ distinct reflections $\rho(a)|_P(C_V|_P)^k$, so $|D|=2m_0$. Distinct elements of $D$ have lifts $\tilde g\in\langle a,b\rangle$ with distinct restrictions to $P$, hence are distinct elements of $W$; by F4 their chamber interiors are distinct and disjoint. Thus the orbit of $S_0:=\mathcal C\cap P$ consists of $2m_0$ distinct sectors of angle $\theta$, each of the form $\rho(\tilde g)\mathcal C\cap P$, with pairwise disjoint relative interiors. Hence $2m_0\theta\le2\pi$, so $j=1$ and $\theta=\pi/m_0$; equality shows the sectors cover $P$. As $m_0\mid h$ by F1, the element $c^{m_0}$ fixes every point of $P$, in particular a point of $\mathcal C^\circ\cap P$; its stabiliser is trivial, so $c^{m_0}=1$ and $h\mid m_0$. Thus $m_0=h$ and $\lambda=2\cos(\pi/h)$, completing (1) and the angle claims of (2). [F1, F2, F4, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.10.1: 10.1 The ray $\mathbb R_{>0}x_J$ lies in the relative interior of the face $\mathcal C_J$, so its stabiliser is $W_J$; similarly the stabiliser of $\mathbb R_{>0}x_K$ is $W_K$. Every element of $W_J$ reduces to a product of a subset $I\subseteq J$ because its simple generators are commuting involutions; the subset products are distinct because their $\rho$-images have different signs on the independent simple roots and $\rho$ is faithful by [F2]. The image of the product for $I$ acts by $-1$ on $\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_s:s\in I\}$ and by $+1$ on its $B$-orthogonal complement, so its $(-1)$-eigenspace has dimension $|I|$; therefore it is a reflection exactly when $|I|=1$, and the reflections in $W_J$ are precisely its $|J|=r$ simple generators. The same reasoning gives exactly $|K|=n-r$ reflections in $W_K$. The $2h$ distinct boundary rays from 8.1 alternate between the two types, so there are $h$ of each; conjugating the stabiliser count around them gives $hr+h(n-r)=hn$ incidences between rays and ambient root hyperplanes. Each hyperplane contributes exactly two incidences because its trace is a line. Hence the arrangement has $hn/2$ hyperplanes, so $|T|=hn/2$ by the root-reflection correspondence of [F7]. [F1, F2, F4, F7, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, step 9.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.12.1: 12.1 Choose the direction around the circle so that the first boundary ray of $S_0$ is $x_J$. The rays then occur in the cyclic order $p_{2k}=C_V^k\mathbb R_{>0}x_J$ and $p_{2k+1}=C_V^k\rho(a)\mathbb R_{>0}x_K$ for $k=0,\dots,h-1$: $\rho(a)$ reflects across the $J$ boundary, while $C_V$ advances by two sector angles. The hyperplanes through $p_{2k}$ are exactly $H_{C_V^k\alpha_s}$ for $s=s_1,\dots,s_r$, and those through $p_{2k+1}$ are exactly $H_{C_V^k\rho(a)\alpha_t}$ for $t=s_{r+1},\dots,s_n$, by the stabiliser counts and the description of the reflections in $W_J,W_K$ from 10.1. These are precisely the blocks $H_{\rho_{kn+1}},\dots,H_{\rho_{kn+r}}$ and $H_{\rho_{kn+r+1}},\dots,H_{\rho_{(k+1)n}}$ by the cyclic prefix definition in 1.2. The first $h$ rays carry $hn/2$ hyperplanes: this is $hn/2$ from $h/2$ complete color pairs when $h$ is even, and $n(h-1)/2+r=hn/2$ when $h$ is odd by 11.1. The opposite semicircle carries the other $hn/2$ hyperplanes. Each half-turn list is pairwise distinct because every trace line meets that semicircle only once, and the listed hyperplanes in each boundary block are distinct simple-root images. [F1, step 9.1, step 10.1, step 11.1, algebra]

facts.fact_text: [F4] The transferred chamber is $\mathcal C=\{x\in V:B(x,\alpha_s)\ge0\ \forall s\}$ with interior defined by strict inequalities; the chambers $w\mathcal C$ tile $V$ with disjoint interiors, and a point in $w\mathcal C_I$ has stabiliser $wW_Iw^{-1}$. proof_step_texts.9.1: 9.1 For every root $\alpha$, the trace $H_\alpha\cap P$ is a line: if $P\subseteq H_\alpha$, the nonidentity reflection $t_\alpha$ fixes a point of $\mathcal C^\circ\cap P$, contradicting its trivial stabiliser; otherwise the nonzero linear functional $x\mapsto B(x,\alpha)$ restricts to a nonzero functional on the two-plane $P$, whose kernel is a line. Each component is connected and the ambient chamber interiors form a disjoint open cover of it, so it lies in one chamber interior. Conversely, if a full-dimensional chamber section contained points from two components, choose them in its relative interior; their segment lies in that relative interior by convexity and crosses a root trace, contradicting disjointness of chamber interiors from the arrangement. facts.fact_text: [F8] The coordinate norm $\|\cdot\|_0$ and inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_0$ are the standard Euclidean ones on $\mathbb R^S$. For $n\ge1$ the coordinate unit sphere is nonempty (it contains each simple basis vector $\alpha_s$) and compact. The identity map is continuous, and a linear map $L$ is continuous because $\|Lx-Ly\|_0\le K\|x-y\|_0$ for some $K\ge0$. The inner product of continuous vector-valued maps is continuous, so $q(x)=\langle x,Ax\rangle_0$ is continuous; every continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact subset of $\mathbb R^n$ attains a maximum. [[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]], [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] (3), [[cor-euclidean-closed-balls-and-spheres-are-compact]], [[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]] (4)

proof_step_texts.2.1: 2.1 The unit sphere for $\|\cdot\|_0$ is compact, so $q$ attains a maximum $\lambda$ there; normalizing $e_s+e_t$ for an edge $\{s,t\}$ gives a positive value of $q$, so $\lambda>0$, and step 1.1 at a maximizer gives $\lambda<2$. Let $p$ be a unit maximizer. For $y$ with $\langle p,y\rangle_0=0$, maximality at $(p+ty)/(1+t^2\|y\|_0^2)^{1/2}$ gives $2t\langle Ap,y\rangle_0+t^2(q(y)-\lambda\|y\|_0^2)\le0$ for every real $t$. If $\langle Ap,y\rangle_0\ne0$, a sufficiently small $t$ of the same sign makes the linear term dominate the quadratic term, a contradiction. Thus $Ap$ is orthogonal to every $y\perp p$, so it is a multiple of $p$; pairing with $p$ gives $Ap=\lambda p$. [F2, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 Write $\|x\|_0^2:=\sum_{s\in S}x_s^2$ for the standard coordinate norm and set $q(x):=x^{\mathsf T}Ax$. If $m(s,t)=\infty$ for distinct $s,t$, then $B(e_s+e_t,e_s+e_t)=0$, contradicting positive definiteness; hence every off-diagonal Coxeter exponent is finite. Therefore $A_{ss}=0$ and $A_{st}=-2B(e_s,e_t)=2\cos(\pi/m(s,t))\ge0$ for $s\ne t$, with $A_{st}>0$ exactly on the edges of the connected diagram. Also $q(x)=2\|x\|_0^2-2B(x,x)<2\|x\|_0^2$ for every nonzero $x$. [F1, F2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.2: 1.2 For $1\le i\le n$, the first $n$ prefix vectors satisfy $\rho_i=\alpha_i$ for $i\le r$ and $\rho_i=\rho(a)\alpha_i=\alpha_i+\sum_{s\in J}A_{si}\alpha_s$ for $i>r$: the earlier reflections in the same color class fix $\alpha_i$, while each reflection in the other class adds its $A_{si}\alpha_s$ and fixes the other roots of that class. Hence the coordinate matrix of $(\rho_1,\dots,\rho_n)$ relative to the ordered basis $(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ is block upper triangular with identity diagonal blocks, so these vectors form a basis. The cyclic definitions give $\rho_{i+n}=C_V\rho_i$ and $\mu_{i+n}=C_V\mu_i$ for every $i\ge1$, because each block of $n$ reflections has product $c$. Each $\rho_i$ is a root, being the image of a simple root by an element of $W$. [F1, F2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.2.1: 2.1 The unit sphere for $\|\cdot\|_0$ is compact, so $q$ attains a maximum $\lambda$ there; normalizing $e_s+e_t$ for an edge $\{s,t\}$ gives a positive value of $q$, so $\lambda>0$, and step 1.1 at a maximizer gives $\lambda<2$. Let $p$ be a unit maximizer. For $y$ with $\langle p,y\rangle_0=0$, maximality at $(p+ty)/(1+t^2\|y\|_0^2)^{1/2}$ gives $2t\langle Ap,y\rangle_0+t^2(q(y)-\lambda\|y\|_0^2)\le0$ for every real $t$. If $\langle Ap,y\rangle_0\ne0$, a sufficiently small $t$ of the same sign makes the linear term dominate the quadratic term, a contradiction. Thus $Ap$ is orthogonal to every $y\perp p$, so it is a multiple of $p$; pairing with $p$ gives $Ap=\lambda p$. [F2, F8, step 1.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 For $1\le i\le n$, duality gives $B(\beta_i,\alpha_j)=0$ for every $j\ne i$, so $R_j\beta_i=\beta_i$ for every $j\ne i$ and in particular $\mu_i=R_1\cdots R_{i-1}\beta_i=\beta_i$. Also $R_i\beta_i=\beta_i-2\alpha_i$. Thus $C_V\beta_i=R_1\cdots R_n\beta_i=R_1\cdots R_{i-1}(\beta_i-2\alpha_i)=\mu_i-2\rho_i=\beta_i-2\rho_i$, so $(C_V-\mathrm{id}_V)\beta_i=-2\rho_i$. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 Put $d':=\sum_{t\in K}p_t^2$. Since distinct simple roots in either color class are orthogonal, $B(u,u)=d$ and $B(v,v)=d'$. Multiplying the eigenvector equations $\sum_{t\in K}A_{st}p_t=\lambda p_s$ by $p_s$ and summing over $s\in J$ gives $\sum_{s\in J,t\in K}p_sA_{st}p_t=\lambda d$; summing the equations indexed by $K$ gives the same left side equal to $\lambda d'$, hence $d=d'>0$. Finally $B(u,v)=-\frac12\sum_{s\in J,t\in K}p_sA_{st}p_t=-\lambda d/2$. The Gram matrix on $(u,v)$ is $d\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-\lambda/2\\-\lambda/2&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $d^2(1-\lambda^2/4)>0$, so $u,v$ are independent and $P$ is a plane. [F1, F2, step 3.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.5.1: 5.1 For $s\in J$, $R_s$ fixes $\alpha_{s'}$ for $s'\in J\setminus\{s\}$ and negates $\alpha_s$; the corresponding statement holds in $K$. Summing with coefficients $p_t$ and $p_s$ and using $Ap=\lambda p$ yields $\rho(a)u=-u$, $\rho(a)v=v+\lambda u$, $\rho(b)v=-v$, and $\rho(b)u=u+\lambda v$. facts.fact_text: [F6] The longest element satisfies $\rho(w_0)\Phi_+=\Phi_-$, $\ell(w_0)=|\Phi_+|=|T|$, $w_0^2=1$, and it is the unique element of length $\ell(w_0)$. [[thm-cg-finite-parabolic-longest-element-and-opposition]] (1)(ii)-(iv)

proof_step_texts.14.1: 14.1 Let $q:=hn/2$. The word $w=c^{h/2}$ for even $h$, or $w=c^{(h-1)/2}a$ for odd $h$, has exactly $q$ letters; in the odd case this uses $r=n/2$ from 11.1. Its prefix roots are $\rho_1,\dots,\rho_q$ by the cyclic definition, and these are positive by 13.1. At each step the root-length criterion therefore increases the prefix length by one, so the word is reduced and $\ell(w)=q=\ell(w_0)$. By uniqueness of the longest element, $w=w_0$, proving the formulas for $w_0$ in (3). [F5, F6, step 11.1, step 13.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.15.1: 15.1 The full word $(s_1\cdots s_n)^h$ represents $1$ and splits after its first $q$ letters, whose product is $w_0$ by 14.1. Every prefix of a reduced word is reduced; applying the root-length criterion at each next letter shows that every prefix root of this suffix is positive. direct_paragraphs: Let $(W,S)$ be an irreducible finite-type Coxeter system with $|S|=n\ge2$, with bipartition $J\sqcup K=S$ and data $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$, $s_1,\dots,s_n$, $a,b,c=ab$, $h=\operatorname{ord}(c)$, $\beta_i,\rho_i,\mu_i$ and conditional map $\mu$ as in [[def-cg-bipartite-coxeter-element-and-root-recursion]]. Put $r:=|J|$, so $J=\{s_1,\dots,s_r\}$ and $K=\{s_{r+1},\dots,s_n\}$. Let $C_V:=\rho(c)\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ denote the linear action of $c$, let $\mathcal C$ be the primal chamber in $V$ and $\mathcal C^\circ$ its interior, and let $H_\alpha=\{x\in V:B(x,\alpha)=0\}$ be the root hyperplanes ([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]], [[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]], [[def-cg-finite-reflection-arrangement-and-spherical-chambers]]). Write $w_0$ for the longest element ([[thm-cg-finite-parabolic-longest-element-and-opposition]]). Then:

facts.fact_text: [F2] $B$ is positive definite, $\rho$ is faithful and preserves $B$, and every root satisfies $B(\alpha,\alpha)=1$; for each $s$, $R_s=\rho(s)$ is the reflection $x\mapsto x-2B(x,\alpha_s)\alpha_s$. proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 Write $\|x\|_0^2:=\sum_{s\in S}x_s^2$ for the standard coordinate norm and set $q(x):=x^{\mathsf T}Ax$. If $m(s,t)=\infty$ for distinct $s,t$, then $B(e_s+e_t,e_s+e_t)=0$, contradicting positive definiteness; hence every off-diagonal Coxeter exponent is finite. Therefore $A_{ss}=0$ and $A_{st}=-2B(e_s,e_t)=2\cos(\pi/m(s,t))\ge0$ for $s\ne t$, with $A_{st}>0$ exactly on the edges of the connected diagram. Also $q(x)=2\|x\|_0^2-2B(x,x)<2\|x\|_0^2$ for every nonzero $x$. [F1, F2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.2: 1.2 For $1\le i\le n$, the first $n$ prefix vectors satisfy $\rho_i=\alpha_i$ for $i\le r$ and $\rho_i=\rho(a)\alpha_i=\alpha_i+\sum_{s\in J}A_{si}\alpha_s$ for $i>r$: the earlier reflections in the same color class fix $\alpha_i$, while each reflection in the other class adds its $A_{si}\alpha_s$ and fixes the other roots of that class. Hence the coordinate matrix of $(\rho_1,\dots,\rho_n)$ relative to the ordered basis $(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ is block upper triangular with identity diagonal blocks, so these vectors form a basis. The cyclic definitions give $\rho_{i+n}=C_V\rho_i$ and $\mu_{i+n}=C_V\mu_i$ for every $i\ge1$, because each block of $n$ reflections has product $c$. Each $\rho_i$ is a root, being the image of a simple root by an element of $W$. [F1, F2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.2.1: 2.1 The unit sphere for $\|\cdot\|_0$ is compact, so $q$ attains a maximum $\lambda$ there; normalizing $e_s+e_t$ for an edge $\{s,t\}$ gives a positive value of $q$, so $\lambda>0$, and step 1.1 at a maximizer gives $\lambda<2$. If $\langle Ap,y\rangle_0\ne0$, a sufficiently small $t$ of the same sign makes the linear term dominate the quadratic term, a contradiction. Thus $Ap$ is orthogonal to every $y\perp p$, so it is a multiple of $p$; pairing with $p$ gives $Ap=\lambda p$. [F2, F8, step 1.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 For $1\le i\le n$, duality gives $B(\beta_i,\alpha_j)=0$ for every $j\ne i$, so $R_j\beta_i=\beta_i$ for every $j\ne i$ and in particular $\mu_i=R_1\cdots R_{i-1}\beta_i=\beta_i$. Every element of $W_J$ reduces to a product of a subset $I\subseteq J$ because its simple generators are commuting involutions; the subset products are distinct because their $\rho$-images have different signs on the independent simple roots and $\rho$ is faithful by [F2]. The image of the product for $I$ acts by $-1$ on $\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_s:s\in I\}$ and by $+1$ on its $B$-orthogonal complement, so its $(-1)$-eigenspace has dimension $|I|$; therefore it is a reflection exactly when $|I|=1$, and the reflections in $W_J$ are precisely its $|J|=r$ simple generators. The same reasoning gives exactly $|K|=n-r$ reflections in $W_K$. The $2h$ distinct boundary rays from 8.1 alternate between the two types, so there are $h$ of each; conjugating the stabiliser count around them gives $hr+h(n-r)=hn$ incidences between rays and ambient root hyperplanes. Each hyperplane contributes exactly two incidences because its trace is a line. Hence the arrangement has $hn/2$ hyperplanes, so $|T|=hn/2$ by the root-reflection correspondence of [F7]. [F1, F2, F4, F7, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, step 9.1, algebra]

facts.fact_text: [F2] $B$ is positive definite, $\rho$ is faithful and preserves $B$, and every root satisfies $B(\alpha,\alpha)=1$; for each $s$, $R_s=\rho(s)$ is the reflection $x\mapsto x-2B(x,\alpha_s)\alpha_s$. [[thm-cg-finite-type-positive-definite-criterion]], [[lem-cg-reflection-representation-descends-and-root-norms]] (1)-(3), [[thm-cg-root-length-criterion-and-faithfulness]] (3)

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 Write $\|x\|_0^2:=\sum_{s\in S}x_s^2$ for the standard coordinate norm and set $q(x):=x^{\mathsf T}Ax$. If $m(s,t)=\infty$ for distinct $s,t$, then $B(e_s+e_t,e_s+e_t)=0$, contradicting positive definiteness; hence every off-diagonal Coxeter exponent is finite. Therefore $A_{ss}=0$ and $A_{st}=-2B(e_s,e_t)=2\cos(\pi/m(s,t))\ge0$ for $s\ne t$, with $A_{st}>0$ exactly on the edges of the connected diagram. Also $q(x)=2\|x\|_0^2-2B(x,x)<2\|x\|_0^2$ for every nonzero $x$. [F1, F2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.2: 1.2 For $1\le i\le n$, the first $n$ prefix vectors satisfy $\rho_i=\alpha_i$ for $i\le r$ and $\rho_i=\rho(a)\alpha_i=\alpha_i+\sum_{s\in J}A_{si}\alpha_s$ for $i>r$: the earlier reflections in the same color class fix $\alpha_i$, while each reflection in the other class adds its $A_{si}\alpha_s$ and fixes the other roots of that class. Hence the coordinate matrix of $(\rho_1,\dots,\rho_n)$ relative to the ordered basis $(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ is block upper triangular with identity diagonal blocks, so these vectors form a basis. The cyclic definitions give $\rho_{i+n}=C_V\rho_i$ and $\mu_{i+n}=C_V\mu_i$ for every $i\ge1$, because each block of $n$ reflections has product $c$. Each $\rho_i$ is a root, being the image of a simple root by an element of $W$. [F1, F2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.2.1: 2.1 The unit sphere for $\|\cdot\|_0$ is compact, so $q$ attains a maximum $\lambda$ there; normalizing $e_s+e_t$ for an edge $\{s,t\}$ gives a positive value of $q$, so $\lambda>0$, and step 1.1 at a maximizer gives $\lambda<2$. Let $p$ be a unit maximizer. For $y$ with $\langle p,y\rangle_0=0$, maximality at $(p+ty)/(1+t^2\|y\|_0^2)^{1/2}$ gives $2t\langle Ap,y\rangle_0+t^2(q(y)-\lambda\|y\|_0^2)\le0$ for every real $t$. If $\langle Ap,y\rangle_0\ne0$, a sufficiently small $t$ of the same sign makes the linear term dominate the quadratic term, a contradiction. Thus $Ap$ is orthogonal to every $y\perp p$, so it is a multiple of $p$; pairing with $p$ gives $Ap=\lambda p$. [F2, F8, step 1.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 For $1\le i\le n$, duality gives $B(\beta_i,\alpha_j)=0$ for every $j\ne i$, so $R_j\beta_i=\beta_i$ for every $j\ne i$ and in particular $\mu_i=R_1\cdots R_{i-1}\beta_i=\beta_i$. Also $R_i\beta_i=\beta_i-2\alpha_i$. Thus $C_V\beta_i=R_1\cdots R_n\beta_i=R_1\cdots R_{i-1}(\beta_i-2\alpha_i)=\mu_i-2\rho_i=\beta_i-2\rho_i$, so $(C_V-\mathrm{id}_V)\beta_i=-2\rho_i$. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 Put $d':=\sum_{t\in K}p_t^2$. Since distinct simple roots in either color class are orthogonal, $B(u,u)=d$ and $B(v,v)=d'$. Multiplying the eigenvector equations $\sum_{t\in K}A_{st}p_t=\lambda p_s$ by $p_s$ and summing over $s\in J$ gives $\sum_{s\in J,t\in K}p_sA_{st}p_t=\lambda d$; summing the equations indexed by $K$ gives the same left side equal to $\lambda d'$, hence $d=d'>0$. Finally $B(u,v)=-\frac12\sum_{s\in J,t\in K}p_sA_{st}p_t=-\lambda d/2$. The Gram matrix on $(u,v)$ is $d\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-\lambda/2\\-\lambda/2&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $d^2(1-\lambda^2/4)>0$, so $u,v$ are independent and $P$ is a plane. [F1, F2, step 3.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.5.1: 5.1 For $s\in J$, $R_s$ fixes $\alpha_{s'}$ for $s'\in J\setminus\{s\}$ and negates $\alpha_s$; the corresponding statement holds in $K$. For $t\in K$, the commuting reflections in $a$ give $\rho(a)\alpha_t=\alpha_t+\sum_{s\in J}A_{st}\alpha_s$, and for $s\in J$, $\rho(b)\alpha_s=\alpha_s+\sum_{t\in K}A_{ts}\alpha_t$. Summing with coefficients $p_t$ and $p_s$ and using $Ap=\lambda p$ yields $\rho(a)u=-u$, $\rho(a)v=v+\lambda u$, $\rho(b)v=-v$, and $\rho(b)u=u+\lambda v$. Thus $P$ is invariant under $\rho(a),\rho(b)$ and $C_V=\rho(a)\rho(b)$. [F1, F2, step 4.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.6.1: 6.1 In the basis $(u,v)$, $\rho(a)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&\lambda\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $\rho(b)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\\lambda&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, and $C_V|_P=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\lambda^2-1&-\lambda\\\lambda&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The vectors $f_1:=u/\sqrt d$ and $f_2:=(v+\frac\lambda2u)/\sqrt{d(1-\lambda^2/4)}$ are $B$-orthonormal, and direct substitution gives $C_Vf_1=(\lambda^2/2-1)f_1+\lambda\sqrt{1-\lambda^2/4}\,f_2$. With $\theta:=\arccos(\lambda/2)\in(0,\pi/2)$ these coefficients are $\cos(2\theta)$ and $\sin(2\theta)$; since $C_V$ preserves $B$ and has determinant $1$ on $P$, it is the rotation through $2\theta$. [F2, step 5.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.7.1: 7.1 For $x=\xi u+\eta v\in P$, one has $B(x,\alpha_s)=p_s(\xi-\frac\lambda2\eta)$ for $s\in J$ and $B(x,\alpha_t)=p_t(\eta-\frac\lambda2\xi)$ for $t\in K$. Thus $\mathcal C\cap P$ is given by $\xi\ge\frac\lambda2\eta$ and $\eta\ge\frac\lambda2\xi$; because $0<\lambda/2<1$, these inequalities imply $\xi,\eta\ge0$, and their strict versions place the relative interior in $\mathcal C^\circ$. Its boundary rays are $x_J:=\lambda u+2v$ (the $J$ simple-root hyperplanes) and $x_K:=2u+\lambda v$ (the $K$ simple-root hyperplanes). Their squared $B$-norms are both $d(4-\lambda^2)$ and $B(x_J,x_K)=\lambda d(2-\lambda^2/2)$, so the sector angle has cosine $\lambda/2$ and equals $\theta$. The restrictions of $\rho(a)$ and $\rho(b)$ are reflections in the lines $\mathbb R x_J$ and $\mathbb R x_K$: they fix those lines, are involutions, and are nonidentity on $P$ by 4.1. [F1, F2, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.8.1: 8.1 Let $m_0$ be the order of $C_V|_P$. Since it rotates through $2\theta\in(0,\pi)$, $m_0\ge3$ and $2\theta=2\pi j/m_0$ for an integer $j$ with $1\le j<m_0/2$ and $\gcd(j,m_0)=1$. The subgroup $D:=\langle\rho(a)|_P,\rho(b)|_P\rangle$ consists of the $m_0$ distinct rotations $(C_V|_P)^k$ and the $m_0$ distinct reflections $\rho(a)|_P(C_V|_P)^k$, so $|D|=2m_0$. Distinct elements of $D$ have lifts $\tilde g\in\langle a,b\rangle$ with distinct restrictions to $P$, hence are distinct elements of $W$; by F4 their chamber interiors are distinct and disjoint. Thus the orbit of $S_0:=\mathcal C\cap P$ consists of $2m_0$ distinct sectors of angle $\theta$, each of the form $\rho(\tilde g)\mathcal C\cap P$, with pairwise disjoint relative interiors. Hence $2m_0\theta\le2\pi$, so $j=1$ and $\theta=\pi/m_0$; equality shows the sectors cover $P$. As $m_0\mid h$ by F1, the element $c^{m_0}$ fixes every point of $P$, in particular a point of $\mathcal C^\circ\cap P$; its stabiliser is trivial, so $c^{m_0}=1$ and $h\mid m_0$. Thus $m_0=h$ and $\lambda=2\cos(\pi/h)$, completing (1) and the angle claims of (2). [F1, F2, F4, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.9.1: 9.1 For every root $\alpha$, the trace $H_\alpha\cap P$ is a line: if $P\subseteq H_\alpha$, the nonidentity reflection $t_\alpha$ fixes a point of $\mathcal C^\circ\cap P$, contradicting its trivial stabiliser; otherwise the nonzero linear functional $x\mapsto B(x,\alpha)$ restricts to a nonzero functional on the two-plane $P$, whose kernel is a line. Each such line is a root-hyperplane trace and cannot meet the relative interior of any sector $\rho(\tilde g)S_0$, because that relative interior lies in the chamber interior $\rho(\tilde g)\mathcal C^\circ$, which is disjoint from the arrangement. Conversely the two boundary lines of $S_0$ are traces of simple-root hyperplanes by 7.1, and their images under $D$ are root-hyperplane traces because $\rho(W)$ permutes roots. These images are all the sector boundary lines: the $2h$ sectors from 8.1 tile $P$ and have $2h$ distinct boundary rays, while every root trace must be one of those lines because it cannot meet a sector interior. Opposite rays define the same line, so the traces are exactly $h$ distinct lines. The connected components of the complement of these lines are the sector interiors. Each component is connected and the ambient chamber interiors form a disjoint open cover of it, so it lies in one chamber interior. Conversely, if a full-dimensional chamber section contained points from two components, choose them in its relative interior; their segment lies in that relative interior by convexity and crosses a root trace, contradicting disjointness of chamber interiors from the arrangement. Hence the full-dimensional chamber sections are exactly the $2h$ sectors. [F2, F4, step 7.1, step 8.1, algebra]

Every element of $W_J$ reduces to a product of a subset $I\subseteq J$ because its simple generators are commuting involutions; the subset products are distinct because their $\rho$-images have different signs on the independent simple roots and $\rho$ is faithful by [F2]. The same reasoning gives exactly $|K|=n-r$ reflections in $W_K$. The $2h$ distinct boundary rays from 8.1 alternate between the two types, so there are $h$ of each; conjugating the stabiliser count around them gives $hr+h(n-r)=hn$ incidences between rays and ambient root hyperplanes. Each hyperplane contributes exactly two incidences because its trace is a line. Hence the arrangement has $hn/2$ hyperplanes, so $|T|=hn/2$ by the root-reflection correspondence of [F7]. [F1, F2, F4, F7, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, step 9.1, algebra]

facts.fact_text: [F5] For every $w\in W$ and $s\in S$, $\ell(ws)>\ell(w)$ if and only if $\rho(w)\alpha_s\in\Phi_+$. [[thm-cg-root-length-criterion-and-faithfulness]] (1)

proof_step_texts.14.1: 14.1 Let $q:=hn/2$. The word $w=c^{h/2}$ for even $h$, or $w=c^{(h-1)/2}a$ for odd $h$, has exactly $q$ letters; in the odd case this uses $r=n/2$ from 11.1. Its prefix roots are $\rho_1,\dots,\rho_q$ by the cyclic definition, and these are positive by 13.1. At each step the root-length criterion therefore increases the prefix length by one, so the word is reduced and $\ell(w)=q=\ell(w_0)$. By uniqueness of the longest element, $w=w_0$, proving the formulas for $w_0$ in (3). [F5, F6, step 11.1, step 13.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.15.1: 15.1 The full word $(s_1\cdots s_n)^h$ represents $1$ and splits after its first $q$ letters, whose product is $w_0$ by 14.1. Its remaining $q$-letter suffix also represents $w_0^{-1}=w_0$, so it is reduced. Every prefix of a reduced word is reduced; applying the root-length criterion at each next letter shows that every prefix root of this suffix is positive. Its corresponding global prefix root is obtained by applying $\rho(w_0)$ and is therefore negative by [F6]. The second half in 12.1 has pairwise distinct hyperplanes, so these negative roots are pairwise distinct as well. Hence the first $q$ roots are all of $\Phi_+$ because $|\Phi_+|=|T|=q$ by [F6] and 10.1, and the second $q$ are all of $\Phi_-=-\Phi_+$. The first and second lists are disjoint by sign, giving pairwise distinctness of all $nh$ roots; $C_V^h=\mathrm{id}_V$ gives period $nh$, and that distinctness makes it exact. This proves (3). [F3, F5, F6, step 10.1, step 12.1, step 13.1, step 14.1, algebra]
