The lower-rank induction gives $c[F_0]=Z(\sigma_0,\tau_{i_0-1})$, a full-dimensional convex cone in $L_0:=M(\sigma_0)$ with facet supports restricted from $\mu(b)^\perp$ for roots $b\in P_{\sigma_0}$. [F2, F3, F5, F7]
proof_step_texts.2.3:
2.3 **Transporting the base facets through an apex.** The following calculation applies both to the base apex $a=	heta_k$ and to an inductive apex $a=	au_{i+1}$. Let $L=M(\sigma)\cap\mu(a)^\perp=M(R(a)\sigma)$, let $F$ be the already established full-dimensional base cone in $L$, and let a facet of $F$ have support the restriction of $\mu(b)^\perp$ for some $b\in P_{R(a)\sigma}\subseteq L$. Put $E:=M(\sigma)$ and $V_a:=F+\mathbb R_{\ge0}a$. For $x\in E$, the decomposition $x=y+t a$, with $t=B(x,\mu(a))$ and $y\in L$, is unique. Thus $x\in V_a$ exactly when $t\ge0$ and $y\in F$. If a facet of $F$ is given by $\varepsilon B(y,\mu(b))\ge0$ with $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$, its transported inequality is $\varepsilon B(x,
u)\ge0$, where $
u:=\mu(b)-B(\mu(b),a)\mu(a)$; it vanishes at $a$ and agrees with $\mu(b)$ on $L$. Since $B(\mu(a),b)=0$ and $\mu+\mu^*=2I$, $B(\mu(b),a)=2B(b,a)$, so $
u=\mu igl(b-2B(b,a)a igr)=\mu(R(a)b)$. The equality of $F$ with the intersection of its active facet halfspaces therefore gives a finite halfspace presentation of $V_a$ in $E$ by $B(x,\mu(a))\ge0$ and the transported inequalities; step 1.3 identifies its nonredundant inequalities with its facets. The vector $R(a)b$ is a signed root in $M(\sigma)$, so its positive representative $r$ belongs to $P_\sigma$ by [F3]. Thus every non-base facet of $V_a$ is a root-wall facet. [F1, F3, F5, F6, F9, F14, step 1.3]
proof_step_texts.2.4: 2.4 **Inductive root-prefix step.** Suppose $i\ge i_0$ and $K_i:=c[X(\sigma,\tau_i)]=Z(\sigma,\tau_i)$. Put $a:=\tau_{i+1}$ and $\sigma':=R(a)\sigma$. Since $R(a)\le_T\sigma\le_Tc$, write $c=\sigma v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-k$ and $\sigma=R(a)\sigma'$. Then $R(a)c=\sigma'v$; also $\ell_T(R(a)c)=n-1$, since $R(a)\le_Tc$, so $\sigma'\le_T R(a)c\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(\sigma')=k-1$. The subspace $M(\sigma')$ lies in $M(\sigma)$ because $\sigma$ and $R(a)$ preserve $M(\sigma)$, and it lies in $M(R(a)c)=\mu(a)^\perp$ by absolute-order monotonicity. Both $M(\sigma')$ and $M(\sigma)\cap\mu(a)^\perp$ have dimension $k-1$: the latter is the kernel of the nonzero functional $x\mapsto B(x,\mu(a))$ on $M(\sigma)$, which is nonzero on $a\in M(\sigma)$ since $B(a,\mu(a))=1$. Hence $M(\sigma')=M(\sigma)\cap\mu(a)^\perp$ and $P_{\sigma'}=P_\sigma\cap\mu(a)^\perp$. The link base $F$ on the old vertices orthogonal to $\mu(a)$ satisfies $c[F]=K_i\cap\mu(a)^\perp$: all old vertices have nonpositive pairing with $\mu(a)$, so a nonnegative combination pairs to zero exactly when it uses only zero-pairing vertices. Thus $F=X(\sigma',\tau_i)$. Let $\epsilon'_1,\dots,\epsilon'_{k-1}$ be the prefix roots for the canonical simple system of $\sigma'$. They lie in $M(\sigma')$, so $B(\mu(a),\epsilon'_j)=0$. If $\epsilon'_j>a$, the distinct reflections $R(a)$ and $R(\epsilon'_j)$ have product length $2$ by the determinant argument in [F9]. Since $R(\epsilon'_j)\le_TR(a)c$, write $R(a)c=R(\epsilon'_j)v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-2$; then $c=R(a)R(\epsilon'_j)v$ is reduced, so $R(a)R(\epsilon'_j)\le_Tc$. By [F10] and the increasing order $a<\epsilon'_j$, this is the endpoint factorization of the rank-two element $w:=R(a)R(\epsilon'_j)$, so $B(a,\epsilon'_j)\le0$. The root $d:=R(a)\epsilon'_j=\epsilon'_j-2B(\epsilon'_j,a)a$ is a nonzero nonnegative combination of the endpoints; hence has nonnegative simple-root coordinates and is positive by [F15]. Since it lies in $M(w)$, [F3] puts it in $P_w$; it cannot equal $a$, since that would imply $\epsilon'_j=R(a)a=-a$. Thus $a<d$ in the global order. Since $a,\epsilon'_j\in M(\sigma)$ and $R(a)$ preserves $M(\sigma)$, this positive root lies in $P_\sigma=\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$. Now $\sigma'^{-1}\epsilon'_j=\sigma^{-1}d$ is negative by step 1.1 applied to $\sigma'$, so step 1.1 applied to $\sigma$ gives $d\in\{\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k\}$, contradicting $d>a\ge\theta_k$. Hence every $\epsilon'_j<a$, and therefore $\theta'_{k-1}\le\tau_i$. Let $b$ be the last root of $P_{\sigma'}$ at or below $\tau_i$; it exists since $\theta'_{k-1}$ is such a root, and $b\ge\theta'_{k-1}$. Then $F=X(\sigma',\tau_i)=X(\sigma',b)$, so lower-rank induction gives $c[F]=Z(\sigma',b)$, full-dimensional and convex in $L=M(\sigma')$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, F9, F10, F13, F15, step 1.1]

facts.fact_text: [F6] For orthogonal $A$, $M(A)=F(A)^\perp$. Every subspace $U\subseteq M(A)$ has an orthogonal restriction with moved space $U$, and for group elements Carter's formula transfers this restriction order to absolute order. [[lem-cg-orthogonal-wall-form-and-subspace-restriction]] (1),(3)-(5) [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]]

proof_step_texts.1.2: 1.2 **The first separator.** Write $s=R(\tau_s)$ and $a=R(\tau_a)$. Since $B(\mu(\tau_s),\tau_a)=0$, [F2] and [F6] give $\tau_a\in M(sc)$ and hence $a\le_Tsc$. The distinct reflections $s,a$ have product determinant $+1$ and nonidentity image, whereas every reflection has determinant $-1$; hence $\ell_T(sa)=2$. Writing $sc=az$ gives $c=saz$ with $2+\ell_T(z)=\ell_T(c)$, so $sa\le_Tc$. Its moved space is contained in $M(\sigma)$ because both normals lie there, hence [F5] gives $sa\le_T\sigma$. The rank-two statement [F10] applied to $sa$ shows that $\tau_s$ and $\tau_a$ are the ordered endpoints of the simple system of $P_{sa}$. Put $\tau_b:=R(\tau_a)\tau_s=\tau_s-2B(\tau_s,\tau_a)\tau_a$. The endpoint pairing in [F10] makes this a nonzero nonnegative combination of the endpoints; [F9] says it is a root, and [F15] makes it positive because its simple-root coordinates are nonnegative. The reflection $R(\tau_a)$ preserves $M(sa)$, so $\tau_b\in P_{sa}$. The endpoints are the least and greatest roots of $P_{sa}$, hence $\tau_s\le\tau_b\le\tau_a$; equality $\tau_b=\tau_a$ would imply $\tau_s=-\tau_a$, so $\tau_b<\tau_a$. Thus $\tau_b\in P_\sigma$ as $sa\le_T\sigma$. The pair $(\tau_b,\tau_a)$ has reverse product $R(\tau_a)R(\tau_b)=sa\le_Tc$ of length $2$, so [F7] gives $B(\mu(\tau_a),\tau_b)=0$. Also $B(\mu(\tau_s),\tau_b)=B(\mu(\tau_s),\tau_s-2B(\tau_s,\tau_a)\tau_a)=1>0$. [F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, F9, F10, F15]
proof_step_texts.2.1: 2.1 **The opposite separator.** Set $\tau_c:=\sigma^{-1}\tau_s$. By [F1], $\tau_s\in P_\sigma$; the hypothesis excludes the inversion roots in [F3], so [F4] and step 1.1 imply $\tau_c\in P_\sigma$. Put $t:=R(\tau_s)$ and $u:=t\sigma$. Write $\sigma=tu_0$ with additive reflection lengths, so $u=u_0$ and $u_0^{-1}\sigma=u_0^{-1}tu_0$ has length $1$; hence $u\le_T\sigma$. If $c=\sigma v$ is reduced, then $tc=u_0v$ and $\ell_T(tc)=n-1=\ell_T(u_0)+\ell_T(v)$ because $t\le_T\sigma\le_Tc$, so also $u\le_Ttc$. The vector $\mu(\tau_s)$ is fixed by $tc$ by [F2], hence by $u$ using [F5]-[F6]. Let $p$ be the orthogonal projection of $\mu(\tau_s)$ onto $M(\sigma)$. Its residual lies in $F(\sigma)\subseteq F(u)$, so $p\in F(u)$ as well; projection preserves its pairing with $\tau_s\in M(\sigma)$, giving $B(p,\tau_s)=1$. Therefore $\sigma p=tp=p-2\tau_s$. Since $\sigma\tau_c=\tau_s$ and $\sigma$ is an isometry, $B(\mu(\tau_s),\tau_c)=B(p,\tau_c)=B(\sigma p,\tau_s)=B(p-2\tau_s,\tau_s)=-1$. By [F2], if $\tau_s<\tau_c$ then this pairing is nonnegative, and equality of the roots would give $1$; thus $\tau_c<\tau_s<\tau_a$. Since $s\sigma=\sigma R(\tau_c)$ and $sa\le_T\sigma$, one has $a\le_Ts\sigma=\sigma R(\tau_c)$. Write $s\sigma=az$ with $\ell_T(z)=k-2$. Then $\sigma=azR(\tau_c)$ and $(aR(\tau_c))^{-1}\sigma=R(\tau_c)zR(\tau_c)$ has length $k-2$ by conjugation invariance. The distinct reflections $a$ and $R(\tau_c)$ have product of determinant $+1$ and this product is nonidentity, so its reflection length is $2$; the length equality therefore gives $aR(\tau_c)\le_T\sigma\le_Tc$. Now [F7] gives $B(\mu(\tau_a),\tau_c)=0$. Together with step 1.2 this proves (1). [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F9]
proof_step_texts.2.3:
2.3 **Transporting the base facets through an apex.** The following calculation applies both to the base apex $a=	heta_k$ and to an inductive apex $a=	au_{i+1}$. Let $L=M(\sigma)\cap\mu(a)^\perp=M(R(a)\sigma)$, let $F$ be the already established full-dimensional base cone in $L$, and let a facet of $F$ have support the restriction of $\mu(b)^\perp$ for some $b\in P_{R(a)\sigma}\subseteq L$. Put $E:=M(\sigma)$ and $V_a:=F+\mathbb R_{\ge0}a$. For $x\in E$, the decomposition $x=y+t a$, with $t=B(x,\mu(a))$ and $y\in L$, is unique. Thus $x\in V_a$ exactly when $t\ge0$ and $y\in F$. If a facet of $F$ is given by $\varepsilon B(y,\mu(b))\ge0$ with $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$, its transported inequality is $\varepsilon B(x,
u)\ge0$, where $
u:=\mu(b)-B(\mu(b),a)\mu(a)$; it vanishes at $a$ and agrees with $\mu(b)$ on $L$. Since $B(\mu(a),b)=0$ and $\mu+\mu^*=2I$, $B(\mu(b),a)=2B(b,a)$, so $
u=\mu igl(b-2B(b,a)a igr)=\mu(R(a)b)$. The equality of $F$ with the intersection of its active facet halfspaces therefore gives a finite halfspace presentation of $V_a$ in $E$ by $B(x,\mu(a))\ge0$ and the transported inequalities; step 1.3 identifies its nonredundant inequalities with its facets. The vector $R(a)b$ is a signed root in $M(\sigma)$, so its positive representative $r$ belongs to $P_\sigma$ by [F3]. Thus every non-base facet of $V_a$ is a root-wall facet. [F1, F3, F5, F6, F9, F14, step 1.3]
proof_step_texts.2.4: 2.4 **Inductive root-prefix step.** Suppose $i\ge i_0$ and $K_i:=c[X(\sigma,\tau_i)]=Z(\sigma,\tau_i)$. Put $a:=\tau_{i+1}$ and $\sigma':=R(a)\sigma$. Since $R(a)\le_T\sigma\le_Tc$, write $c=\sigma v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-k$ and $\sigma=R(a)\sigma'$. Then $R(a)c=\sigma'v$; also $\ell_T(R(a)c)=n-1$, since $R(a)\le_Tc$, so $\sigma'\le_T R(a)c\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(\sigma')=k-1$. The subspace $M(\sigma')$ lies in $M(\sigma)$ because $\sigma$ and $R(a)$ preserve $M(\sigma)$, and it lies in $M(R(a)c)=\mu(a)^\perp$ by absolute-order monotonicity. Both $M(\sigma')$ and $M(\sigma)\cap\mu(a)^\perp$ have dimension $k-1$: the latter is the kernel of the nonzero functional $x\mapsto B(x,\mu(a))$ on $M(\sigma)$, which is nonzero on $a\in M(\sigma)$ since $B(a,\mu(a))=1$. Hence $M(\sigma')=M(\sigma)\cap\mu(a)^\perp$ and $P_{\sigma'}=P_\sigma\cap\mu(a)^\perp$. The link base $F$ on the old vertices orthogonal to $\mu(a)$ satisfies $c[F]=K_i\cap\mu(a)^\perp$: all old vertices have nonpositive pairing with $\mu(a)$, so a nonnegative combination pairs to zero exactly when it uses only zero-pairing vertices. Thus $F=X(\sigma',\tau_i)$. Let $\epsilon'_1,\dots,\epsilon'_{k-1}$ be the prefix roots for the canonical simple system of $\sigma'$. They lie in $M(\sigma')$, so $B(\mu(a),\epsilon'_j)=0$. If $\epsilon'_j>a$, the distinct reflections $R(a)$ and $R(\epsilon'_j)$ have product length $2$ by the determinant argument in [F9]. Since $R(\epsilon'_j)\le_TR(a)c$, write $R(a)c=R(\epsilon'_j)v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-2$; then $c=R(a)R(\epsilon'_j)v$ is reduced, so $R(a)R(\epsilon'_j)\le_Tc$. By [F10] and the increasing order $a<\epsilon'_j$, this is the endpoint factorization of the rank-two element $w:=R(a)R(\epsilon'_j)$, so $B(a,\epsilon'_j)\le0$. The root $d:=R(a)\epsilon'_j=\epsilon'_j-2B(\epsilon'_j,a)a$ is a nonzero nonnegative combination of the endpoints; hence has nonnegative simple-root coordinates and is positive by [F15]. Since it lies in $M(w)$, [F3] puts it in $P_w$; it cannot equal $a$, since that would imply $\epsilon'_j=R(a)a=-a$. Thus $a<d$ in the global order. Since $a,\epsilon'_j\in M(\sigma)$ and $R(a)$ preserves $M(\sigma)$, this positive root lies in $P_\sigma=\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$. Now $\sigma'^{-1}\epsilon'_j=\sigma^{-1}d$ is negative by step 1.1 applied to $\sigma'$, so step 1.1 applied to $\sigma$ gives $d\in\{\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k\}$, contradicting $d>a\ge\theta_k$. Hence every $\epsilon'_j<a$, and therefore $\theta'_{k-1}\le\tau_i$. Let $b$ be the last root of $P_{\sigma'}$ at or below $\tau_i$; it exists since $\theta'_{k-1}$ is such a root, and $b\ge\theta'_{k-1}$. Then $F=X(\sigma',\tau_i)=X(\sigma',b)$, so lower-rank induction gives $c[F]=Z(\sigma',b)$, full-dimensional and convex in $L=M(\sigma')$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, F9, F10, F13, F15, step 1.1]
proof_step_texts.3.2: 3.2 The new prefix is $X(\sigma,\tau_{i+1})=X(\sigma,\tau_i)\cup(a*F)$ by [F7], so its cone is $K_{i+1}=K_i\cup V_a$ with $V_a=c[F]+\mathbb R_{\ge0}a$. Apply step 2.3 to each facet of $F$; every facet of $V_a$ is supported by $\mu(a)^\perp$ or by $\mu(r)^\perp$ for $r\in P_\sigma$. Each side facet contains $a$, so $B(\mu(r),a)=0$. If $r<a$ and $r$ is not a $\theta$-root, step 2.1 produces two vertices of $F$ on opposite sides of $\mu(r)^\perp$, contradicting support. Thus every facet label is a $\theta_j$, $a$, or a root $r>a$. Its containing halfspace is respectively $\mu(\theta_j)^+$, $\mu(a)^+$, or $\mu(r)^-$, by the sign inequalities in [F2]-[F3]. The cone $Z(\sigma,\tau_{i+1})\cap\mu(a)^+$ satisfies all these facet halfspaces; step 1.3 therefore puts it in $V_a$. Its other half $Z(\sigma,\tau_{i+1})\cap\mu(a)^-$ equals $Z(\sigma,\tau_i)=K_i$. Consequently $Z(\sigma,\tau_{i+1})\subseteq K_{i+1}$. The reverse containment follows from step 1.4, proving $K_{i+1}=Z(\sigma,\tau_{i+1})$. The active-facet list is a subset of the defining inequalities; any omitted or repeated inequality is recorded as redundant. [F2, F3, F6, F7, step 2.1, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 2.3, step 2.4]

facts.fact_text: [F3] $W_\sigma=\{w:M(w)\subseteq M(\sigma)\}$ is the finite reflection subgroup whose positive roots are $P_\sigma$. Since $M(t_\alpha)=\mathbb R\alpha$, this gives $P_\sigma=\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$. For $n\ge2$ it has a simple system $\Delta=\{\delta_1,\dots,\delta_k\}$, every root in $P_\sigma$ is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$, and the reordered roots $\theta_1<\dots<\theta_k$ give a reduced factorization $\sigma=R(\theta_k)\cdots R(\theta_1)$. The prefix roots $\epsilon_j=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{j-1})\delta_j$ are positive. [[lem-cg-ordered-root-pairings-and-simple-systems]] (4)(i)-(iv) [[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (1)

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 **Inversion inside a subinterval.** If $n=1$, (1) is vacuous because $P_\sigma$ has only its single positive root. Assume $n\ge2$. Fix $u\le_Tc$, $u\ne1$, and let $\Delta_u=\{d_1,\dots,d_m\}$ be the simple system of $P_u$ given by [F3]. The item-18 factorization, in its second form with index $1$, is $u=R(d_1)\cdots R(d_m)$; it is reduced because $\ell_T(u)=m$. Apply the inversion formula [F4] to the finite Coxeter system $W_u$ with simple system $\Delta_u$. Its positive roots are exactly $P_u$, so $\{\alpha\in P_u:u^{-1}\alpha\in-P_u\}=\{\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_m\}=\{\theta_1,\dots,\theta_m\}$, where the prefix roots are $\varepsilon_j=R(d_1)\cdots R(d_{j-1})d_j$. The action of $u$ preserves $M(u)$, so a root in $M(u)$ is negative in this subsystem exactly when it is negative in the ambient positive system. Thus for $\alpha\in P_u\setminus\{\theta_1,\dots,\theta_m\}$, $u^{-1}\alpha\in P_u$. [F3, F4]

proof_step_texts.1.4: 1.4 **The inclusions and rank base.** The root-reflection dictionary and the definition of $W_\sigma$ give $P_\sigma=\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$. For $n\ge2$, the wall statement (4)(iii) of item 18 and $B(\mu(\epsilon_j),\epsilon_j)=1$ from [F2] show that $\mu(\epsilon_j)\cdot\delta_l=1$ for $l=j$ and $0$ otherwise: the wall makes the off-diagonal pairings zero, and $\epsilon_j-\delta_j$ is a combination of earlier simple roots. Thus the restrictions $B(\mu(\epsilon_j),-)|_{M(\sigma)}$ form the basis dual to $\Delta$. Since the $\theta_j$ are a reordering of the $\epsilon_j$, the restricted pairing functionals $B(\mu(\theta_j),-)|_{M(\sigma)}$ are this same dual basis in a different order. Therefore [F3] gives $B(\mu(\theta_j),\tau)\ge0$ for every $\tau\in P_\sigma$. For $n=1$ the same inequalities follow directly from $P_\sigma=\{\theta_1\}$. If $\tau\le\tau_i$ and $j>i$, then $\tau<\tau_j$, so [F2] gives $B(\mu(\tau_j),\tau)\le0$. Consequently $Y(\sigma,\tau_i)\subseteq Z(\sigma,\tau_i)$; by definition $c[X(\sigma,\tau_i)]\subseteq Y(\sigma,\tau_i)$. If $k=1$, then $P_\sigma=\{\theta_1\}$: it is the positive root set on the one-dimensional space $M(\sigma)$, and unit normalization leaves one positive root. The only eligible prefix is the singleton, $c[X(\sigma,\theta_1)]=\mathbb R_{\ge0}\theta_1=M(\sigma)\cap\mu(\theta_1)^+$, whose sole facet is the origin in $\mu(\theta_1)^\perp$; this includes the empty base $X(1)=\{\emptyset\}$ with cone $\{0\}$. Suppose henceforth $k\ge2$, and let $i_0$ be the unique index with $\tau_{i_0}=\theta_k$. [F1, F2, F3, F7, F8, F9, F12]

By [F1], $\tau_s\in P_\sigma$; the hypothesis excludes the inversion roots in [F3], so [F4] and step 1.1 imply $\tau_c\in P_\sigma$. Put $t:=R(\tau_s)$ and $u:=t\sigma$. proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 **Base of the root-index induction.** Put $\sigma_0:=R(\theta_k)\sigma=R(\theta_{k-1})\cdots R(\theta_1)$. The prefix $\{\theta_1,\dots,\theta_{k-1}\}$ is a face of the canonical $k$-simplex by [F7], so $\sigma_0\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(\sigma_0)=k-1$. The tuple $\theta_1<\dots<\theta_{k-1}$ is eligible for $\sigma_0$, so [F3]'s componentwise minimality makes its canonical tuple $\theta'_1<\dots<\theta'_{k-1}$ satisfy $\theta'_j\le\theta_j$ for every $j$. In particular $\theta'_{k-1}<\theta_k$, and appending $\theta_k$ to this tuple gives an increasing reduced tuple for $\sigma$; componentwise minimality for $\sigma$ gives $\theta_j\le\theta'_j$ for $j<k$. Thus $\theta'_j=\theta_j$ for every $j<k$. Also $M(\sigma_0)=\operatorname{span}(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_{k-1})$. The dual-basis result of step 1.4 makes $B(\mu(\theta_k),\tau)\ge0$ for every $\tau\in P_\sigma$, while root order makes this pairing nonpositive when $\tau<\theta_k$ by [F2]; hence every such $\tau$ lies in $M(\sigma)\cap\mu(\theta_k)^\perp$. This hyperplane has dimension $k-1$ and contains the independent roots $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_{k-1}$, so $M(\sigma_0)=M(\sigma)\cap\mu(\theta_k)^\perp$. Since $\theta_{k-1}<\theta_k=\tau_{i_0}$, the prefix ending at $\tau_{i_0-1}$ is eligible for $\sigma_0$. Every $\tau_j<\theta_k$ has $B(\mu(\theta_k),\tau_j)\ge0$ by the dual-basis result above and $\le0$ by the global order, so these earlier roots lie in $M(\sigma_0)=M(\sigma)\cap\mu(\theta_k)^\perp$. Conversely $P_{\sigma_0}\subseteq P_\sigma$ by [F3]. Thus the two prefix vertex sets, and hence their full subcomplexes, agree: $F_0:=X(\sigma,\tau_{i_0-1})=X(\sigma_0,\tau_{i_0-1})$. The lower-rank induction gives $c[F_0]=Z(\sigma_0,\tau_{i_0-1})$, a full-dimensional convex cone in $L_0:=M(\sigma_0)$ with facet supports restricted from $\mu(b)^\perp$ for roots $b\in P_{\sigma_0}$. [F2, F3, F5, F7]

Since $a,\epsilon'_j\in M(\sigma)$ and $R(a)$ preserves $M(\sigma)$, this positive root lies in $P_\sigma=\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$. Hence every $\epsilon'_j<a$, and therefore $\theta'_{k-1}\le\tau_i$. Let $b$ be the last root of $P_{\sigma'}$ at or below $\tau_i$; it exists since $\theta'_{k-1}$ is such a root, and $b\ge\theta'_{k-1}$. proof_step_texts.3.1: 3.1 **Initial cone and its facets.** Let $K_{i_0}:=c[X(\sigma,\theta_k)]$. By [F7], $K_{i_0}=c[F_0]+\mathbb R_{\ge0}\theta_k$, so it is a full-dimensional convex cone. The base support is $\mu(\theta_k)^\perp$; each other facet has support $\mu(r)^\perp$ for a positive root $r\in P_\sigma$ by step 2.3. It contains the apex, so $B(\mu(r),\theta_k)=0$. Hence every side facet is labelled by a $\theta_j$ or a root $r>\theta_k$. The $\theta_j$ inequalities have positive sign on $K_{i_0}$ by [F3], the base apex inequality is positive on $\theta_k$ and zero on $F_0$, and each later-root inequality is nonpositive on all vertices of the prefix. The finite facet test of step 1.3 therefore gives $Z(\sigma,\theta_k)\subseteq K_{i_0}$. With the reverse inclusion from step 1.4, equality holds at $i_0$; the same facet argument records that any other listed halfspace not defining one of these facets is redundant. proof_step_texts.3.2: 3.2 The new prefix is $X(\sigma,\tau_{i+1})=X(\sigma,\tau_i)\cup(a*F)$ by [F7], so its cone is $K_{i+1}=K_i\cup V_a$ with $V_a=c[F]+\mathbb R_{\ge0}a$. Apply step 2.3 to each facet of $F$; every facet of $V_a$ is supported by $\mu(a)^\perp$ or by $\mu(r)^\perp$ for $r\in P_\sigma$. Each side facet contains $a$, so $B(\mu(r),a)=0$. If $r<a$ and $r$ is not a $\theta$-root, step 2.1 produces two vertices of $F$ on opposite sides of $\mu(r)^\perp$, contradicting support. Thus every facet label is a $\theta_j$, $a$, or a root $r>a$. Its containing halfspace is respectively $\mu(\theta_j)^+$, $\mu(a)^+$, or $\mu(r)^-$, by the sign inequalities in [F2]-[F3]. The cone $Z(\sigma,\tau_{i+1})\cap\mu(a)^+$ satisfies all these facet halfspaces; step 1.3 therefore puts it in $V_a$. Its other half $Z(\sigma,\tau_{i+1})\cap\mu(a)^-$ equals $Z(\sigma,\tau_i)=K_i$. Consequently $Z(\sigma,\tau_{i+1})\subseteq K_{i+1}$. The reverse containment follows from step 1.4, proving $K_{i+1}=Z(\sigma,\tau_{i+1})$. facts.fact_text: [F4] The inversion set is $N(w)=\{\alpha\in\Phi_+:w\alpha\in\Phi_-\}$. For a reduced expression $w=s_1\cdots s_m$, its prefix roots $s_1\cdots s_{i-1}\alpha_{s_i}$ are exactly $N(w^{-1})$, and are pairwise distinct positive roots. [[def-cg-geometric-inversion-set]] [[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (2)

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 **Inversion inside a subinterval.** If $n=1$, (1) is vacuous because $P_\sigma$ has only its single positive root. Assume $n\ge2$. Fix $u\le_Tc$, $u\ne1$, and let $\Delta_u=\{d_1,\dots,d_m\}$ be the simple system of $P_u$ given by [F3]. The item-18 factorization, in its second form with index $1$, is $u=R(d_1)\cdots R(d_m)$; it is reduced because $\ell_T(u)=m$. Apply the inversion formula [F4] to the finite Coxeter system $W_u$ with simple system $\Delta_u$. Its positive roots are exactly $P_u$, so $\{\alpha\in P_u:u^{-1}\alpha\in-P_u\}=\{\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_m\}=\{\theta_1,\dots,\theta_m\}$, where the prefix roots are $\varepsilon_j=R(d_1)\cdots R(d_{j-1})d_j$. The action of $u$ preserves $M(u)$, so a root in $M(u)$ is negative in this subsystem exactly when it is negative in the ambient positive system. Thus for $\alpha\in P_u\setminus\{\theta_1,\dots,\theta_m\}$, $u^{-1}\alpha\in P_u$. [F3, F4]
proof_step_texts.2.1: 2.1 **The opposite separator.** Set $\tau_c:=\sigma^{-1}\tau_s$. By [F1], $\tau_s\in P_\sigma$; the hypothesis excludes the inversion roots in [F3], so [F4] and step 1.1 imply $\tau_c\in P_\sigma$. Put $t:=R(\tau_s)$ and $u:=t\sigma$. Write $\sigma=tu_0$ with additive reflection lengths, so $u=u_0$ and $u_0^{-1}\sigma=u_0^{-1}tu_0$ has length $1$; hence $u\le_T\sigma$. If $c=\sigma v$ is reduced, then $tc=u_0v$ and $\ell_T(tc)=n-1=\ell_T(u_0)+\ell_T(v)$ because $t\le_T\sigma\le_Tc$, so also $u\le_Ttc$. The vector $\mu(\tau_s)$ is fixed by $tc$ by [F2], hence by $u$ using [F5]-[F6]. Let $p$ be the orthogonal projection of $\mu(\tau_s)$ onto $M(\sigma)$. Its residual lies in $F(\sigma)\subseteq F(u)$, so $p\in F(u)$ as well; projection preserves its pairing with $\tau_s\in M(\sigma)$, giving $B(p,\tau_s)=1$. Therefore $\sigma p=tp=p-2\tau_s$. Since $\sigma\tau_c=\tau_s$ and $\sigma$ is an isometry, $B(\mu(\tau_s),\tau_c)=B(p,\tau_c)=B(\sigma p,\tau_s)=B(p-2\tau_s,\tau_s)=-1$. By [F2], if $\tau_s<\tau_c$ then this pairing is nonnegative, and equality of the roots would give $1$; thus $\tau_c<\tau_s<\tau_a$. Since $s\sigma=\sigma R(\tau_c)$ and $sa\le_T\sigma$, one has $a\le_Ts\sigma=\sigma R(\tau_c)$. Write $s\sigma=az$ with $\ell_T(z)=k-2$. Then $\sigma=azR(\tau_c)$ and $(aR(\tau_c))^{-1}\sigma=R(\tau_c)zR(\tau_c)$ has length $k-2$ by conjugation invariance. The distinct reflections $a$ and $R(\tau_c)$ have product of determinant $+1$ and this product is nonidentity, so its reflection length is $2$; the length equality therefore gives $aR(\tau_c)\le_T\sigma\le_Tc$. Now [F7] gives $B(\mu(\tau_a),\tau_c)=0$. Together with step 1.2 this proves (1). [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F9]

[[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (1) [[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]] (3) [[thm-cg-root-sign-and-simple-reflection-positivity]]

proof_step_texts.1.2: 1.2 **The first separator.** Write $s=R(\tau_s)$ and $a=R(\tau_a)$. Since $B(\mu(\tau_s),\tau_a)=0$, [F2] and [F6] give $\tau_a\in M(sc)$ and hence $a\le_Tsc$. The distinct reflections $s,a$ have product determinant $+1$ and nonidentity image, whereas every reflection has determinant $-1$; hence $\ell_T(sa)=2$. Writing $sc=az$ gives $c=saz$ with $2+\ell_T(z)=\ell_T(c)$, so $sa\le_Tc$. Its moved space is contained in $M(\sigma)$ because both normals lie there, hence [F5] gives $sa\le_T\sigma$. The rank-two statement [F10] applied to $sa$ shows that $\tau_s$ and $\tau_a$ are the ordered endpoints of the simple system of $P_{sa}$. Put $\tau_b:=R(\tau_a)\tau_s=\tau_s-2B(\tau_s,\tau_a)\tau_a$. The endpoints are the least and greatest roots of $P_{sa}$, hence $\tau_s\le\tau_b\le\tau_a$; equality $\tau_b=\tau_a$ would imply $\tau_s=-\tau_a$, so $\tau_b<\tau_a$. Also $B(\mu(\tau_s),\tau_b)=B(\mu(\tau_s),\tau_s-2B(\tau_s,\tau_a)\tau_a)=1>0$. [F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, F9, F10, F15]

If $k=1$, then $P_\sigma=\{\theta_1\}$: it is the positive root set on the one-dimensional space $M(\sigma)$, and unit normalization leaves one positive root. The only eligible prefix is the singleton, $c[X(\sigma,\theta_1)]=\mathbb R_{\ge0}\theta_1=M(\sigma)\cap\mu(\theta_1)^+$, whose sole facet is the origin in $\mu(\theta_1)^\perp$; this includes the empty base $X(1)=\{\emptyset\}$ with cone $\{0\}$. Suppose henceforth $k\ge2$, and let $i_0$ be the unique index with $\tau_{i_0}=\theta_k$. [F1, F2, F3, F7, F8, F9, F12]

proof_step_texts.2.3:
2.3 **Transporting the base facets through an apex.** The following calculation applies both to the base apex $a=	heta_k$ and to an inductive apex $a=	au_{i+1}$. Let $L=M(\sigma)\cap\mu(a)^\perp=M(R(a)\sigma)$, let $F$ be the already established full-dimensional base cone in $L$, and let a facet of $F$ have support the restriction of $\mu(b)^\perp$ for some $b\in P_{R(a)\sigma}\subseteq L$. Put $E:=M(\sigma)$ and $V_a:=F+\mathbb R_{\ge0}a$. For $x\in E$, the decomposition $x=y+t a$, with $t=B(x,\mu(a))$ and $y\in L$, is unique. Thus $x\in V_a$ exactly when $t\ge0$ and $y\in F$. If a facet of $F$ is given by $\varepsilon B(y,\mu(b))\ge0$ with $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$, its transported inequality is $\varepsilon B(x,
u)\ge0$, where $
u:=\mu(b)-B(\mu(b),a)\mu(a)$; it vanishes at $a$ and agrees with $\mu(b)$ on $L$. Since $B(\mu(a),b)=0$ and $\mu+\mu^*=2I$, $B(\mu(b),a)=2B(b,a)$, so $
u=\mu igl(b-2B(b,a)a igr)=\mu(R(a)b)$. The equality of $F$ with the intersection of its active facet halfspaces therefore gives a finite halfspace presentation of $V_a$ in $E$ by $B(x,\mu(a))\ge0$ and the transported inequalities; step 1.3 identifies its nonredundant inequalities with its facets. The vector $R(a)b$ is a signed root in $M(\sigma)$, so its positive representative $r$ belongs to $P_\sigma$ by [F3]. Thus every non-base facet of $V_a$ is a root-wall facet. [F1, F3, F5, F6, F9, F14, step 1.3]
proof_step_texts.2.4: 2.4 **Inductive root-prefix step.** Suppose $i\ge i_0$ and $K_i:=c[X(\sigma,\tau_i)]=Z(\sigma,\tau_i)$. Put $a:=\tau_{i+1}$ and $\sigma':=R(a)\sigma$. Since $R(a)\le_T\sigma\le_Tc$, write $c=\sigma v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-k$ and $\sigma=R(a)\sigma'$. Then $R(a)c=\sigma'v$; also $\ell_T(R(a)c)=n-1$, since $R(a)\le_Tc$, so $\sigma'\le_T R(a)c\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(\sigma')=k-1$. The subspace $M(\sigma')$ lies in $M(\sigma)$ because $\sigma$ and $R(a)$ preserve $M(\sigma)$, and it lies in $M(R(a)c)=\mu(a)^\perp$ by absolute-order monotonicity. Both $M(\sigma')$ and $M(\sigma)\cap\mu(a)^\perp$ have dimension $k-1$: the latter is the kernel of the nonzero functional $x\mapsto B(x,\mu(a))$ on $M(\sigma)$, which is nonzero on $a\in M(\sigma)$ since $B(a,\mu(a))=1$. Hence $M(\sigma')=M(\sigma)\cap\mu(a)^\perp$ and $P_{\sigma'}=P_\sigma\cap\mu(a)^\perp$. The link base $F$ on the old vertices orthogonal to $\mu(a)$ satisfies $c[F]=K_i\cap\mu(a)^\perp$: all old vertices have nonpositive pairing with $\mu(a)$, so a nonnegative combination pairs to zero exactly when it uses only zero-pairing vertices. Thus $F=X(\sigma',\tau_i)$. Let $\epsilon'_1,\dots,\epsilon'_{k-1}$ be the prefix roots for the canonical simple system of $\sigma'$. They lie in $M(\sigma')$, so $B(\mu(a),\epsilon'_j)=0$. If $\epsilon'_j>a$, the distinct reflections $R(a)$ and $R(\epsilon'_j)$ have product length $2$ by the determinant argument in [F9]. Since $R(\epsilon'_j)\le_TR(a)c$, write $R(a)c=R(\epsilon'_j)v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-2$; then $c=R(a)R(\epsilon'_j)v$ is reduced, so $R(a)R(\epsilon'_j)\le_Tc$. The root $d:=R(a)\epsilon'_j=\epsilon'_j-2B(\epsilon'_j,a)a$ is a nonzero nonnegative combination of the endpoints; hence has nonnegative simple-root coordinates and is positive by [F15]. Since it lies in $M(w)$, [F3] puts it in $P_w$; it cannot equal $a$, since that would imply $\epsilon'_j=R(a)a=-a$. Thus $a<d$ in the global order. Since $a,\epsilon'_j\in M(\sigma)$ and $R(a)$ preserves $M(\sigma)$, this positive root lies in $P_\sigma=\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$. Now $\sigma'^{-1}\epsilon'_j=\sigma^{-1}d$ is negative by step 1.1 applied to $\sigma'$, so step 1.1 applied to $\sigma$ gives $d\in\{\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k\}$, contradicting $d>a\ge\theta_k$. Hence every $\epsilon'_j<a$, and therefore $\theta'_{k-1}\le\tau_i$. Let $b$ be the last root of $P_{\sigma'}$ at or below $\tau_i$; it exists since $\theta'_{k-1}$ is such a root, and $b\ge\theta'_{k-1}$. Put $E:=M(\sigma)$ and $V_a:=F+\mathbb R_{\ge0}a$. For $x\in E$, the decomposition $x=y+t a$, with $t=B(x,\mu(a))$ and $y\in L$, is unique. Thus $x\in V_a$ exactly when $t\ge0$ and $y\in F$. If a facet of $F$ is given by $\varepsilon B(y,\mu(b))\ge0$ with $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$, its transported inequality is $\varepsilon B(x,
u)\ge0$, where $
u:=\mu(b)-B(\mu(b),a)\mu(a)$; it vanishes at $a$ and agrees with $\mu(b)$ on $L$. Since $B(\mu(a),b)=0$ and $\mu+\mu^*=2I$, $B(\mu(b),a)=2B(b,a)$, so $
u=\mu igl(b-2B(b,a)a igr)=\mu(R(a)b)$. The equality of $F$ with the intersection of its active facet halfspaces therefore gives a finite halfspace presentation of $V_a$ in $E$ by $B(x,\mu(a))\ge0$ and the transported inequalities; step 1.3 identifies its nonredundant inequalities with its facets. The vector $R(a)b$ is a signed root in $M(\sigma)$, so its positive representative $r$ belongs to $P_\sigma$ by [F3]. Thus every non-base facet of $V_a$ is a root-wall facet. proof_step_texts.2.4: 2.4 **Inductive root-prefix step.** Suppose $i\ge i_0$ and $K_i:=c[X(\sigma,\tau_i)]=Z(\sigma,\tau_i)$. Put $a:=\tau_{i+1}$ and $\sigma':=R(a)\sigma$. Since $R(a)\le_T\sigma\le_Tc$, write $c=\sigma v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-k$ and $\sigma=R(a)\sigma'$. Then $R(a)c=\sigma'v$; also $\ell_T(R(a)c)=n-1$, since $R(a)\le_Tc$, so $\sigma'\le_T R(a)c\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(\sigma')=k-1$. The subspace $M(\sigma')$ lies in $M(\sigma)$ because $\sigma$ and $R(a)$ preserve $M(\sigma)$, and it lies in $M(R(a)c)=\mu(a)^\perp$ by absolute-order monotonicity. Both $M(\sigma')$ and $M(\sigma)\cap\mu(a)^\perp$ have dimension $k-1$: the latter is the kernel of the nonzero functional $x\mapsto B(x,\mu(a))$ on $M(\sigma)$, which is nonzero on $a\in M(\sigma)$ since $B(a,\mu(a))=1$. Hence $M(\sigma')=M(\sigma)\cap\mu(a)^\perp$ and $P_{\sigma'}=P_\sigma\cap\mu(a)^\perp$. The link base $F$ on the old vertices orthogonal to $\mu(a)$ satisfies $c[F]=K_i\cap\mu(a)^\perp$: all old vertices have nonpositive pairing with $\mu(a)$, so a nonnegative combination pairs to zero exactly when it uses only zero-pairing vertices. Thus $F=X(\sigma',\tau_i)$. Let $\epsilon'_1,\dots,\epsilon'_{k-1}$ be the prefix roots for the canonical simple system of $\sigma'$. They lie in $M(\sigma')$, so $B(\mu(a),\epsilon'_j)=0$. If $\epsilon'_j>a$, the distinct reflections $R(a)$ and $R(\epsilon'_j)$ have product length $2$ by the determinant argument in [F9]. Since $R(\epsilon'_j)\le_TR(a)c$, write $R(a)c=R(\epsilon'_j)v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-2$; then $c=R(a)R(\epsilon'_j)v$ is reduced, so $R(a)R(\epsilon'_j)\le_Tc$. By [F10] and the increasing order $a<\epsilon'_j$, this is the endpoint factorization of the rank-two element $w:=R(a)R(\epsilon'_j)$, so $B(a,\epsilon'_j)\le0$. The root $d:=R(a)\epsilon'_j=\epsilon'_j-2B(\epsilon'_j,a)a$ is a nonzero nonnegative combination of the endpoints; hence has nonnegative simple-root coordinates and is positive by [F15]. Since it lies in $M(w)$, [F3] puts it in $P_w$; it cannot equal $a$, since that would imply $\epsilon'_j=R(a)a=-a$. Thus $a<d$ in the global order. Since $a,\epsilon'_j\in M(\sigma)$ and $R(a)$ preserves $M(\sigma)$, this positive root lies in $P_\sigma=\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$. Now $\sigma'^{-1}\epsilon'_j=\sigma^{-1}d$ is negative by step 1.1 applied to $\sigma'$, so step 1.1 applied to $\sigma$ gives $d\in\{\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k\}$, contradicting $d>a\ge\theta_k$. Hence every $\epsilon'_j<a$, and therefore $\theta'_{k-1}\le\tau_i$. Let $b$ be the last root of $P_{\sigma'}$ at or below $\tau_i$; it exists since $\theta'_{k-1}$ is such a root, and $b\ge\theta'_{k-1}$. Then $F=X(\sigma',\tau_i)=X(\sigma',b)$, so lower-rank induction gives $c[F]=Z(\sigma',b)$, full-dimensional and convex in $L=M(\sigma')$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, F9, F10, F13, F15, step 1.1]

**(2) Inversion formula.** For every $w\in W$ one has $|N(w)|=\ell(w)$ (with $N$ as in [[def-cg-geometric-inversion-set]]); and for every reduced expression $w=s_1\cdots s_n$,
$$N(w)=\bigl\{\rho(s_{i+1}\cdots s_n)^{-1}e_{s_i}:1\le i\le n\bigr\},\qquad N(w^{-1})=\bigl\{\rho(s_1\cdots s_{i-1})e_{s_i}:1\le i\le n\bigr\},$$

[F5] The inversion set is $N(w)=\{\alpha\in\Phi_+:\rho(w)\alpha\in\Phi_-\}$; it satisfies $N(1)=\emptyset$, $N(w^{-1})=-\rho(w)N(w)$, and the step recursion: for $u\in W$, $s\in S$ with $\ell(us)>\ell(u)$ one has $N(us)=\{e_s\}\sqcup sN(u)$ with $sN(u)\subseteq\Phi_+\setminus\{e_s\}$ and $e_s\notin N(u)$, while for $\ell(us)<\ell(u)$ one has $N(us)=s(N(u)\setminus\{e_s\})$ ([[def-cg-geometric-inversion-set]]).

proof_uses.text: 1.2 **The inversion formula (2).** We prove by induction on $m$ the assertion: for every $x$ with $\ell(x)=m$ and every reduced expression $x=s_1\cdots s_m$ one has $N(x)=\{\rho(s_{i+1}\cdots s_m)^{-1}e_{s_i}:1\le i\le m\}$ with pairwise distinct elements, and $|N(x)|=m$. For $m=0$ this is $N(1)=\emptyset$ by [F5]. For the step let $x=us_m$ with $u:=s_1\cdots s_{m-1}$, so $\ell(u)=m-1$ and $\ell(us_m)=m>\ell(u)$; the first case of the step recursion of [F5] gives $N(x)=\{e_{s_m}\}\sqcup s_mN(u)$, the union being disjoint with $s_mN(u)\subseteq\Phi_+\setminus\{e_{s_m}\}$. By induction $N(u)=\{\rho(s_{i+1}\cdots s_{m-1})^{-1}e_{s_i}:1\le i\le m-1\}$ with pairwise distinct elements; since $\rho(s_m)\rho(s_{i+1}\cdots s_{m-1})^{-1}=\rho(s_ms_{m-1}\cdots s_{i+1})=\rho(s_{i+1}\cdots s_m)^{-1}$ for $i\le m-1$ by [F6], one has $s_mN(u)=\{\rho(s_{i+1}\cdots s_m)^{-1}e_{s_i}:1\le i\le m-1\}$, and the term $i=m$ with the empty product contributes $e_{s_m}$. Hence $N(x)=\{\rho(s_{i+1}\cdots s_m)^{-1}e_{s_i}:1\le i\le m\}$ with pairwise distinct elements, and $|N(x)|=1+|N(u)|=m$. Applying the same formula to the reversed reduced expression $x^{-1}=s_m\cdots s_1$ and using $\rho(s_{i-1}\cdots s_1)^{-1}=\rho(s_1\cdots s_{i-1})$ gives $N(x^{-1})=\{\rho(s_1\cdots s_{i-1})e_{s_i}:1\le i\le m\}$, again with pairwise distinct elements. The induction principle [F8] gives (2) for every element. [F5, F6, F8, given]

proof_uses.text: 2.1 **The dictionary (iii) and (iv).** Let $\alpha,\beta\in\Phi$. Since $\rho(s)e_s=-e_s$ by [F6], the root $-\alpha$ has the representation $-\alpha=-\rho(w)e_s=\rho(ws)e_s$, so $t_{-\alpha}=(ws)s(ws)^{-1}=wsw^{-1}=t_\alpha$. If $t_\alpha=t_\beta$, then $r_\alpha=\rho(t_\alpha)=\rho(t_\beta)=r_\beta$ by 1.3 (ii); by [F3] and $B(\alpha,\alpha)=1$ of [F1] the $(-1)$-eigenspace of $r_\alpha$ is $\mathbb R\alpha$, and that of $r_\beta$ is $\mathbb R\beta$, so $\mathbb R\alpha=\mathbb R\beta$ and $\beta=\lambda\alpha$ with $\lambda\ne0$; then $1=B(\beta,\beta)=\lambda^2B(\alpha,\alpha)=\lambda^2$, so $\lambda=\pm1$. Conversely $t_\alpha=t_{\pm\alpha}$ by the first part. Hence $t_\alpha=t_\beta$ if and only if $\beta=\pm\alpha$, which is (iii). For (iv), the map $[\alpha]\mapsto t_\alpha$ on classes $\{\pm\alpha\}$ is well defined by (i) and (iii) and injective by (iii); it is surjective because every element of $T$ is of the form $wsw^{-1}=t_{\rho(w)e_s}$ by 1.1. Hence it is a bijection. Since $\Phi=\Phi_+\sqcup\Phi_-$ with $\Phi_-=-\Phi_+$ by [F6], every class $\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$ contains exactly one positive root; composing $\alpha\mapsto[\alpha]$ with the class bijection $[\alpha]\mapsto t_\alpha$ gives a bijection $\Phi_+\to T$, $\alpha\mapsto t_\alpha$. [F1, F3, F6, step 1.1, step 1.3, algebra]

proof_uses.text: 1.1 **Set-up.** Fix a reduced expression $w=s_1\cdots s_n$ of an element $w\in W$, write $w_j:=s_1\cdots s_j$ and $r_i:=w_{i-1}s_iw_{i-1}^{-1}\in T$ for the prefix reflections, and note $\rho(w_j)=\rho(s_1)\cdots\rho(s_j)$ by [F6] and $\rho(r_i)=\rho(w_{i-1}s_iw_{i-1}^{-1})=r_{\rho(w_{i-1})e_{s_i}}$. [F1, F4, F6, given]

1.4 **The shorteners are exactly the prefix reflections.** Keep the reduced expression of 1.1 and let $r\in T$. If $r=r_i$ is a prefix reflection of the word, then $r_iw=w_{i-1}s_iw_{i-1}^{-1}w_{i-1}s_is_{i+1}\cdots s_n=w_{i-1}s_{i+1}\cdots s_n=s_1\cdots\widehat{s_i}\cdots s_n$, so $\ell(r_iw)<n=\ell(w)$; and by [F4] the set $\{r_1,\dots,r_n\}$ equals $\Phi(w)=\{r:\eta(r,w)=-1\}$ and its members are pairwise distinct. Conversely let $r\in T$ with $\ell(rw)<\ell(w)$ and suppose $\eta(r,w)=+1$. The formula of [F4] implies the cocycle identity $\eta(x,uv)=\eta(x,u)\eta(u^{-1}xu,v)$ for all $x\in T$, $u,v\in W$: indeed $(\varepsilon,x)\cdot(uv)=((\varepsilon,x)\cdot u)\cdot v$, and comparing first coordinates of the displayed formula gives the identity. With $x=r$, $u=r$, $v=w$ this gives $\eta(r,rw)=\eta(r,r)\eta(r,w)=\eta(r,r)$; also $\eta(r,1)=1$, since the action of $1$ is the identity. We claim $\eta(r,r)=-1$. Write $r=usu^{-1}$ with $s\in S$, $u\in W$, so that $u^{-1}ru=s$; applying the action formula of [F4] successively along the word $usu^{-1}$ to $(\varepsilon,r)$ gives $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot u=(\varepsilon\eta(r,u),u^{-1}ru)=(\varepsilon\eta(r,u),s)$, then $U_s(\varepsilon\eta(r,u),s)=(-\varepsilon\eta(r,u),s)$ by the definition of $U_s$ in [F4], and then $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot(usu^{-1})=(-\varepsilon\eta(r,u)\eta(s,u^{-1}),r)$. Comparing with $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot r=(\varepsilon\eta(r,r),r)$ from [F4] yields $\eta(r,r)=-\eta(r,u)\eta(s,u^{-1})$. facts.actual_text: [F12] [[lem-cg-sortable-skips-basis-and-cover-decomposition]] (5)(ii): if $s$ is final in $c$ and $v$ is $c$-sortable with $v\ge_Rs$, then $v=s\vee v_J$.

facts.label: F10
facts.actual_text: [F10] [[lem-cg-uniform-omega-positive-and-aligned-sortability]] (3): if $v$ is $c$-sortable, its $W_J$-prefix is sortable for the restricted Coxeter element on $W_J$; conversely a sortable element of $W_J$ is $c$-sortable in $W$.

facts.label: F6
facts.actual_text: [F6] [[def-cg-left-right-weak-order-and-descents]] (1),(3) and [[lem-cg-weak-order-is-a-graded-partial-order]] (2),(4)-(5): $x\le_Ry$ means $y=xv$ with additive length; a simple left multiplication changes length by $1$ or $-1$; $s\le_Rw$ iff $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$; and $x\le_Ry$ iff $N(x^{-1})\subseteq N(y^{-1})$.

facts.label: F4
facts.actual_text: [F4] [[lem-cg-weak-parabolic-projection-and-cover-joins]] (1)-(3): $N(w_J^{-1})=N(w^{-1})\cap\Phi_{J,+}$; $w_J$ is the greatest $W_J$-element below $w$ and prefix projection is order-preserving; the prefix projection preserves joins; and its largest lift is $z w_0(J)w_0$.

facts.label: F16
facts.actual_text: [F16] [[thm-cg-finite-lattice-interval-congruence-criterion]] (i)-(ii): for an equivalence relation on a finite lattice whose classes are intervals, the relation is a congruence if and only if its lower and upper endpoint maps are order-preserving.

facts.label: F5
facts.actual_text: [F5] [[thm-cg-finite-parabolic-longest-element-and-opposition]] (1)(i)-(v): $w_0^2=1$, $\rho(w_0)\Phi_+=\Phi_-$, $N(w_0v)=\Phi_+\setminus N(v)$, $\ell(w_0w)=\ell(ww_0)=\ell(w_0)-\ell(w)$, and conjugation by $w_0$ permutes $S$.

facts.label: F17
facts.actual_text: [F17] [[thm-cg-finite-parabolic-longest-element-and-opposition]] (2), applied to $W_J$: $w_0(J)$ is the longest element of the finite parabolic $W_J$ and is an involution; applying the opposition assertion of [F5] within $W_J$ gives $N(w_0(J)v)=\Phi_{J,+}\setminus N(v)$ for $v\in W_J$.

facts.label: F14
facts.actual_text: [F14] [[thm-cg-sortable-meet-join-closure-and-cambrian-quotient]] (2): $c$-sortable elements are closed under nonempty joins, and their joins are $c$-sortable.

facts.label: F18
facts.actual_text: [F18] [[thm-cg-sortable-meet-join-closure-and-cambrian-quotient]] (4): the kernel relation $\sim_c$ is a lattice congruence with the quotient operations and quotient map already defined in [[def-cg-recursive-sortable-projection-and-cambrian-congruence]].

facts.label: F11
facts.actual_text: [F11] [[thm-cg-sortable-skip-basis-cover-roots-and-chamber-unions]] (1): $\pi_c(w)$ is the unique greatest $c$-sortable element below $w$.

facts.label: F8
facts.actual_text: [F8] [[thm-cg-weak-order-meet-semilattice-and-finite-lattice]] (2): $W$ is finite and its right weak order is a lattice.

dispositions.notes: Finite-type recursion, full cone criterion and skip basis assemble exactly their proved clauses. Negative roots correspond to explicitly typed cover reflections. The reverse chamber-union inclusion uses a single generic interior witness and least-integer approximants avoiding finitely many hyperplanes; closed chambers handle boundary points and rank-zero case. Group fibers index geometric chambers and are never asserted to be subsets of V themselves. facts.label: F5
facts.actual_text: [F5] [[def-cg-sortable-element-skip-roots-and-cone]] (3),(4): $\mathrm{Cone}_c(v)=\{x:B(x,C^r_c(v))\ge0\text{ for every }r\in S\}$ is the intersection of the halfspaces with normals the skip roots.

facts.label: F2
facts.actual_text: [F2] [[lem-cg-sortable-cone-criterion-and-projection-monotonicity]] (1),(2),(3),(4): for comparable pairs $\pi_c(w)=v\iff wC\subseteq\mathrm{Cone}_c(v)$; $\pi_c$ is order preserving for $\le_R$; $\pi_c(w)$ is the unique greatest $c$-sortable element below $w$ and $\pi_c(w)=v\iff wC\subseteq\mathrm{Cone}_c(v)$ for every $c$-sortable $v$ and every $w$; and $\pi_{c'}(w_J)=\pi_c(w)_J$.

facts.label: F1
facts.actual_text: [F1] [[lem-cg-sortable-recursion-output-and-initial-choice-independence]] (1),(2),(3),(4),(5): $\pi_c$ is well defined and independent of the initial-letter choices, $\pi_c(w)$ is $c$-sortable, $\pi_c(w)\le_Rw$ with equality if and only if $w$ is $c$-sortable, $\pi_c$ is idempotent, $w\ge_Rs$ if and only if $\pi_c(w)\ge_Rs$ for initial $s$, and $\pi_c$ restricts to $\pi_{c|_J}$ on $W_J$.

facts.label: F3
facts.actual_text: [F3] [[lem-cg-sortable-skips-basis-and-cover-decomposition]] (1),(2),(3): $C^r_c(v)=\pm\beta_t$, the set $C_c(v)=\{C^r_c(v):r\in S\}$ is a basis of $V$ independent of all choices, and $\mathcal A_c(v)=\{-\beta_t:t\in\mathrm{Cov}(v)\}$, $\mathcal B_c(v)=\{\beta_t:t\in ufs_c(v)\}$ with $fsc(v)=\mathrm{Cov}(v)$.

facts.label: F6
facts.actual_text: [F6] [[lem-cg-weak-parabolic-projection-and-cover-joins]] (4): the positive-root set $\operatorname{cov}(w)$ consists of roots $\alpha\in N(w^{-1})$ with $t_\alpha w=ws$ and $\ell(ws)=\ell(w)-1$ for some $s\in S$, together with the cover-join formulas (i) and (ii).

facts.label: F4
facts.actual_text: [F4] [[thm-cg-finite-chamber-tiling-and-coset-face-identification]] (1),(2): the closed chambers $wC$ tile $V$ and are the closures of the connected components of the complement of the root hyperplanes; there are only finitely many of them in finite type; and the walls of $wC$ are the hyperplanes $H_{\rho(w)e_s}$.
